metadata.title: Whistleblower 101: Navigating the False Claims Act | Justia Webinars
metadata.author: Justia
metadata.shortDescription:
Many attorneys are unaware of the high-stakes, high-impact world of qui tam litigation — a practice area where legal advocacy meets public accountability. In this dynamic one-hour CLE, you'll gain a practical introduction to whistleblower representation under the False Claims Act (FCA), including how relators initiate claims, the government’s role in intervention, and the ethical and strategic considerations that arise throughout the process.

Whether you’re a litigator, employment lawyer, or corporate counsel, this session will equip you with insights that could surface in your own practice — from healthcare fraud and defense contracting to financial market misconduct.

The faculty are all members of The Anti-Fraud Coalition (TAF Coalition), a public interest, non-profit organization dedicated to defending and empowering whistleblowers who expose fraud on the government and the financial markets.

Lawyers: Want CLE credit for watching this video?
Join Justia Connect Pro and watch it on Justia Learning - details at https://j.st/5cM4

03:30 Understanding the False Claims Act
09:40 Elements and Procedures of FCA Cases
29:33 Whistleblower Roles and Challenges
41:50 The Litigation Process
52:41 State False Claims Act

----------------------

Introduction to the False Claims Act
Purpose
Brief History
Types of Cases

Claim

Damages

First to file and public disclosure considerations

Other Kinds of False Claims Act Violations
Reverse FCA
Anti-Kickback Statute
Stark Law

Whistleblowers
Who can be a whistleblower
How FCA whistleblowing works
FCA retaliation provisions

State False Claims Acts
Variations among states
Medicaid only False Claims Acts

Conclusion
When to consult an FCA attorney
Other whistleblower programs

Q&A (as time permits)

----------------------


Speakers

MaryAnne Hamilton
Attorney
Miller Law Group, PLLC
https://connect.justia.com/webinars/speakers/maryanne-hamilton

MaryAnne Hamilton is an attorney at Miller Law Group, PLLC, in Raleigh, North Carolina. She represents clients in whistleblower and retaliation, products liability/toxic tort, medical negligence, and civil rights cases. In her practice, MaryAnne combines an intense focus on the needs of her clients with an ability to distill complex issues in a way that both makes them understandable and highlights the key issues.


Darth M. Newman
Founding Attorney
Law Offices of Darth M. Newman
https://connect.justia.com/webinars/speakers/darth-m-newman

Darth M. Newman is a skilled trial attorney and a certified mediator with more than a decade of litigation experience in complex commercial and plaintiff’s side whistleblower cases. He has tried shareholder disputes, fraud, insider dealing, and fiduciary duty matters worth millions of dollars. He has also represented whistleblowers from across the country helping to shed light on all manner of fraud against the government from dangerous healthcare systems, devices, and doctors to government contracting and loan fraud.

metadata.title: A Guide to the False Claims Act for Whistleblowers | Brown, LLC
metadata.author: Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
This comprehensive guide for whistleblowers explains the power of the False Claims Act. Unmask the truth behind fraudulent schemes and learn how to navigate the legal landscape to protect justice and expose wrongdoing. Gain insights, strategies, and essential knowledge to champion integrity and fight against false claims. 

00:01 What Is the False Claims Act?
00:37 What Actions Are Considered Violations Under the False Claims Act?
01:29 Who Can File a Qui Tam Action?
03:42 Can I Work With My Colleagues to Bring a Qui Tam Action, or Do I Have to Do It Alone?
05:49 What Happens After the Case Is Filed?
08:34 I Went Along With the Fraud for a While - Does That Mean I Can’t Bring a Qui Tam Now?
10:13 What if It Turns Out We’re Not the First to File?
12:19 Can I Use Information I Get From the Newspaper, Other Cases, or Other Public Sources?

Visit out website https://IFightForYourRights.com to learn more or call (877) 561-0000 to schedule a free confidential consultation.

metadata.title: Recurring Issues in False Claims Act Litigation
metadata.author: Phillips & Cohen LLP
metadata.shortDescription: Whistleblower attorney Colette Matzzie of Phillips & Cohen LLP moderated a webinar on the False Claims Act and qui tam cases for the Federal Judiciary Center in December of 2013. The webinar was aimed at attorneys and judges who handle FCA and qui tam cases. Participants included a federal judge, a Department of Justice official, whistleblower lawyers, and an attorney who represents companies accused of wrongdoing in qui tam lawsuits. Please note that the webinar was previously recorded, so do not email questions to the on-screen address. If you have any questions, please contact us www.phillipsandcohen.com

metadata.title: Qui Tam 101: False Claims Act, Whistleblowers, Corporate Fraud and Employer Misconduct
metadata.author: Beverly Hills Bar Association
metadata.shortDescription:
This program will cover basic whistleblower concepts, with particular emphasis on qui tam actions, which are civil suits brought by whistleblowers with evidence of fraud in federal, state, or local government programs or contracts, who sue the wrongdoer on behalf of the government under the federal or state False Claims Act.

"Speaking truth to power" has an honorable, if often tragic lineage. A leading civil rights organizer of the mid-century quoted the Prophet Muhammad as saying "the most excellent jihad is when one speaks a true word in the presence of a tyrannical ruler." Nowhere is this more evident than the workplace.

The program will be presented by Mark Kleiman, Esq., an attorney who has long advocated for whistleblowers, with particular emphasis on qui tam actions. False Claims Act cases filed by Mr. Kleiman have recovered over seven hundred million dollars, with particular emphasis on healthcare, in cases involving matters such as pharmaceutical fraud, hospitals giving kickbacks to doctors or submitting false bills and unacceptable patient care amounting to Medicare fraud. Mr. Kleiman has served as a Special Master during investigations of fraudulent medical-legal activities in cooperation with the California Department of Insurance and the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office.

Qui Tam 101: A Field Guide to False Claims Act and Other Whistleblower Actions That Address Corporate Fraud and Employer Misconduct.

metadata.title: Medicare and Medicaid Fraud: When Does Improper Billing Violate the False Claims Act?
metadata.author: Stephen Teller - Teller Law
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode Summary:
In this episode of False Claims, Real Consequences, host Leann Lyon is joined by Stephen Teller, a seasoned employment and whistleblower attorney with over 25 years of experience. The discussion centers on fraud involving Medicare and Medicaid, highlighting how billing mistakes can escalate into potential fraud under the False Claims Act. Stephen explains the nuances of healthcare fraud, including upcoding, unbundling, and the implications of billing for services not medically necessary. He also delves into the complexities of healthcare kickbacks and self-referrals, providing real-world examples of how these practices can lead to significant legal consequences. The episode offers valuable insights for healthcare employees, particularly billing staff and coders, who are often the first to notice fraudulent activities. Listeners will gain a deeper understanding of the legal landscape surrounding healthcare fraud and the importance of vigilance in billing practices. 

Key Timestamps:
00:01 – Introduction
0:33 – Focus on Medicare and Medicaid Fraud
1:32 – Billing Mistakes vs. Fraud
2:24 – Types of Healthcare Fraud
3:35 – Unbundling Charges Explained
4:38 – Incident-to Billing and Supervision
5:28 – Medical Necessity and False Claims
6:15 – Healthcare Kickbacks and Self-Referrals
7:17 – False Information About Provider Qualifications
8:40 – Role of Billing Staff in Detecting Fraud
10:19 – Common Healthcare Billing Practices Leading to Fraud
11:21 – Falsifying Patient Qualifications
11:45 – False Claims Act and Private Insurers

About the Show:
False Claims, Real Consequences is a podcast dedicated to exploring the intricacies of whistleblower law and the False Claims Act. Hosted by experienced legal professionals, the show provides listeners with in-depth discussions on topics such as healthcare fraud, employment law, and government compliance. Aimed at individuals interested in understanding the legal ramifications of fraud and misconduct, the podcast offers expert insights and practical advice. Whether you're a legal practitioner, a healthcare professional, or someone interested in whistleblower cases, False Claims, Real Consequences delivers valuable content with clarity and precision.

For more information, visit our website:
www.stellerlaw.com

metadata.title: Protections for SEC Whistleblowers
metadata.author: Zuckerman Whistleblower Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
The SEC whistleblower program has been effective in combatting fraud and protecting investors.  Whistleblower tips have enabled the SEC to recover more than $3 billion and as a result, the SEC has paid whistleblowers more than $500 million in awards.
Understandably, whistleblowers are reluctant to come forward because they fear retaliation.  Fortunately, the SEC whistleblower program permits a whistleblower to disclose fraud anonymously by retaining an attorney to represent them at the Commission.
And federal whistleblower laws protect SEC whistleblowers against retaliation.  In particular, the whistleblower protection provisions of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and Dodd-Frank Act protect employees disclosing potential violations of federal securities law.
The whistleblower protection provision of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act prohibits employers from retaliating against whistleblowers for reporting to a supervisor, law enforcement, regulatory authorities or Congress,  mail fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, securities fraud, a violation of any rule or regulation of the SEC, or any provision of federal law relating to fraud against shareholders.
These whistleblower retaliation laws authorize a variety of remedies for retaliation, including lost pay and benefits and reinstatement or front pay.  And SOX authorizes the recovery of uncapped damages for emotional distress and reputational harm.
There are, however, critical differences between these two whistleblower protection laws, including the scope of protected whistleblowing, the statute of limitations, and the requirement to exhaust administrative remedies.  State laws can provide additional protection and potentially enable the whistleblower to recover additional damages.
It is critical to retain a firm with substantial experience representing whistleblowers and a thorough understanding of whistleblower protection laws.
If you have suffered retaliation for reporting potential violations of federal securities laws to your employer or to the SEC, call us today for a case evaluation.

metadata.title: Strengthening the SEC Whistleblower Program
metadata.author: Whistleblower Network News
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of the Whistleblower of the Week podcast, host Jane Turner speaks with whistleblower attorney and former SEC official Andrew Feller.

Feller is currently Senior Special Counsel at the leading whistleblower firm Kohn, Kohn & Colapinto, where as co-Chair of the firm’s Securities and Commodities Whistleblower Group, he represents whistleblowers who seek to report fraud and other legal violations to financial regulators including the SEC, CFTC, DOJ, IRS, and FinCEN. Prior to joining Kohn, Kohn & Colapinto, Feller investigated and litigated securities fraud matters as Senior Counsel in the SEC’s Division of Enforcement.

Turner and Feller discuss his career and why he decided to represent whistleblowers. Drawing on Feller’s firsthand experience as both an attorney for SEC whistleblowers and an SEC official, they discuss the successes and importance of the SEC Whistleblower Program and the key role whistleblowers play in fighting fraud.

Feller explains why the bipartisan SEC Whistleblower Reform Act of 2025 is a critical bill which would strengthen the SEC Whistleblower Program. The National Whistleblower Center is calling for the passage of the SEC Whistleblower Reform Act and has created an Action Alert allowing individuals to write to members of Congress calling for the bill’s passage.

Visit www.whistleblowersblog.org for more information.

metadata.title: False Claims Act Enforcement in 2026
metadata.author: Foley & Lardner LLP
metadata.shortDescription: The DOJ and relators’ bar continues to aggressively deploy the False Claims Act across a variety of subject areas, including health care, cybersecurity, and customs. Drawing on the DOJ’s latest enforcement data and 2025 recoveries, this program will highlight key FCA trends, practical lessons learned, and what organizations should expect and prepare for in 2026.

Allied Stone was importing quartz surface products from China. Quartz was among uh the the goods that were uh subject to anti-du- anti-dumping countervailing duty tariffs. Um but they misclassified these as marble or crystallized glass. A relator filed suit way back in 2021. So again, took 4 years to resolve this. And uh the relator there will receive $2.1 million out of the 12.4. So, it really shows the power of the financial incentives in key key tam cases. So, this slide has the same sort of uh key areas that I called out earlier that are high-risk areas. And it's it's how you as a company want to be thinking about your importing and whether you have I'm going to do a very self-interested shout-out to Foley's uh trade practice. We um have some uh true subject matter experts in this area. Foley has a whole part of its uh website that has a lot of excellent resources and goods that you can do that proactive work to consider how to do, for example, an assessment of your customs work and to try to get ahead of uh ahead. This is an area in particular where self-reporting to customs uh can often lead to much better results than if you were uh subject to a False Claims Act enforcement. Uh with that, I will turn it back over to our colleagues. >> Thanks, Matt. Um next up is False Claims Act in the use of the False Claims Act in anti-discrimination cases. Um Recent remarks by DOJ leadership have outlined how DOJ is sort of frameworking DEI and other employment discrimination uh theories. The first quote is, "DOJ is not investigating companies for having a DEI program. Companies can discriminate with or without DEI programs and can operate DEI programs without violating the law." And their framework is also that no one should be advantaged or disadvantaged in this country based on their immutable characteristics. Um So I So I want to say, with the way DOJ is framing this, calling it DEI enforcement is really a misnomer. It's It's about anti-discrimination enforcement and using the False Claims Act like as a vehicle for that. Per DOJ comments, this is from Brenna Jenny again, the Deputy Assistant Attorney General. She said DOJ is currently the busiest in this space with corporate government contractors and claims of race and sex discrimination. She also indicated that they have the most whistleblower suits filed following under those two umbrellas. She said the two main categories these fall under are preferential hiring, promotion, or compensation decisions based on immutable characteristics like race or sex, as well as the selection of candidates for special programs such as internships or trainings that that discriminate on the basis of race or sex in terms of who can participate in those programs. She also gave examples that could draw DOJ attention in this space. I want to be clear again, we're defense lawyers here and just because something draws DOJ's attention or just because DOJ thinks that they have a theory here, does not mean that they have a viable theory here. But I thought it was important to amplify DAG Jenny's comments just so folks know like what DOJ is looking at in terms of their enforcement interests here. So some of the things that she listed in recent remarks are um measuring leader performance by progress towards DEI goals and particularly companies that are tying promotion or compensation decisions to progress towards those goals. Next is encouraging employees to develop DEI goals as their personal employment goals and then evaluating or compensating those employees on meeting those goals. She added tra She added an interest in tra in companies that are tracking diversity goals in a manner that expresses preference for people of a particular race or sex. Here she gave an interesting example, which is tracking mechanisms that show certain races in in in green, which she thinks suggests that there's a preference expressed for those people and that is something that uh draws her enforcement interest. Um she acknowledged that some some federal contractors are required to do some tracking here, right? And so something that that they're also looking for is whether it's actually addressing underutilization or other requirements um pursuant grants versus just tracking for different purpose. Um and I think in general there is a tension between um some language of grants and some requirements on companies and what um what in for what how the enforcement landscape has been shifting here and I think that creates opportunity for for discussion with DOJ um to the extent that they see something as um discrimination when it's really something that is required by grant terms for instance. Um other examples she gave lowering standards to obtain an interview or to obtain a promotion um for individuals with certain immutable characteristics like based on race or sex. Um and also companies that track promotion alongside participation in special programs such as if you have this program that's only available to a particular race for instance and then you're tracking um the success of that program in terms of promotions or something like that. That will draw her enforcement interest. Something that struck me during her remarks and her remarks were focused in the DEI space, but something that struck me is this can be applicable to traditional race-based discrimination cases as well, right? So, if you are a company and you're facing a claim that someone of, you know, whether it's a minority race, a member of a minority race, or majority race, if you're facing a discrimination claim, it can now be amplified into the False Claims Act space if there's a certification that was a whistleblower or DOJ thinks was breached or was made falsely. Um so, I think while the headlines have been DEI here, this is also, I think, just a headline in in risks in general in employment law in the employment law space um that that folks should be aware of um generally. Um in terms of the False Claims Act elements for uh for the False Claims Act lawyers on the phone um on the line, um she said materiality, the element of materiality, of course, has to be the false certification actually mattered to the government um when paying out the funds. And so, one could argue, is this employment action really material to the government's decision to pay for these goods? She would argue, and DOJ would argue, yes, cuz federal contracting is also about choosing a partner. In terms of damages, she expressed her view that DOJ could go after the full value of a government contract, or they could go after just the costs uh that they see uh the of the allegedly unlawful program that were passed along to the government, or some hybrid approach, just really depending on facts and circumstances. Um so, that to me was super interesting um in terms of how they're looking at damages models. Um multiplier, like any other FCA case, they're looking at the same types of cooperation and remediation factors. Um and she expressed that penalties here are important um in her view, including for deterrence. So, even if the damages number is relatively small, you're still looking at that per um per False Claims Act penalty. Um these cases are active, they're under seal, they're under investigation, they are not very public, but they are definitely out there, so we wanted folks to be aware um that they are going on. >> I uh I was just going to say hand it off to to Matt Krieger to to walk us through the constitutionality of the qui tam provisions uh something that he knows uh quite a bit about uh thanks to his recent work in that space. >> All right, thanks, Joe. Um so something to uh very much watch in 2026 is whether the qui tam provisions uh continue to exist in a way. Uh there are significant questions about the constitutionality of them that are being litigated right now. So to put context on this, uh we've been talking in a various contexts today about the qui tam provisions and what what those mean, what those are is that private individuals can file suit in the name of the United States and then uh even continue to litigate on behalf of the United States uh if for example, the government declines the suit, it may allow the relator to keep going, or even if the government does join the suit, the relator still gets to participate as a party. And this makes the False Claims Act of particularly unique and peculiar uh because relators do not have their own personal injury, which is usually required under Article 3 in order to be litigating. Instead, um the Supreme Court has on the standing question said that relators have an assignment of the government's injury and therefore are able to be suing for for government. That may address the Article 3 question for standing, uh but there are live questions about whether this uh framework is constitutional under Article 2. Article 2 is the executive branch uh article, and it says that executive power, all of it, is vested in the president, who shall take care to faithfully uh execute the laws. And then Article 2 goes on to explain how officers of the United States can be appointed to help uh help uh execute uh the the the the the things that Congress has enacted. So, the questions are whether relators, who are private individuals, uh are infringing on those Article 2 powers. A couple of years ago in a case called Polansky, uh three justices of the Supreme Court, Justices Thomas, Breyer, and Kavanaugh, uh wrote a uh a side set of opinions raising questions about whether qui tam suits were constitutional or not, and in essentially signaled to uh to the defense bar and to others that they wanted to see that question litigated. Uh and so, there have been a number of motions to dismiss or motions for motions for judgment on the pleading that are raising these Article 2 arguments. Uh Foley proudly, uh I worked on a case with Joe Swanson and others here at Foley who filed a motion for judgment on the pleadings in the case cited at the bottom there, United States ex rel. Afuera versus Florida Medical Associates, uh in the Middle District of Florida, uh raising these Article 2 questions. And there, uh the district judge agreed with us and uh dismissed that suit holding that the qui tam provisions are unconstitutional because of the appointments clause, finding that relators were acting as officers of the United States without having been duly appointed. And so, uh that case uh sent a bit of a shockwave through a False Claims Act bar and has now been appealed to the 11th Circuit. Uh oral argument on that case occurred in December, and so we're waiting for a decision now. If the 11th Circuit affirms, it will very likely go to the Supreme Court because you would then have a circuit split and more fundamentally in one of the circuits, you would have uh key town provisions not not be constitutional, not not existing. If they love if the 11th Circuit reverses, it's um much harder to say uh whether and when a case might reach the Supreme Court, but this issue is being litigated in a number of cases. The Third Circuit, for example, is to is is likely to weigh in on this soon. Uh so, very very interesting issue that would change the nature of False Claims Act in a fundamental way. We do think that there are uh let's say the Supreme Court invalidates the key town provisions. Um there are a number of other federal enforcement statutes that have whistleblower features to them. For example, uh the SEC has whistleblower features where people can um raise a a concern to the government and then get a bounty, a reward, but they're not given authority to actually litigate for the government. And so, that that again makes the False Claims Act unique in that way. So, that's uh that's the nature of the False Claims Act uh its constitutional challenges. >> Thanks, Matt. So, certainly something to keep an eye on everybody uh in this space. Um I think 2026 will be an interesting year for the development of the law uh as we get the Safir off decision and and see where the law goes um in that case and and in others. So, um let's spend the last few minutes here just looking forward uh into the current year and beyond uh, with some takeaways here, uh, over the next two slides. Um, yeah, to state the obvious, uh, the last fiscal year was a record-setting year for False Claims Act enforcement. That followed a record-setting year before it. So, clearly this is a hot area and has been for the last couple of years. Um, that clearly indicates the DOJ is going to continue, uh, this as a a priority, uh, in the next fiscal year. And we do think that key tam relators, um, will likely remain very critical to DOJ's enforcement efforts. You saw that in, you know, 1,300 key tam cases filed in the last year, 400 DOJ initiated cases. I mean, that's a ratio. And so, you know, relators are going to continue to play a a significant role. Again, particularly if, um, some of the resources at main justice and in some US attorney's offices across the country are constrained due to, um, uh, you know, lower staffing levels and so forth. I think then the the impact that the relators bar have will be, uh, even greater. We expect health care to continue to be a primary focus of False Claims Act enforcement, both from DOJ and from the relators bar. Uh, and, um, we also expect, uh, continued interest in some of these other areas we've talked about today, whether it's cybersecurity, trade-related, uh, and DEI. Um, what should you do, uh, in the face of of this risk? You know, step one, review your existing compliance programs, uh, focus on generating contemporaneous records that reflect compliant intent, because scienter is such a an important part of these cases. Uh, contemporaneous records showing compliant intent is going to be very, very important to mounting a defense and trying to knock out that scienter element. It also creates a culture that facilitates internal reporting. One of the cybersecurity cases I talked about uh involved um you know, vulnerabilities being raised through a complaint tip line and allegedly not being followed up on. And so, uh you know, it's very important that you have a false you have a culture that facilitates internal reporting. In the cyber security space, um you know, not only would companies be well served by focusing on their cyber security programs to try to ward off breaches, but that also would go a long way to defending against a false claims act case um and at least offering uh evidence in mitigation. Uh and look, when problems arise, um proactively investigate and remediate and consider the risks and benefits of self-disclosure, particularly in things like the custom space for the reasons Matt talked about. Um I see we've got a few questions that have come up. We've got a few more minutes for uh answering as many of those as we can. Any that we don't get to, we will follow up with you offline. Uh Matt, I see a question here about I think this is a fear of discussion. Could the government simply refile on its own if the key tam provision is deemed unconstitutional? Do you want to handle that one? >> Um Sure. Yeah, certainly there is not a constitutional concern if the uh if the government is filing and litigating. Um but the government often declines uh a great number of false claims act cases. And so, I think um it it probably wouldn't have the resources or the interest to intervene and litigate nearly as many as uh relators end up continuing to litigate themselves. >> And Matt, I see another question on the constitutionality. Would rules promulgated to allow the appointment of the relator via petition um you know, upon filing the key tam case, would would that be constitutionally sufficient in in your view? >> Um the Constitution lays out how officers have to be appointed and so to avoid that issue, you'd have to satisfy the appointment procedure. So, um, creative workarounds would probably run into the same problems. But, on the other hand, there are established practices, for example, of special assistant U.S. attorneys or SAUSAs, as they're sometimes called, being appointed by the government to litigate uh, certain matters where the government can under the control of a contractor or a contractor can be under the control of the government to litigate cases. So, there there probably are different models where things could could happen, but, um, it'd have to be thought through and obviously, uh, follow the Constitution's requirements. >> Sounds good. Thank you for that, Matt. And, uh, I see one other question. What happens if an auditing entity reports a supplier, but didn't fully review or understand CMS guidelines? I imagine that's a question focused on a healthcare fact pattern. Um, Lori, uh, in the 30 seconds we have left, any thoughts on that? >> Yeah, I mean, I think if if if the government's investigating a case and there's not merit to it, that's an opportunity for counsel to advocate to the government about why the auditor got it wrong or didn't understand. Um, DOJ is also, at least theoretically, consulting in close contact with the agencies. So, hopefully, HHS or CMS would would set the record straight in those situations. There's my 30-second answer. >> Love it. Thanks. Thanks, Lori, and thanks to my colleagues for, uh, a great discussion over the last hour. And and thanks to all of you for joining us and sending so many questions along the way. There were a handful we could not get to, but we will follow up with each of you offline who have a unanswered question and we really thank everyone for their time. Have a great rest of the day.

segments.text: Recently a U.S. appeals court upheld a $26 million penalty against an importer
that lied about where its products came from. Their mistake? Saying Chinese-made goods were
from Taiwan to avoid antidumping duties. That’s a violation of the False Claims
Act—and it’s a costly warning for importers. I’m Kari Crane, editor of Shipping Solutions
International Trade Blog Passages. Today, you’ll learn how mistakes in
undervaluing goods, misclassifying products, and misrepresenting country of origin can all get
you into serious trouble under the False Claims Act—and what steps you can take to stay compliant.
But before we dive in, make sure you subscribe to our channel! We publish
Basics of Exporting and Importing videos twice a week to help you succeed in international trade.
The False Claims Act, or FCA, is a federal law that holds companies and individuals liable for
knowingly providing false or fraudulent information to the U.S. government.
Under the FCA: “Knowingly” includes actual knowledge, deliberate
ignorance, or reckless disregard for the truth. Whistleblowers can bring cases on behalf of the
government and receive a share of the recovery. While the FCA is often used in healthcare or
government contracting, it’s increasingly being applied to customs fraud.
Importers can run into FCA trouble in three common ways:
If you declare a lower value than what you actually paid—or fail to
include certain add-ons—Customs may see it as fraud. This can happen if:
The invoice price is influenced by a related-party relationship.
The goods are sold on consignment. You omit assists or other additions from the
declared value or don’t charge for samples. Make sure you keep detailed records,
educate your suppliers, and make sure your customs broker has all the necessary
information to properly value your goods. Using the wrong HTS code to avoid higher
duties or qualify for FTA benefits you’re not entitled to can trigger FCA liability.
Even small differences—like whether pliers are slip-joint or not—can
affect the correct code and duty rate. If you discover a past misclassification,
consider voluntarily disclosing it to Customs to reduce your risk.
If you need help with classification, click the link in the right-hand corner
to try our Product Classification Software for free. It eliminates the need to manually
search through hundreds of pages of HTS codes. Claiming a product comes from one country when
it’s actually from another—whether through relabeling, transshipping, or ignoring
origin rules—can lead to serious penalties. Legitimate “substantial transformation” can
change a product’s origin, but simple repackaging does not. And if you’re sourcing components
from multiple countries, getting country of origin right is tricky—but getting it wrong,
intentionally or accidentally—can cost you. Document your origin determination carefully,
and use the correct certificates of origin for free trade agreements. You’ll find links to free
COO templates in the upper righthand corner or in the description below.
So, how do you keep the False Claims Act from becoming your problem? It really comes
down to tightening up your import process. Make sure you’re classifying your products
correctly, double-check the declared value, and be absolutely certain about your country-of-origin
claims. Train your team so they know what to look for, and keep your documentation in order so you
can back up every number and statement you make to Customs. And don’t just set it and forget it—check
in on your processes regularly to catch small mistakes before they turn into big penalties.
If you want to make that job a whole lot easier, click here to get a free trial of our Product
Classification and Import Controls Software. It’ll help you find the right codes, check for
extra tariffs, and avoid compliance mistakes. Or watch the video linked here to see it in action.
And for even more resources, check out the hundreds of articles on
exporting and compliance available on our International Trade Blog, linked below.

Your career, reputation, and livelihood – a lot is at stake when you decide to call out fraud or other wrongdoing to blow the whistle. Our team of dedicated whistleblower attorneys understands the challenges you face as a whistleblower. We have decades of experience helping courageous men and women navigate the complicated and daunting process of bringing whistleblower claims to a just and rewarding conclusion.

Whistleblower programs contain provisions that protect the privacy and confidentiality of whistleblowers while providing anti-retaliation protections that prohibit employers from lashing out at employees who report wrongdoing.

The federal False Claims Act allows those who report fraud against the government to receive 10 to 30% of the recovered damages. Beasley Allen has a talented team of attorneys dedicated to pursuing whistleblower lawsuits.

For Disclaimers, see our Terms of Use: 
https://www.beasleyallen.com/terms-of-use/

metadata.title: How to Become an IRS Whistleblower (and Get Paid) | Law Minded EP. 11
metadata.author: Law Minded
metadata.shortDescription:
How does the IRS Whistleblower Program work, and who can get paid for reporting tax fraud? Tax attorney Alina Veneziano of Oberheiden, P.C. explains eligibility, award amounts, and how to file an IRS whistleblower claim the right way.

The short answer: the IRS pays whistleblowers who voluntarily report specific, credible tax fraud as the original source of the information. Successful claims can earn an award of 15% to 30% of what the IRS collects.

In this episode of Law Minded, host Gerrid Smith sits down with tax attorney Alina Veneziano of Oberheiden, P.C. to break down the IRS Whistleblower Program from start to finish.

The discussion covers who is eligible to file a whistleblower claim, why people come forward, what kinds of tax fraud can be reported, and how to submit a claim that the IRS takes seriously.

Alina explains that to qualify, a whistleblower must provide information voluntarily, be the original source, and sign the submission under penalty of perjury. Current and former Treasury employees, federal employees who learned the information through their jobs, and anyone legally barred from sharing it are excluded.

She walks through the most common violations reported, including offshore tax evasion, unreported foreign accounts and FBAR violations, unpaid payroll taxes, abusive micro-captive insurance, syndicated conservation easements, cryptocurrency noncompliance, Employee Retention Credit (ERC) fraud, pandemic relief loan fraud, and underreported income. Claims can target individuals as well as corporations, partnerships, LLCs, trusts, and tax-exempt organizations. When the conduct also involves the Bank Secrecy Act, securities law, or sanctions, the case may involve FinCEN, the SEC, the CFTC, or OFAC alongside the IRS.

Alina also explains how to file IRS Form 211, the Application for Award for Original Information, and warns about a common mistake: filing a similar form that reports the tip but carries no award. She covers what supporting documents matter most and why working with a whistleblower attorney can add credibility with the IRS.

This episode is designed for employees, former employees, business insiders, and anyone who has seen tax fraud and wants to know whether they qualify for an IRS whistleblower award.

Alina Veneziano is a tax attorney at Oberheiden, P.C., where she represents IRS whistleblowers and taxpayers in federal tax matters.

00:23 What is the IRS Whistleblower Program and who is eligible
01:35 Why people become IRS whistleblowers and award amounts
03:00 Types of tax fraud you can report to the IRS
04:27 Reporting corporations, LLCs, trusts, and other entities
05:52 How to file IRS Form 211 for a whistleblower award
07:23 Why supporting evidence makes or breaks a claim
08:18 How a whistleblower attorney adds credibility with the IRS
09:29 Closing remarks

About Law Minded

Law Minded is a podcast that takes a clear, practical look at how the legal system works behind the scenes. Hosted by Oberheiden, P.C., the show focuses on government investigations, enforcement actions, and regulatory issues that often feel complex or hard to follow from the outside.

Each episode features conversations with former government officials, attorneys, and professionals who have worked directly inside the system. They share real-world experience on how investigations begin, how enforcement decisions are made, and what these processes look like in practice, not just in theory.

Law Minded is designed for lawyers, attorneys, business leaders, compliance professionals, and clients who want a better understanding of government enforcement and legal risk. The discussions are thoughtful, straightforward, and focused on practical insight, without unnecessary jargon or oversimplification.

is the IRS whistleblower program? How
does it work? Who is actually eligible
to uh you know, apply for it? Uh walk us
through that.
>> Absolutely. So, the IRS whistleblower
program is the process by which the IRS
pays monetary awards to people who come
forward with specific credible
information about tax fraud or other
violations of the tax laws. The program
is run by the IRS whistleblower office.
To be eligible, a whistleblower
generally must um provide information
voluntarily, must be the original source
of the information, and must sign the
submission under the penalty of perjury.
And uh not not everyone qualifies for
the program. So, for example, current
and former employees of the US Treasury
Department are excluded, you know, as
are federal employees who learned the
information through their official
duties. And anyone who's legally
required or or actually legally barred
from disclosing it. But outside that,
generally the pool of eligible
whistleblowers is quite broad.
>> Okay. And why would somebody consider
becoming an IRS whistleblower?
>> So, generally I'd say there are two
motivations for doing so, and often they
come together. The first is financial.
Congress built a real incentive into the
program, and that's that successful
claims
can lead to a monetary award between 15
and 30% of what the IRS collects. And
some individual awards have run into the
tens of millions of dollars.
The second one is more personal. So,
most most of the whistleblowers I
represent, you know, they didn't start
out thinking solely about the money.
They're often current or former
employees who saw something happen
internally that troubled them or made
them uncomfortable about their continued
employment and didn't have anywhere else
to take it.
And maybe a third um
miscellaneous point is there's also that
broader public interest at stake.
>> Yeah.
>> And the IRS, they estimate that, you
know, unpaid taxes literally cost uh the
country roughly trillion dollars
annually. And that gap, it gets filled
in part by taxpayers
who do file and pay honestly. So, the
whistleblowers, they generally help
level the playing field. So, the IRS
does rely on these whistleblowers.
>> Yeah, they play a very important role,
especially with our country's debt the
way it is. You know, if everybody just
kind of paid their fair share, uh maybe
we'd be in a different position. Talk to
me about the types of tax violations or
misconduct that can be reported as I'm
sure there's, you know, a lot of
different things going through people's
minds as they watch and listen to this.
>> Yes, exactly. That's a good question.
So, generally almost any violation of
the tax laws the IRS is authorized to
enforce can be reported. Now, I would
say a few categories come up constantly
in my practice. So, we have offshore tax
evasion is a big one. Unreported foreign
accounts, FBAR violations, money moved
abroad specifically to avoid being
taxed.
I see a lot of employment-related
tax gap, particularly employers who
withhold payroll taxes from workers
paychecks
and then never actually deposit them
with the IRS. Beyond that, I would say
we regularly handle claims involving
abusive micro capped insurance companies
and syndicated conservations,
cryptocurrency related noncompliance,
fraud connected to programs such as the
employee retention credit and pandemic
era relief
loans. And then we get our typical
underreported income cases.
>> Okay.
Now, [snorts] can you turn in
corporations and and various different
kinds of entities or is it just like,
you know, personal individuals?
>> So, the program absolutely covers
entities. So, partnerships,
corporations, LLCs, trusts, even
tax-exempt organizations. They can they
can all be subject to a claim, not just
those individual taxpayers. That said,
you know, the IRS tends to be especially
receptive when a a company's
noncompliance has that ripple effect.
So, for example, when the tax returns of
the companies' employees, for example,
are also inaccurate. So, then you have
the corporate inaccurate tax returns and
all the tax returns of the employees as
well. So, that's a more attractive case
to the IRS.
The IRS will still take a case that's
purely about corporate noncompliance
and particularly when the dollar amount
figures are large or the issues cross
borders, for example. And sometimes that
same underlying conduct implicates more
than the IRS, and that's an interesting
point, too. So, if a company's
misconduct
also touches the Bank Secrecy Act, for
example, security laws or sanctions
violations, you know, we may end end
working with FinCEN, SEC, CFTC, OFAC
alongside the IRS.
>> Okay, interesting. Now, if somebody
actually wants to go through the process
of becoming a an IRS whistleblower, what
does that look like? Is there a special
form that they have to have? Do they
need an attorney involved in this?
What's the best way to go about it?
>> Yes, there is. Um absolutely, I would
recommend having an attorney for this to
guide them through the entire process
because it can definitely get
complicated. You know, even the form
two, there's a specific form here, the
form 211, the application for award for
original information, and it looks
strikingly like another form that just
reports information, but there's no
award attached to it. So, these can be
common but devastating mistakes.

enormously. So, you need to identify the

entity that had violated the tax laws to

recollection. So, their name, address,

information. And disclose your
relationship. So, how did you find out

attach whatever supporting documentation

thing is signed under penalty of
perjury, so accuracy does matter from

supporting documentation is maybe one of
the more important things, obviously.
You know, you you could be sitting at a
restaurant or you're with a friend, you
overhear something, you know, that
probably doesn't make a very strong case
to the IRS. They want text messages,
emails, they want something that
probably backs up, you know, the fraud
that you're alleging. Is that correct?
>> That's exactly correct. You know,
otherwise it's just a speculative too.
You know, we have to remember that the
IRS receives countless of these tips on
an annual basis. So, there has to be a
way to narrow them down and pick them.
And honestly, a lot of
good claims with substantiation are also
not investigated too. So, we have to

You know, if everybody just kind of paid their fair share, uh maybe we'd be in a different position. Talk to me about the types of tax violations or misconduct that can be reported as I'm sure there's, you know, a lot of different things going through people's minds as they watch and listen to this. >> Yes, exactly. That's a good question. So, generally almost any violation of the tax laws the IRS is authorized to enforce can be reported. Now, I would say a few categories come up constantly in my practice. So, we have offshore tax evasion is a big one. Unreported foreign accounts, FBAR violations, money moved abroad specifically to avoid being taxed. I see a lot of employment-related tax gap, particularly employers who withhold payroll taxes from workers paychecks and then never actually deposit them with the IRS. Beyond that, I would say we regularly handle claims involving abusive micro capped insurance companies and syndicated conservations, cryptocurrency related noncompliance, fraud connected to programs such as the employee retention credit and pandemic era relief loans. And then we get our typical underreported income cases. >> Okay. Now, [snorts] can you turn in corporations and and various different kinds of entities or is it just like, you know, personal individuals? >> So, the program absolutely covers entities. So, partnerships, corporations, LLCs, trusts, even tax-exempt organizations. They can they can all be subject to a claim, not just those individual taxpayers. That said, you know, the IRS tends to be especially receptive when a a company's noncompliance has that ripple effect. So, for example, when the tax returns of the companies' employees, for example, are also inaccurate. So, then you have the corporate inaccurate tax returns and all the tax returns of the employees as well. So, that's a more attractive case to the IRS. The IRS will still take a case that's purely about corporate noncompliance and particularly when the dollar amount figures are large or the issues cross borders, for example. And sometimes that same underlying conduct implicates more than the IRS, and that's an interesting point, too. So, if a company's misconduct also touches the Bank Secrecy Act, for example, security laws or sanctions violations, you know, we may end end working with FinCEN, SEC, CFTC, OFAC alongside the IRS. >> Okay, interesting. Now, if somebody actually wants to go through the process of becoming a an IRS whistleblower, what does that look like? Is there a special form that they have to have? Do they need an attorney involved in this? What's the best way to go about it? >> Yes, there is. Um absolutely, I would recommend having an attorney for this to guide them through the entire process because it can definitely get complicated. You know, even the form two, there's a specific form here, the form 211, the application for award for original information, and it looks strikingly like another form that just reports information, but there's no award attached to it. So, these can be common but devastating mistakes. And the form itself, it's fairly short, but what accompanies it matters enormously. So, you need to identify the taxpayer, which is the individual or entity that had violated the tax laws to the best of your knowledge and recollection. So, their name, address, taxpayer identification number if you have it. You need to describe the alleged violations in specific terms. Explain how and when you learned the information. And disclose your relationship. So, how did you find out about this? What was your role? And attach whatever supporting documentation you have. I would say that the entire thing is signed under penalty of perjury, so accuracy does matter from the time of the very first submission, so that's an important point as well. >> Yeah. And I would imagine that the supporting documentation is maybe one of the more important things, obviously. You know, you you could be sitting at a restaurant or you're with a friend, you overhear something, you know, that probably doesn't make a very strong case to the IRS. They want text messages, emails, they want something that probably backs up, you know, the fraud that you're alleging. Is that correct? >> That's exactly correct. You know, otherwise it's just a speculative too. You know, we have to remember that the IRS receives countless of these tips on an annual basis. So, there has to be a way to narrow them down and pick them. And honestly, a lot of good claims with substantiation are also not investigated too. So, we have to make sure that everything from start to finish is adequately substantiated, that there's nothing that makes an individual ineligible, and we guide our clients through that entire process. >> Yeah, given the fact that the IRS, I'm sure, receives, I don't even know, countless millions maybe tips a year, would it be fair to say that going through this process with an attorney offers legitimacy maybe in the eyes of the IRS cuz they know, okay, at least a law firm has vetted this, you know, they have all the right stuff in place. Does that help in case at all, do you think? >> It does. It does substantially. And the reason for that is that they know that the attorney will be submitting something that satisfies all the criteria. You know, that's our job. We have to go through everything, make sure that everything that, you know, we're submitting on behalf of our client, that we're writing, you know, is adequately supported either by the substantiation, good faith recollection of our clients. And that's important too because, you know, sometimes when we're reviewing cases, we get to a situation where we find a case where the individual is ineligible or something is not adequately substantiated, and we don't proceed with those cases anymore. But, so with that said, the IRS knows, has reason to believe that things submitted by law firms are are genuine. >> Yeah. Mason, thank you so much for your time today. >> Thank you so much, Jared. A pleasure. >> [music] >> Mhm.

metadata.author: Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you aware of significant tax underpayments, offshore accounts, or corporate tax evasion? Tax fraud robs the public of critical resources—and the IRS Whistleblower Program gives insiders the opportunity to make a difference and receive a substantial reward.

In this video, former FBI Special Agent and founding attorney Jason T. Brown of Brown, LLC walks you through the entire IRS Whistleblower process. Learn how to report tax fraud confidentially, safely, and strategically.

Timestamps: 
00:00 – Introduction
01:26 – What Qualifies for an IRS Whistleblower Award
02:36 – Tax Evasion
02:42 – False Accounting
02:51 – Business Misclassification
03:02 – Crypto Tax Fraud
03:10 – Strong IRS Whistleblower Case Examples
04:00 – Risks of Reporting Without Legal Help
04:46 – Gathering Key Evidence
05:33 – Filing IRS Form 211
07:18 – IRS Review & Investigation
09:37 – Appeal Process
10:32 – Confidentiality & Whistleblower Protections

At Brown, LLC, we've helped whistleblowers recover hundreds of millions of dollars for the government while safeguarding their identity and future. If you have inside information about significant tax fraud, consult with our whistleblower attorneys for a free, confidential case evaluation.

📞 Contact Us
Website: https://ifightforyourrights.com/
Email: info@jtblawgroup.com
Call: (877) 561-0000

Disclaimer: No attorney-client relationship is created by watching this video. This content is for informational purposes only and should not be considered legal advice. This may be considered attorney advertising.

segments.text: The IRS whistleblower process from start
to finish. How to report those tax
cheats and potentially receive an IRS
whistleblower reward. Hi everybody.
Thank you for joining me today to
discuss one of the most important
whistleblower programs, albeit one of
the slowest, the IRS whistleblower
program and how to report tax cheats.
I'm Jason T. Brown, former FBI special
agent and legal adviser and the
privilege to now head the whistleblower
law firm Brown LLC. I'm also licensed in
US tax court, so hopefully I won't put
you to sleep, though, among other
jurisdictions. Today, I'm going to walk
you through the IRS whistleblower
program from start to finish. I'll also
let you know what types of cases to be
on the lookout for and mention that
although we offer free and confidential
consultations, we're very selective
about the IRS whistleblower cases that
we pursue. Now, I'm wearing green today,
not just because this was filmed on St.
Patrick's Day, because there's large IRS
whistleblower awards out there for the
right information that can get you the
green. I'm also wearing blue because
unfortunately most cases are blue and
sadly don't result in any award. At
Brown LLC, our goal is to go after the
green and steer you clear of the blue.
So, if you uncovered serious tax fraud
and want to know how to report it and
potentially receive an IRS whistleblower
reward, this session is for you. So,
let's dive right in. What qualifies as
an IRS whistleblower award? Not all tax
issues qualify for a whistleblower
award. The IRS focuses on substantial
tax underpayments. typically involving 2
million or more in tax liability, not
income liability. Let me clarify that
with an example. If someone fails to
declare 2 million in income and their
effective tax rates around 50%, their
tax liability is only a million, which
would fall short of the 2 million
threshold for an award. And the truth
is, even at 2 million in liability, the
IRS, due to very limited resources, is
unlikely to act unless the case is
extremely blatant, well documented, and
likely to result in a collection of 10
million or more. For individuals,
there's also the additional requirement,
they must also have had gross income
over $200,000 in at least one of the tax
years at issue. By the way, let me just
say, God bless some of the hard workers
at the IRS and the great work that they
do. I know not many people say that, but
I've worked alongside of them at the FBI
and some of them are very dedicated,
hardworking individuals. And these tax
fraud cases typically involve under
reportported income, fraudulent or
outright fake deductions like writing
off personal expenses as business ones,
or just making them up, which we've seen
in some cases. Big ones may include
offshore tax evasion, like using foreign
accounts to hide income or assets, false
accounting, manipulating records to
misstate the taxable income. Whenever
there's two sets of books, they're
always suspicious. Makes for a great
complaint. And business
mclassifications, including classifying
employees as independent contractors to
avoid paying payroll taxes or
intentionally misstating the business
structure to reduce tax liability. Also,
cryptocurrency is pretty hot. If
somebody's using crypto to invade tax
liability, the IRS wants to know and
CFTC wants to know. Different
whistleblower program. The best IRS
whistle cases involve large dollar
amounts with very clear documented
evidence against deep pocketed targeted
defendants with collectible assets,
especially when the acts are willful and
not just a misunderstanding and ideally
cases where you're an insider and have
direct access to the information. The
stronger your evidence and the larger
the potential recovery, the more likely
the IRS will act. The weaker the case,
the poorer the documentation or the
smaller the potential recovery, the more
likely it's ignored. Also, keep in mind
tax cheats can face criminal exposure.
If you participated in the scheme or
feel you may be at risk, speak to IRS
counsel first. Your safety and liberty
should always come before any potential
award. Reporting a matter to criminal
authorities might accelerate the case,
but can increase the risk that your
identity is revealed or subject you to
criminal exposure, which has happened in
the past to some other IRS
complaintants. If you're clean and your
IRS whistleblower attorney reports it
criminally, there may be a strategy to
try to stimulate the case, but that's an
important decision to talk over with
your council. You also have state
options. A few states, including New
York, Illinois, have programs that allow
whistleblowers to report tax fraud under
their state statutes. and generally
state false claims act statute. It could
be a powerful tool and runs it parallel
to the federal IRS program, but with
completely different mechanisms and
protections. So, run it by your law
firm. If they're one of the best IRS
whistleblower law firms out there, they
probably navigated those state statutes
before like we have. Step two, gathering
the evidence. The IRS does not act on
speculation. They want specific,
credible, and verifiable information.
Some examples include internal emails or
spreadsheets, two sets of books, tax
returns or amended returns, bank
statements and financial ledgers,
contracts and invoices, communications
like emails that or text messages that
show an intent to deceive. That said,
gathering evidence must always be done
legally and ethically. Taking documents
you're not authorized to have,
especially from an employer, could
backfire, get you fired, get you
arrested. This is why you should engage
experienced whistleblower counsel early
to advise you on what you can and can't
use and how to best build that case of
yours without exposing yourself to the
risk. Step three, filing form 211, the
IRS whistleblower form. Maybe it's the
moment you've waited for. To apply for
this reward, you must file IRS form 211,
officially titled the application for
award for original information. Already
a mouthful. Your IRS whistleblower
attorney will do this for you and it's a
critical step. If you file it wrong,
consider yourself dead in the water or
at best delayed by a couple years,
couple years. If you have access to the
tax information because of your role as
an attorney or accountant, you really
need to work that out ahead of time or
could sit in a taint process anywhere
for three to five years before anything
gets done with it. That's right, a half
a decade you'll be waiting because you
filed it improperly. And speaking of
that, many cases come to us after
someone has submitted on their own the
form 211 and they're trying to have us
salvage the matter. In those instances,
we'll review your submission and
determine whether we're even able to
clean up the mess that generally people
make on their own. And if we can't, we
just decline it on the spot. The form
211 is the heart of your submission. You
need to explain the W's. Who, what,
when, and where, who committed the
fraud, what they did, when and how did
they do it? Why did they do it? Their
intent, the estimated tax loss, and how
you arrive at that figure, and the
documentation that supports your claim.
At Brown LLC, we typically submit a
comprehensive written memo alongside the
form 211 walking the IRS through the
facts, applicable laws, and documents
trying to make their job as easy as
possible to maximize the chance that the
IRS will take action. The IRS wants
these things silver plattered, not quick
value meal. A quick value mail often
doesn't sit well and is immediately
discarded. And you know how it's
discarded. Step four, IRS review and
investigation. Once submitted, the IRS
whistleblower office reviews your claim.
If they believe it has some merit, they
may open a civil audit or criminal
investigation. But here's the reality.
These cases take forever. Forever. The
average time for a successful claim is
about 10 years. You heard that right? A
decade. So, you need patience and better
select the correct council to work with
because you're going to be in this for a
very long time together. Each year, your
IRS whistleblower attorney may try to
obtain an update, but most updates are
actually quite vague or nonsubstantive.
Here's the most common updates. No
action, which often means nothing is
happening or they don't want to tell
you. Refer to audit. This can be
promising, but just a little promising.
It doesn't mean too much yet. Refer to
collections. Ding, ding, ding. That's
more helpful as that generally signals
the IRS has found liabilities of
pursuing the money. But even then, you
wait and wait and wait. Step five,
potential IRS whistleblower award. The
good part, if the IRS uses your
information and collects proceeds,
whether it's taxes, penalties, or
interests, you may receive a IRS
whistleblower reward. For eligible
cases, you may receive 15 to 30% of the
collected amount. If your claim doesn't
meet the thresholds, still may fall
under a discretionary program with a
smaller non-appealable reward or no
reward at all. Critically, there's no
guaranteed award when you file, even if
the IRS audits or penalizes the target.
You're only paid if they collect and
credit your submission with having made
a substantial contribution.
On the flip side, some IRS
whistleblowers have received
lifechanging amounts for coming forward
with solid information. One landmark
case, a former banker was ordered 104
million after helping expose offshore
tax schemes, tax evasion at a major
Swiss bank. That's an interesting case.
So, you got to file these the right way.
Other whistleblowers have received
awards ranging from 10 million to 30
million depending on the amount
collected and the quality of the
information. While results like these
are rare, they show it's possible when
the right case is paired with strong
evidence and skilled advocacy. Step six,
appeal if needed. If you're at the
appellet stage, you have a problem. If
your award is denied or you feel is
unfairly low, you could appeal to US tax
courts where unlicensed. That's a
specialized process, and it's worth
saying appeals rarely succeed in tax
court.
It's rare for the court to find the IRS
didn't act favorably in the first place
or why it didn't act correct. They won't
reinvestigate the underlying fraud. It
only reviews whether the whistleblower
office abused its discretion and almost
impossible standard to meet. We handle
IRS whistleblower cases on a contingency
basis. Means we're only paid if we win.
But because of the time complexity and
risk involved, we're extremely selective
about the cases we take on. For us, the
case must involve at least over 10
million tax liability. The information
provided must be detailed, well
documented, and timely. So, it's not
stale or outdated, and it has to be we
want to work with you just like you want
to work with us. Confidentiality and
risk. The IRS attempts to keep
whistleblowers confidential, but
absolute anonymity is not guaranteed,
especially for criminal prosecution or
civil litigation results. That's one
thing to go over with your counsel. If
you're reporting your employer, a
business porter, a partner, or someone
close to you, there can be retaliation
risks. That's why whistleblower strategy
matters, and we help clients weigh when,
how, and even whether to report. Some
final thoughts. Let's recap the IRS
whistleblower process. Number one,
evaluate your case qualifies under the
program. Two, lawfully and ethically
gather information to support your case.
Three, retain experienced IRS
whistleblower counsel firms like Brent
LLC. Four, file the form 211 with a
compelling submission. Five, wait
patiently and strategically for
investigation and collection. Takes a
long time. Six, receive an award only if
funds are collected and your info made a
difference. Seven, appeal if needed, but
keep your expectations realistic.
Probably not going to succeed at the
appellet process. The process is long.
It's complex. For the right case, it can
lead to massive rewards and meaningful
accountability, but for most, it's going
to just languish and die. If you believe
you have a viable IRS whistleblower
case, don't go at it alone. Contact
experienced IRS whistleblower counsel
who know the process inside out and can
guide you toward the green and keep you
away from the blow. Thank you for
watching.

In this video, whistleblower attorney Emily Stabile explains what the IRS Whistleblower Program is, its history, some of its awards, and how potential whistleblowers can file a case.

segments.text: I'm Emily Stibil, a whistleblower
attorney and a partner at the law firm
Phillips and Cohen. Modern day IRS
whistleblower program was started in
2006 after the passage of the tax relief
and healthcare act. The programs
administered by the IRS whistleblower
office. Whistleblowers submit tips to
the IRS whistleblower office on form
211, application for award for original
information. Unlike some other
whistleblower programs, tips cannot be
submitted anonymously to the IRS, but
the IRS does protect whistleblowers
confidentiality. You don't need a lawyer
to file a TIP, but a lawyer can help you
navigate the process and craft the tip
in a way that might heighten the
likelihood of success. The program
mandates that eligible whistleblowers
receive awards of 15 to 30% of the
collected proceeds recovered by the IRS.
The final determination of the award
amount is made by the IRS's
whistleblower office. To date, the
program's paid out over 1 billion in
awards to whistleblowers since its
inception, and it's recovered over 6
billion in collected proceeds based on
tips received from whistleblowers. There
are some thresholds that have to be met
um in order to be an IRS whistleblowers.
First, tips have to be filed by
individuals. Some types of individuals,
such as employees of the Department of
the Treasury, are excluded from
eligibility. In order for an award to be
paid, the tax non-compliance reported
must concern tax penalties, interest,
additions to tax, and additional
proceeds in dispute that exceed $2
million. For an action that's concerning
an individual taxpayer, not a company,
that taxpayers's income has to exceed
200,000 for at least one of the tax
years in question in order for the
whistleblower to be eligible for an
award from that action. Recently,
there's been some improvements to the
IRS's whistleblower program. In 2019,
the Taxpayer First Act made several
improvements to the program, most
notably to improve communications
between the IRS whistleblower office and
the whistleblower. For example, the act
requires that the IRS whistleblower
office notify the whistleblower when a
case for which the whistleblower
provided information is either referred
to an audit or for examination by the
IRS. It also requires that the IRS
whistleblower office notify the
whistleblower
when the taxpayer makes a tax payment
with respect to uh an enforcement action
which the whistleblower's information is
related to. It also provides that the
IRS whistleblower office provides
written responses to requests from the
whistleblower or their attorney for
information on the status and the stage
of their whistleblower claim. Several
notable awards given from the IRS
whistleblower program. The largest award
issued by the whistleblower program was
a 104 million award issued in 2012 to
the whistleblower Bradley Birkinfeld,
the banker who blew the whistle on UBS.
The IRS recovered $780 million from UBS.
UBS admitted that it had helped its US
clients evade taxes. Other large awards
made by the IRS to whistleblowers
included a $20 million award made to a
whistleblower who filed a tip under the
discretionary award program before the
mandatory award program existed. His
information about an abusive tax shelter
resulted in the recovery and in his $20
million award. In another notable case,
husband and wife whistleblower team were
awarded $17 million from the IRS program
for reporting a tax fraud scheme in
which a foreign business helped US
taxpayers evade federal income tax. The
IRS collected $74 million in the matter,
which was alleged to have hidden over
$1.2 2 billion of income in secret
accounts.

metadata.title: How Whistleblowers Power CFTC Enforcement | Raagnee Beri at National Whistleblower Day 2026
metadata.author: National Whistleblower Center
metadata.shortDescription:
More than 40% of Commodities Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) enforcement matters in 2024 involved whistleblowers. At National Whistleblower Day 2026, Raagnee Beri, Director of the CFTC Whistleblower Office, explains why whistleblowers are central to the agency's fight against fraud and misconduct in U.S. derivatives markets.

In her remarks, Beri calls the CFTC whistleblower program "a true heavyweight in a small but mighty agency," and she brings the numbers to back it up:
📊 About 42% of FY2024 enforcement matters involved whistleblowers
📊 One-third of FY2025 enforcement leads came from whistleblower tips
📊 More than $430 million in whistleblower awards since 2014, tied to $3.7 billion in sanctions
📊 A record 19 final award decisions so far this fiscal year

She also explains what's next for the program: more staff, a proposed 30% award presumption to speed up claims, and new technology and AI tools. She closes with thanks to the people who come forward, often at great personal and professional risk: "We could not succeed without the countless individuals who come forward."

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 – Raagnee Beri, Director of the CFTC Whistleblower Office
0:39 – Honoring whistleblowers
1:36 – The program by the numbers
3:09 – What's next for the CFTC Whistleblower Program
4:13 – A message to the whistleblower community

🔗 Learn about the CFTC Whistleblower Program: whistleblower.gov

metadata.title: DOJ and HHS Launch FCA Fraud Task Force
metadata.author: DarshanTalks
metadata.shortDescription:
In Fiscal Year 2024, whistleblower cases reached an all-time high of 979, signaling increased scrutiny of healthcare fraud. Just days after announcing a massive $14.6 billion healthcare fraud takedown involving 324 defendants, the Department of Justice (DOJ) and Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) launched a False Claims Act (FCA) Working Group on July 2, 2025.
This cross-agency task force is laser-focused on tightening enforcement and closing regulatory loopholes across the life sciences sector. 
Key targets include:

Clinical Trials: Fraud related to consent forms, fabricated data, improper enrollment, and documentation mismanagement.

Promotional Activities: Off-label claims, misleading speaker content, disguised kickbacks, and FTC violations.

Pharmacy Operations: Compounding without clinical rationale, patient steering, and questionable reimbursement schemes.

Corporate Transactions: M&A due diligence gaps that allow FCA risks to carry into deals.

Everyone from clinical research site owners and pharmacy operators to advertising managers and corporate lawyers is in the spotlight. The DOJ and HHS are encouraging voluntary self-disclosure of compliance issues, offering potential penalty mitigation—but only if disclosures are thorough and proactive.

The message is clear: life sciences companies must act now to audit their operations, re-evaluate risk, and fix known gaps before enforcement comes knocking.

At the Kulkarni Law Firm, we’re helping clients navigate this heightened enforcement landscape—whether in research, promotion, or pharmacy operations.

metadata.title: Can an Algorithm Find Fraud? The New False Claims Act #falseclaims  #healthcarefraud #legaltech
metadata.author: HB Litigation News
metadata.shortDescription:
⚖️📊 Could the next major False Claims Act case begin with a dataset instead of a whistleblower?

Data mining, statistical analysis, and AI are changing how potential fraud is identified—and healthcare organizations may be particularly exposed because of the enormous volume of Medicare and Medicaid billing data available for analysis.

In this episode of the Emerging Litigation Podcast, Tom Suddath and David Bender of Reed Smith join the conversation to examine the rise of data-driven False Claims Act litigation, DOJ’s Focus Initiative—Broad Oversight Through Careful Use of Statistics—and what these developments could mean for FCA enforcement.

The discussion explores:

▪️ How data miners are identifying potential healthcare fraud
▪️ Why an unusual billing pattern doesn’t necessarily prove fraud
▪️ The role of Rule 9(b) in testing data-driven allegations
▪️ Why scienter and proof of intent can be critical weaknesses in cases built primarily on statistics
▪️ How AI can strengthen—and challenge—data-driven fraud theories
▪️ How healthcare organizations can use their own data to identify compliance risks before a potential relator does

💡 The central question: An algorithm may be able to identify an anomaly. But can the evidence show that someone knowingly submitted a false claim?

▶️ Watch “When Algorithms Find Fraud: The New False Claims Act with Tom Suddath and David Bender” and subscribe to the Emerging Litigation Podcast for more conversations on the legal trends shaping litigation and risk.

#FalseClaimsAct #HealthcareFraud #HealthcareCompliance #ArtificialIntelligence #DataAnalytics #DOJ #LegalTechnology #Litigation #EmergingLitigation
