segments.text: for our panel this afternoon on the
False Claims Act one year after the
Supreme Court's decision in Escobar
I'm Chris Manning I'm a partner at
Williams and Connolly I'm a co-chair of
the key Tam subcommittee of the criminal
justice section and thank you for your
time today
we have a great panel here today I'm
joined by Tom McConville who's a partner
at orc in Los Angeles
Tom's practice focuses on representing
companies that are involved in some
issues with the federal government
including False Claims Act litigation
he's represented health care providers
and defense contractors in False Claims
Act matters and prior to working at
auric he spent 10 years working as an
assistant US attorney in both California
and Ohio and Tom's received a number of
honors including being named California
lawyer of the year for litigation by the
California lawyer magazine I'm also
joined by rich Hayes rich is the deputy
chief of the Civil Division of the US
Attorney's Office in the Eastern
District of New York and he supervises
the offices False Claims Act matters
civil fraud practice areas and he also
oversees the offices environmental
practice on the civil side and he's
overseen investigations involving
mortgage residential mortgage-backed
securities issues under faria civil RICO
issues as well as controlled substance
at Controlled Substances Act cases and
rich is a two-time recipient of the
Attorney General's Award for
distinguished service and a two-time
recipient of the directors award for
superior performance from the executive
office of the US Attorney's robb vogel
is a partner with Vogel Slate in
Goldstein in Washington DC Rob focuses
on representing relators plaintiffs in
key Tam cases involving the healthcare
industry defense contracting and other
types of False Claims Act matters
Robb's represented more than 90
plaintiffs in civil quitan matters that
have resulted in more than a billion
dollars of recoveries for the US
Treasury and before going into private
practice rob was a trial attorney in the
commercial fraud section of
Department of Justice and since 2008
he's also served as a co-chair of the
procurement fraud committee of the ABA
z-- public contract law section so
thanks to the three of you for joining
us so we'll get started I know a lot of
you are here because you know something
about the False Claims Act but some of
you may not be as familiar with it so we
wanted to start with some background
about the False Claims Act it's a
statute that provides both for civil and
criminal liability for false claims made
for money or property from the US
government the elements under the civil
statute involved knowingly presenting
false claims knowingly making false
statements revert what what are called
reverse false claims trying to keep
money or property that you've gotten
from the from the government as well as
conspiracy claims under the False Claims
Act there is a criminal statute and
there are anti-retaliation provisions
that protect individuals who are raising
concerns complaints within companies or
to the government about False Claims Act
issues the False Claims Act started as a
Civil War era statute when the Union
Army was finding that it was dealing
with some unscrupulous defense
contractors who were selling them guns
that wouldn't shoot ships that had
rotten hulls rent rancid rations there's
a case about the same mule being sold to
the Army over and over again and there
was no redress at the time under
existing federal law to go after the the
fraudsters so President Lincoln had
petitioned Congress for a statute that
would allow the federal government to go
after the defense contractors who are
engaging in those kinds of activities
and so the False Claims Act became known
as Lincoln's law
one of the most important aspects of the
False Claims Act are the key tam
provisions and the phrase key Tam comes
from a much longer Latin phrase that
talks about someone who's bringing a
lawsuit for the king as well as
themselves and it means that a private
citizen or later can bring claims on
behalf of the United States the
government gets to see the complaint
under seal and make an initial
determination whether to intervene in
the case or to decline to intervene in
which case the relator can proceed with
the case on their own or in some cases
the government can choose to dismiss the
case if they don't want the relator to
proceed and they don't want to intervene
the private relator can then get a share
of any recovery that the government gets
for the lawsuit and the percentage of
the share will change depending on
whether the government intervenes and
takes over the case or whether the
government declines to intervene and the
relator has to go on their own and False
Claims Act litigation has led to some
very high-stakes cases and some big
incentives for both the government and
private relators to go forward with
cases it provides for treble-damages
three times the amount of the damages
and civil penalties so every every false
claim has a statutory penalty that now
under current law has increased to
between a little over $10,000 to a
little over $21,000 per claim so if
you're talking about certain industries
where you're making thousands and
thousands of claims if those are all
part of the lawsuit just the penalties
alone can add up to millions of dollars
in it and that's before you get into any
damages that are going to be traveled
under the statute the False Claims Act
also provides for statutory attorneys
fees and costs and it's led to the cases
have led to a lot of long protracted
discovery very expensive cases for
government for relators and for the
companies to defend
and in one recent decision the DC
Circuit they spell that out they said
that the case had been pending for 12
years there have been three years of
discovery this was all prior to motion
motion for summary judgment a million

metadata.title: False Claims Act: Latest Trends and Developments
metadata.author: American Health Law Association
metadata.shortDescription:
Joe Wolfe, Attorney, Hall Render Killian Heath & Lyman PC, speaks with Robert S. Salcido, Partner, Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld LLP, about the current landscape of the False Claims Act (FCA) in the health care industry. They discuss the “falsity” element and the interaction between the FCA and the Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute, the constitutionality of the FCA’s qui tam provisions and possible Supreme Court intervention, the uptick in FCA investigations and other enforcement developments, the legacy of the SuperValu case and the impact on how FCA actions are litigated, and potential emerging government enforcement priorities. Robert is the author of AHLA’s False Claims Act & The Health Care Industry: Counseling & Litigation, Sixth Edition. From AHLA’s Fraud and Abuse and Hospitals and Health Systems Practice Groups.

Learn more about AHLA’s False Claims Act & The Health Care Industry: Counseling & Litigation, Sixth Edition: https://store.lexisnexis.com/ahla/products/ahla-false-claims-act-the-health-care-industry-counseling-litigation-ahla-members-grpussku69720.html 

Learn more about AHLA’s Fraud and Abuse Practice Group: https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/practice-groups/practice-groups/fraud-and-abuse 

Learn more about AHLA’s Hospitals and Health Systems Practice Group: https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/practice-groups/practice-groups/hospitals-and-health-systems 

Subscribe to AHLA's Speaking of Health Law: https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/education-events/speaking-of-health-law-podcasts

Learn more about AHLA and the educational resources available to the health law community: https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/

Get all your health law news from the major media outlets on AHLA's Health Law Daily podcast, exclusively for AHLA Comprehensive members. To subscribe and add this private podcast feed to your podcast app, go to https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/dailypodcast

videos.full_text: This episode of AHLA [music] Speaking of Health Law is brought to you by AHLA members and donors like you. For more information, [music] visit americanhealthlaw.org. >> Welcome everyone to today's AHLA podcast where I'll be talking to Robert Salcido from Akin Gump about the False Claims Act where we'll be calling it the FCA and key trends and developments that we're seeing in the healthcare industry. Robert recently published the sixth edition of the AHLA's False Claims Act and healthcare industry book. I have a copy of it right here. It's a great resource. Today's podcast is brought to you by the AHLA's Fraud and Abuse Practice Group and the Hospitals and Health System Practice Group. The Fraud and Abuse Practice Group's mission is to help all of you stay informed about healthcare fraud and abuse and compliance issues and HHS Practice Group focuses on the legal, financial, and operational issues raised by healthcare business strategies and transactions from the perspective of hospitals and health systems which of course would include the the FCA like we'll be talking about today. Again, going to be talking to Robert Salcido and his about his sixth edition of the book. It has some great information. It's broken out into the history of the FCA, substantive provisions of the FCA, how FCA civil actions work procedurally, the whistleblower concepts, damages and penalties, procedure and jurisdiction, CIDs, civil investigative demands, and voluntary disclosures. So, there's a lot covered in that book that's really helpful for healthcare attorneys those in healthcare compliance. Thanks Robert for participating. Before we get started, Robert, why don't you introduce yourself? >> Uh, thank you, Joe. Um, my name's Robert Saltzman. My just very briefly, my background is I started my career as a trial attorney with the Civil Fraud Section of DOJ, which has nationwide jurisdiction over the the False Claims Act. So, I've seen enforcement actions from that vantage point. Um, since 1993, I've been an attorney with Akin Gump. Now, I'm currently based in Los Angeles as a partner with Akin Gump. >> Great, thanks, Robert. Again, I'm Joe Wolf. I'm a vice chair of the Hospitals and Health Systems Practice Group. Previously chaired the Fraud and Abuse Practice Group at HLA. And in my day-to-day, I'm a shareholder and and healthcare practice group leader at Hall Render. And we're a boutique healthcare law firm with practice about 20 years in the industry. Now, we're going to get into some questions for Robert about about the FCA and the book. But just wanted to start off with a high-level overview of the False Claims Act. You know, many of us that work in the space, there's a talk about it being called the Lincoln Law, originally enacted back during the Civil War to combat procurement fraud. And then prior to, I would say mid-80s, it was largely used in the defense industry. And and through a number of amendments that have strengthened its its reach. You know, notably the the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act has really positioned it as the government's primary litigation tool for combating fraud against the government. And you know, looking at it from a very high level, Um, just the mechanics of it can be helpful. Uh, the False Claims Act has a few elements. It It uh any person who knowingly presents or causes to be presented a false claim for payment and and know it or knowingly makes or uses or causes to be made a false record or statement material to a false or fraudulent claim or conspires towards that um can be uh held liable for civil penalties. Um, and the damages involved in a False Claims Act type litigation uh can be staggering, dramatic. And Robert will get into more of the mechanics, but at a high level when we talk about False Claims Act liability, we're talking about how does a a situation align with some key elements? And, you know, when we we we work through the False Claims Act, there are a number of key elements um that that we want to be thinking about. You know, one, you know, was there a claim? You know, was there some type of a request for payment? Was it presented? Was Did Do we make a request of payment through some type of a claim? You know, whether that was an electronic electronic filing like a CMS 1500. Uh, did a party cause a false claim to be submitted? Uh, defendants in these cases may not actually be the ones who filed the claim, but there could be an allegation that they caused the claim to be to be filed. And there are some other key terms to the analysis. It's all in Robert's book, but you know, materiality um it under the materiality concept, was there was there was there a natural tendency to influence or be capable of influencing payment um from the government? Um, did the party act knowingly? Um, and that's an interesting analysis, you know, looking at actual knowledge or deliberate ignorance or reckless disregard as as concepts as well. Um, and was there an obligation to pay in in the often in the context of a retention of of an overpayment. And so, um, those of us that work in the space you have to interact with these issues. One of the more interesting sides of the the False Claims Act from my perspective is just some of the procedures involved. Um, that uh, that allegations are often brought as key tam actions. Uh, the plaintiffs tend to be uh, those that have um, knowledge of the of the underlying facts involved in the case. Um, they're they must follow certain key tam procedures. Um, the complaint is filed under seal. Uh, the government investigation occurs while the case is under under seal. And then there's ultimately an intervention decision by the government where the government decides to proceed with the action or notify the court that it's going to decline. Um, and the whistleblower continue can continue with the case on their own. Um, and then that impacts the amount of the whistleblower's proceeds depending on how it's handled. Uh, the DOJ also has dismissal authority um, notwithstanding the objections of the relator. So, again, I'm not trying to steal Robert's thunder here, but it's it's a very interesting law um, from a lot of different angles and we want to hear Robert's take on it. Um, and and Robert, I just provided a very high level overview of the FCA. Um, in when we when we talked last time in the podcast, you discussed the the falsity element and the interaction between the FCA and the and Stark and Kickback. Uh, can you dig in on those areas again or maybe touch on other areas where you're seeing FCA development? >> Yes. Um, in terms of the the first part, um, Joe, in terms of the falsity element and, um, kickback and and Stark actions, um, brought in a context of a False Claims Act alleged violation. There's been a few developments. Um, one is, uh, with respect to falsity, what what is a false claim? Uh, there has been a very recent decision coming out this year, uh, US ex rel Sheldon versus Allergan in the Fourth Circuit, that, um, further describes what constitutes a false claim. So, there the court wrote that a statute in and of itself being ambiguous, there the drug rebate standard, um, statute, um, isn't enough to constitute falsity for purposes of the False Claims Act. So, um, we have that decision out there. We now have to reconcile that decision with other decisions like United States versus Asara Care, the 11th Circuit case, which says that if reasonable experts can disagree, uh, regarding, um, clinical judgment, there is no falsity there because it's it's merely a manifestation of of reasonable disagreement. So, we'll have to see how the Fourth Circuit's recent case and Allergan is ultimately going to be reconciled, uh, with the 11th Circuit's decision in Asara Care. That that will be a development to watch for this year. In terms of Stark and Anti-Kickback Statute, uh, there's been a phenomenal decision just recently, um, about a month ago, uh, issued also by the Fourth Circuit, uh, US ex rel Khoury versus Thomas Health System, which will be very important, >> [clears throat] >> um, in terms of defending False Claims action actions based on an alleged violation of the Stark Law and anti-kickback statute. And the reason for that, as as I'm sure you know, and and for the audience, a common theme or common narrative by either whistleblowers or the government in Stark and anti-kickback cases, um involves the various factors. One is that the hospital purportedly tracked physicians' referrals and the profitability of those referrals. Another is that physicians are highly paid, sometimes in a 90th uh percentile or higher. Another is that the physician component of the the health system operated at a loss. And another is either the hospital or executives of the hospital has been involved in False Claims Act actions in the past and manifested a desire of capturing physician referrals. All those themes uh were developed by the the relator, the whistle-proported whistleblower in the prior case, and the court rejected each of those as as really being kind of a dispositive grounds for believing either a kickback violation or Stark Stark Law violation occurred. The court noted that tracking referrals isn't the same as overpaying on compens- compensation. Paying physicians at the [clears throat] 90th percentile, of course, there's another 10% who are paid higher, and that doesn't tell you necessarily whether um appropriate payment was was made at the end of the day or not. And the fact that for reimbursement purposes, um payments to physicians might operate at a loss doesn't tell you either whether there's a violation of either the Stark [clears throat] Law or the anti-kickback statute. So, that that was very favorable. However, leaving aside the the falsity and the stark and kickback components, uh the biggest development in in my view and what to watch for over the next couple years is really the constitutionality debate. Uh we've now had um the 11th Circuit in US ex rel Safarov versus Florida Medical Associates um in December hear oral argument. And then, of course, we had US ex rel Pena Law versus Jansen, the Third Circuit hear oral argument uh in March in terms of whether the qui tam provisions of the False Claims Act are constitutional. Um we have the Safarov district court decision, which found the um False Claims Act qui tam provisions to breach the Appointments Clause of the Constitution. Um we we suspect that that's going to ultimately reach the Supreme Court. We know that three justices, Justice um Thomas going back to the Planski case, US ex rel Planski versus Executive Health Resources, um said that this raises substantial questions that should be addressed by the Supreme Court. And in the same case, there was a concurrence by Justices Barrett and Kavanaugh saying the same thing. So, we suspect eventually this issue's going to get there. And of course, if it does, it will have enormous consequences uh for the future of the False Claims Act. Um if if it finds it constitutional, that issue will will ultimately be finally resolved. If it finds it to be unconstitutional, then it's an open question what what the remedy's going to be. Is Is the court going to try to rewrite the statute? Or is Or is it going to say it can't rewrite it and leave it to Congress to rewrite it? So, so I think that's that's the biggest issue looming over this year and and probably the next couple years. >> It's great. Um, really appreciate you you stepping through that. Um, and I I want from my my perspective and some developments in the industry, um, you know, from an enforcement standpoint, I I I think we're seeing a significant uptick, um, in in investigations. If you look at some of the data, um, it it's play it it's showing that. Um, if you look at data from 2024 as compared to 2025, the number of of new filed key tam actions in 2025 was around 1,300, up from about 700 the year before. So, there just so many cases are are unfolding, so we we're continuing to see lots and lots of false claims act developments. Um, um, and then within that, we look at recoveries, uh, under the False Claims Act. Um, if you look at the 2025 data, I think numbers I saw were about 6.8 billion in total FCA recoveries, and 5.7 billion of that, um, in healthcare-related cases. So, this continues to be a an area that has a return on investment as we look at, uh, bringing False Claims Act actions, um, and significant recoveries in the healthcare sector, uh, when we look at the totality of of False Claims Act recoveries beyond that. So, and I was actually, you know, Robert and I didn't compare notes, but um, prior, uh, but that the Thomas Healthcare case in in my from my perspective was a was a significant case. And those issues you mentioned that it clarified around provider compensation, uh, was was very helpful for the fourth circuit to take that on, um, and to and to articulate some of those those concepts. And I thought, uh, the the way that the um, the the circuit framed those arguments was helpful. Um And the judges in that case noted that um some of the what are what I would call ordinary healthcare business practices um were were framed as as being fraudulent and and the the court here was saying, "Look, that uh ordinary healthcare business practices like hospital subsidies um does not necessarily constitute an FCA claim um if there haven't been specific allegations of fraudulent actions." So, I think that's uh you know, that the the industry can breathe a sigh of relief there because I think as you would parse through complaints from prior cases, there there was a thought that some of the allegations were being framed um as fraud when when I think many of us know that there are appropriate business rationale uh for for many of of those business practices. So, I'm glad you mentioned the Thomas Healthcare case. I think that was an important one um from my perspective as well. Uh question for you, Robert. Um in 2024, uh the Supreme Court issued its decision in the SuperValu case uh where they touched on on how to interpret the FCA's knowledge element. Uh has that decision made a big impact on how FCA actions are litigated from your from your perspective? >> The the the answer is yes, a very uh big impact um for for the industry, I believe. And and the reason why is just as in um the Supreme Court's decision in Escobar regarding a materiality standard, the uh Supreme Court said that we had to in assessing materiality move from an objective standard to subjective. The Supreme Court did the same thing with respect to False Claims Act knowledge, in the the SuperValu case. And the reason that's so important for the industry, I believe, is before the Supreme Court took that case, we had six circuit courts of appeal who said that if there is if if the health system has a reasonable interpretation of ambiguous law, and there is no official governmental guidance to warn them away from that um interpretation, then you can't, as a matter of law, establish a False Claims Act violation. And we all know the long litany of ambiguous um statutes um for which industry could have a reasonable interpretation. I mean, what is a usual and customary charge? Or how do you how do you calculate best price for the Medicaid drug rebate? Courts are all over the place on on those issues. Um what the Supreme Court said in in SuperValu is that um it's not a dispositive defense merely to show that you had a reasonable interpretation of ambiguous law. Instead, it it said what had to be evaluated was a company's subjective knowledge of or interpretation of the law. Um meaning that you could act with reckless disregard or deliberate ignorance in light of an inherently ambiguous statute, if it shows that you had contextual clues of what the right answer is in terms of interpreting that particular statute. Now, the reason why that is so important uh is because now, instead of resolving a case as a matter of law just based on reading a statute, now it authorizes, arguably, the government and whistleblowers to dig into the whole health system's files to see what its subjective intent really was. How did it understand the operation of that statute? statute? So, what that means is it's much more difficult to get rid of cases at the pleading stage. Um and also more difficult to get rid of cases at the summary judgment stage because if you turn everything into the uh an intent question, what did the writer mean in that email or text message? Um and and was it acting in recklessness or or deliberate of the actual meaning of that that statute? Then it creates a triable issue of fact for ultimately a a jury to to resolve. So, um we've seen cases that have show that litany of of consequences occur. One is US ex rel versus um Eli Lilly. Now, on on the good news side is very recently within the last couple months, um the second circuit has ruled in US ex rel Hanick versus um amazon.com that you have to plead FCA knowledge with specificity for purposes of Rule 9B. Even though Rule 9B says general knowledge is sufficient, you still have to allege sufficient facts. So, the coming development for our audience to watch over the the short term regarding the construction of the knowledge element is we have some decisions like US ex rel Sheldon versus Allergan that says essentially you can never resolve the knowledge issue on emotions um uh stage of the case. Um and now we could juxtapose that with the second circuit decision in Hanick which says that if you do not plead any type of factual predicate for showing that the company knew that it they had conscious knowledge that the conduct was wrongful. Um or or otherwise act with reckless disregard or deliberate ignorance. You can get rid of the case on on 9B. So, I I think that's the the future to to watch for in that particular issue. Um how much knowledge has to be asserted at the pleading stage to have an an operative um complaint. Um in in that regard, Joe, I I know some of your practice has to do with uh proactive compliance and FCA defenses and investigations. Are Are you seeing any recent trends in that area? >> Yeah, thanks, Robert. I I think that many of the I would say themes or best practices around uh s- you know, reacting or responding to a a CID, um performing investigations, that some of those themes are similar to what we uh where we would have looked historically. I mean, if you're responding to a CID from um my perspective, it's it's good to involve uh counsel um as as soon as possible. Um the uh it's important to know that any interactions with the government um in connection with that investigation is is creating a record. Um we want to make sure that we're we're being truthful um in our discussions. Um making false statements um in in an investigation, that that that creates its own list of prob- set of problems. And so, we want to make sure that our responses to the government are accurate. I think uh maintaining control over the investigation um i- i- and who is involved in responding and who has knowledge of the existence of the investigation can help mitigate risk. We want to make sure um that there aren't unintended consequences uh related just how the investigation is handled, um need to be thinking about um information technology um in response to you know document preservation um in in connection with the CID uh having a strategy um where um we we consider the allegations made, how we're going to respond to them, understanding the potential damages at stake. Um determining um and collecting those responsive materials uh that the government's asking for, making sure those are analyzed as they're um you know as you you strategize how they're going to be produced, performing your own internal investigation as part of your response strategy, remedying potential areas of compliance concern, um and presenting uh the facts uh in and responses in in the uh light that uh is most aligned with your strategy as in working with the government. And so I mean, the response to CIDs, those are some themes I I think about. Um you know if you want to think about the most proactive compliance strategy, of course having a compliance program um that that meets the elements of uh effectiveness that the government has has uh uh articulated as important. And then also really considering self-disclosure as a proactive uh compliance strategy to help mitigate future um risk with regard to FCA. And so um you know self-disclosure uh should be a a part of any healthcare organization's um uh strategy around compliance. Um we're often asked, "Well, if if we pursue self-disclosure, won't that uh you know call attention to our organization?" Um and the government says, "Well, one, if if self-disclosure is is required due to some type of um some type of False Claims Act theory around retention or reverse False Claims Act theory, it may be the only option for an organization. And two, in our experience, the government uh views self-disclosure as a an appropriate compliance activity. And and I don't think it it raises the temperature in in most instances if you if you [clears throat] an appropriate uh self-disclosure. So, those are some areas that that that I've we we've been focusing on. That uptick in investigations is is one that we we have seen we're we're we're seeing and and those are some of the themes we consider as we work with clients in that area. Um Robert, uh just just kind of wrapping up here and and thinking about looking forward, what do you see as some uh potential enforcement priorities of the government and some emerging hot topics? >> Yeah, in in terms of emerging actions and and hot topics, um what what we see currently um are some enforcement trends that um expand um more broadly than we've seen historically. So, we we see some False Claims Act investigations having to do with diversity um inclusion equity programs and certifications made um in in that regard. We've seen an uptick in um naturally cases having to do with compliance with custom duties and and payment of tariffs um which involves to some degree that the health care sector, but is is obviously broader than that. Um we we've seen a lot of activity with respect to gender-affirming care investigations um, that also impact to to a significant degree health care um, industry as well. So, those are a relatively new trends, but it it it appears at least in my practice that um, the vast bulk of investigations are more on what we've historically experienced on the health care side. And what I mean by that is cases questioning medical necessity, um, investigations having to do with alleged breaches of the False Claims Act because of an alleged breach of the Stark Law and anti-kickback statute. And coming out of the post-COVID area, um, still a healthy supply of um, Paycheck Protection Program cases. There there is a sliver to watch for in terms of data mining cases where um, private entities are attempting to mine publicly available data having to do with coding practices or whether people qualified for PPP loans, uh, Paycheck Protection Program loans um, are uh, arising as well. There's there's defenses involved in in managing those those cases. But those the those are the trends I I'm seeing overall. >> Thanks, Robert. Um, do you have any any final remarks for our audience? >> Yes, um, it and and largely kind of reiterates points that that you've already raised as as well, Joe. One is that enforcement is upticking and you see that partly in the the numbers. Um, a record amount of qui tam actions were filed last year, almost 1,300. It was it was 1,297. Which dramatically was an increase from the prior year, which had a record number of 979. So, we see huge uptick in qui tam actions. We also saw a huge uptick in recoveries. 6.8 billion uh 5.7 billion of which involved the the healthcare industry. And the total recoveries, the the 6.8 billion was more than double than last year. So, we're we're seeing more enforcement actions and in in actions filed. And because those are qui tam actions, as as you know, those are filed under seal. So, we're we're just starting to see those come unsealed now, and they will for the next couple of years. So, um one is to keep keep in mind that that that's coming. The the other final thought, and this this too reiterates on something you said earlier, which is um what what steps can you take to be proactive? And tying this to the the points I referenced earlier about the change in in False Claims Act knowledge, where a company's subjective knowledge is um really being scrutinized by the courts. So, what one of the best practices, of course, for companies in light of that change in law resulting from the Supervalu decision, is to be mindful that whenever red flags are raised internally, the company is going to want to be able to explain why at the end of the day there was no violation of the False Claims Act. Because otherwise, the way it'll be weaponized against them by either the government or other private whistleblowers is to say, you know, my my God, this employee said that this fraud is occurring. Um see that email or text message. What did you do in light of that? Now, if the company does nothing, then your argument's going to be made that by definition those acting with reckless disregard or deliberate ignorance. So, now you have to be mindful those emails and text messages are going to be scrutinized no matter how ambiguous standard line statute is. And two, you have to have an answer to that question. What did you do when you received that email or text message in order to assure yourself that there was no known overpayment to the government. So, that's that's really the the final thought at least that I have um in terms of what to do moving forward in light of the trending case law. >> Great. Thanks. Thanks, Robert. And and thanks to everyone for listening in to to this AHLA podcast. Um and you know, please try to find opportunities to get involved in AHLA. I mentioned earlier the the Fraud and Abuse Practice Group and the Hospitals and Health Systems Practice Group. Uh we're always looking for for new members and and volunteers and to to try to expand and and get others involved. So, please reach out. Um and I hope you all have a great day and thanks for tuning in. Um and uh thanks for your time today, Robert. >> Thank you very much, Joe. >> Take care. >> If you enjoyed this episode, be sure to subscribe to AHLA's [music] Speaking of Health Law wherever you get your podcasts. metadata.shortDescription:
Episode three of McGuireWoods’ video series “Healthcare Headlines” is now available. Hosted by McGuireWoods partner Amber McGraw Walsh, chair of the firm’s nationally recognized Healthcare Department, this episode focuses on trends in False Claims Act investigations across the healthcare industry. Amber will be joined by partner David Pivnick, co-chair of McGuireWoods’ healthcare and life sciences industry team, and partner Michael Podberesky, a former prosecutor in the U.S. Department of Justice Civil Fraud Section. 

Series playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLIhiURlywxrj-hFAp3bRFy5QDQ_zxjVLi
For more about the series, please visit: https://www.mcguirewoods.com/healthcare-headlines
Videos may include attorney advertising and aren’t legal advice/opinion. Prior successes ≠ future results. © 2021 McGuireWoods LLP. All rights reserved.

metadata.title: Trump DOJ Sharpens Its Focus on Healthcare Fraud
metadata.author: Husch Blackwell
metadata.shortDescription:
Host Jonathan Porter (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/jonathan-porter)  welcomes to the show Husch Blackwell attorney Brandon Hall (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/brandon-hall) , a St. Louis-based member of the firm’s Healthcare group, to discuss how the Department of Justice’s reshuffling of priorities could lead to a greater focus on healthcare fraud enforcement. Jonathan and Brandon begin by exploring Brandon’s career prior to entering private practice, when he served as a sales representative for a medical device firm and how this background helped inform Brandon’s interest in and approach to the government’s efforts to regulate healthcare. 


The conversation then pivots to the Eliminating Kickbacks in Recovery Act (EKRA), a criminal law enacted by Congress in 2018 as part of a larger package of legislation addressing the opioid crisis. EKRA, however, has broader implications, and Jonathan and Brandon dive into how it intersects with the False Claims Act and how its willfulness provisions and lack of a right of private action have impacted enforcement. They also discuss EKRA case law that has shaped how compliance programs operate and how courts have interpreted the law’s provisions, including its unique preemption scope vis-à-vis state law and other federal statutes.


With recent reports noting redeployment of DOJ resources toward greater healthcare fraud enforcement, EKRA could emerge as a key piece of criminal law that healthcare providers need to consider.


Jonathan Porter | Full Biography (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/jonathan-porter) 


Jonathan focuses on white collar criminal defense, federal investigations brought under the False Claims Act, and litigation against the government and whistleblowers, where he uses his experience as a former federal prosecutor to guide clients in sensitive and enterprise-threatening litigation. At the Department of Justice, Jonathan earned a reputation as a top white-collar prosecutor and trial lawyer and was a key member of multiple international healthcare fraud takedowns and high-profile financial crime prosecution teams. He serves as a vice chair of the American Health Law Association’s Fraud and Abuse Practice Group and teaches white collar crime as an adjunct professor of law at Mercer University School of Law.


Brandon Hall | Full Biography (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/brandon-hall) 


Brandon counsels clients on healthcare regulatory matters, government enforcement actions, employee benefits, and ERISA. His clients include hospitals, health systems, physicians and other providers, physician groups, pharmacies, ERISA plan fiduciaries, and healthcare private equity investors. 


Prior to his legal career, Brandon sold medical devices for a national cardiac monitoring company. He also serves as adjunct faculty at Saint Louis University School of Law’s Center for Health Law Studies, where he co-teaches the course Grassroots Policy and Advocacy, a class which works with legislators to draft and pass legislation during the spring semester by taking frequent trips to the state capital to lobby legislators and testify before various committees.

videos.full_text: Welcome to another episode of Hush Blackwell's False Claims Act Insights podcast. I'm your host, Jonathan Porter. A couple of weeks ago, the Wall Street Journal wrote an interesting article about all the changes that we're seeing at the Justice Department. The article talked about DOJ's pause on enforcing foreign bribery and how DOJ is ending some corporate monitorships early. The article talked about how DOJ has signaled coming changes in antitrust and securities fraud enforcement, too. But then the Wall Street Journal article asked this question. If DOJ isn't doing all of those other things, what will it do? And the answer was healthcare fraud. The journal noted that their sources told them that DOJ is moving people out of those antitrust and securities fraud areas and moving them into healthcare fraud. Meaning the healthcare industry will likely be seeing more investigations soon once those new prosecutors get a handle on, you know, the basics of healthcare. Believe me, that takes some time. This is coming at a fascinating time because the seventh circuit just narrowed up what can be enforced under the Annie kickback statute in the Sorenson case. And so this healthcare enforcement landscape is going to be changing and we're going to follow it on this podcast as best we can. One potential DOJ pivot with more healthcare fraud focus but a narrowed up anti- kickback statute is to look to ECRA, the eliminating kickbacks in recovery act of 2018. That's what we're talking about on the podcast today, ECRA, whether ECRA enforcement could be about to take off and what people in those fields covered by ECRA might want to think about right now. Joining me to talk about ECRA is my Hush Blackwell colleague Brandon Hall. Brandon is a healthcare regulatory lawyer in Hush Blackwell's St. Louis office. Brandon is a lot like me in the sense that we both spend a lot of time keeping on top of new developments in healthcare, figuring out how those developments could impact various healthcare sectors, and then helping our clients in a proactive way get ready for changes. It's always fun for me to compare notes with Brandon, and ECRA is one of the many areas I've enjoyed picking Brandon's brain on recently, and that's what we're doing on the podcast today, talking ECRA with Brandon. And so Brandon, welcome to the podcast. Thanks for joining me and telling our listeners a little bit about ECRA. Thanks, Jonathan. Thanks for having me and and it's a pleasure to be with you today. All right, Brandon, before we get started with ECRA, I actually want to take us in a slightly different direction at first. So, one of the things that I like about you, Brandon, is that you've got realworld healthcare experience, and that's something that I know our clients value in you. So, before you went to law school, you sold medical devices. Regular listeners may remember a podcast episode I did with my friends Mara Smith and Tinyan Cougler about how life sciences companies can market products to healthcare providers without crossing a kickback line. But I want to take a few minutes Brandon to talk with you about that topic as well and then we'll talk ECRA. So Brandon, could you tell us how you and other sales reps went about educating physicians while not crossing any compliance lines? and and did you ever hear stories of anyone, you know, egregiously crossing some sort of a compliance line? Nov. 19, 2020
This is the first webinar in our Healthcare and Life Sciences Webinar Series.
Featuring McGuireWoods partner David J. Pivnick and attorney Brett W. Barnett
We will discuss recent developments in FCA litigation, along with recent trends and developments in the DOJ’s areas of focus.
For more details, please visit: https://www.mcguirewoods.com/events/firm-events/2020/12/healthcare-and-life-sciences-webinar-series
Videos may include attorney advertising and aren’t legal advice/opinion. Prior successes ≠ future results. © 2020 McGuireWoods LLP. All rights reserved.

metadata.title: Whistleblowers, CMMC & the DOJ: The Hidden Triggers Behind False Claims Act Investigations
metadata.author: Cape Endeavors, Inc.
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Bytes & Brew (formerly Bourbon & Bytes), Terry McGraw sits down with Zach Terwilliger, Managing Partner of Vinson & Elkins’ Washington, D.C. office and former U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia — one of the most cyber-heavy federal districts in the country.

Zach brings rare, dual-sided insight: decades inside the Department of Justice, including senior leadership roles overseeing criminal matters, and now leading one of the nation’s top government investigations and white-collar defense practices.

Together, Terry and Zach unpack one of the most misunderstood but dangerous forces bearing down on government contractors today:

The False Claims Act and DOJ’s Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative.

They cover:

How the False Claims Act really works — and why it creates extinction-level financial risk for unprepared contractors.

The rising wave of whistleblower (qui tam) complaints targeting SPRS scores, NIST 800-171 compliance, and CMMC assertions.

Why CIDs (Civil Investigative Demands) can cost millions before a case even begins — and why companies should never face one without experienced counsel.

How DOJ decides whether a case stays civil or becomes criminal.

The growing priority on procurement fraud, cyber misrepresentation, and compliance failures across the Defense Industrial Base.

Practical steps leaders should take now to avoid FCA exposure — and the three things you must do immediately if a CID shows up.

Zach also shares what DOJ’s current administration is signaling, why whistleblowers are a powerful and unstoppable pipeline for new cases, and how AI will reshape both compliance and risk.

Whether you’re in the DIB, a federal contractor, counsel, CISO, or anyone navigating government cybersecurity obligations — this is required listening.

Chapters / Timestamps
00:00 – Introduction
01:00 – Zach’s DOJ Background
03:10 – What the False Claims Act Really Is
06:00 – Why FCA Penalties Are Devastating
08:30 – When Civil Becomes Criminal
10:50 – Whistleblowers: The Hidden Engine Behind DOJ Cases
13:00 – The CID: The Letter That Can Bankrupt You
16:00 – Can You Just Pay the Penalty and Move On?
18:15 – How to Choose the Right Law Firm
20:40 – Is DOJ Increasing FCA Enforcement?
22:55 – The Cyber Fraud Initiative Explained
25:15 – Why CMMC & SPRS Scores Are FCA Landmines
27:45 – How to Avoid Becoming an FCA Target
29:40 – What To Do If a CID Hits Your Company
32:20 – What’s Next in White Collar & Cyber Enforcement
34:50 – The Executive Blind Spot: Cyber vs. Finance Oversight
36:15 – The Role of AI in Compliance & New Risks
37:15 – Closing Thoughts

*About Cape Endeavors*
Cape Endeavors is dedicated to providing top-tier Managed CMMC Secure Enclave services tailored to the defense industrial base. Our team of experts ensures that you can achieve rapid compliance with NIST 800-171/CMMC 2.0 Lvl2 while focusing on your existing business with little interruptions to existing operations.  Learn more: www.capeendeavors.com 

*About Zach Terwilliger*
Zachary (“Zach”) Terwilliger, a highly ranked Chambers white collar practitioner and the former Senate confirmed United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, has both extensive experience in the trenches of all manner of complex investigations at the Department of Justice as well as in the private sector. Those frontline skills combine with his mastery of strategy, problem solving, and crisis management—skills honed by prosecuting multi-national complex cases and then serving in the highest levels of the Department of Justice and leading one of the most prominent U.S. Attorney’s Offices in the country. Over the past years in private practice, Zach has rapidly advanced from a former government official to serving as go-to counsel on a series of complex and high profile representations. His matters, which involve top corporate clients as well as C suite executives and other prominent officials, have been recognized by his peers and the market, where after just four years in private practice Zach has been recognized as part of the Global Investigations Review 100, The Best Lawyers in America for False Claims Act, and as part of The 500 Leading Litigators in America and The 500 Leading Cybersecurity Lawyers in the World by Lawdragon, as well as the previously mentioned Chambers USA, where he is now ranked with those who are a decade or more his senior.

Zach rounds out his extensive executive branch and private practice Washington experience by having served as Associate Deputy Attorney General and Chief of Staff to the Deputy Attorney General, whose office manages the entire Department of Justice and its various agencies, and as counsel to the Chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee.

This is to incentivize people to come forward because there's a financial component to it. Um, to your point about the C, the civil investigative demand, what happens is DOJ gets the complaint and very rarely do they say, "Hey, we're not doing anything." So you work with the the trial attorney or the a USA on that. metadata.title: False Claims Act EXPLAINED  Real Cases & Massive Penalties
metadata.author: K2 GRC
metadata.shortDescription:
In 2024, the U.S. government recovered nearly $3 billion through lawsuits under the False Claims Act. While over half of these settlements involved health care providers, other major sectors also faced serious consequences and penalties, such as defense contracting, education, and technology. So what does this mean for you? If you work in any of these industries, and that's not the entirety of the list, keep in mind, you could be exposed to False Claims Act risk and not even know it. Today we'll break down what the False Claims Act is, real world violations, the massive penalties involved, and what you can do to stay compliant.

The False Claims Act, or FCA, dates back to 1863. Its introduction was in response to defense contractor fraud during the American Civil War. During the war, contractors would sell damaged goods to the Union army, including horses and mules in poor health, faulty rifles, and rancid provisions. It was in response to this that Congress passed the federal law. Today, it's one of the most powerful tools the government uses to fight fraud against federal programs.

If your business, knowingly or even unknowingly, submits false information to the government, you could be held liable. You could get stuck paying three times the government's damages plus a penalty that is directly linked to inflation, even if it was an accident. So what counts as a fraudulent claim? Here are common violations. Submitting false claims for services not rendered. Using false documentation to secure government funds. Conspiring to defraud a federal program. Withholding or misreporting government funds. Illegally buying government property. Accepting kickbacks or bribes. Referring patients to entities you're financially connected to.

Let's take a look at some real False Claims Act settlements to get a better idea of what not to do. One. Areva Medical and Allir Inc. Find $160 million for overbilling a diabetic testing supplies company. Submitted false claims to Medicare by paying kickbacks to patients and billed Medicare under deceased patients' accounts. Two. St. Jude Medical. Knowingly sold defective medical devices and failed to disclose safety issues to regulators. Submitted false or fraudulent claims to Medicare and other federal programs. Settled for $27 million. Three. Booze Allen Hamilton. Improperly allocated indirect costs and failed to disclose cost accounting methods. They also mischarged commercial and international costs to government contracts. They settled for $377.45 million.

I mentioned the term kickback in one of my previous examples, but what is it? A kickback is illegal payments intended as compensation for preferred treatment. This is a common issue in the healthcare industry specifically, even though the law prohibits it. Under the anti-kickback statute, medical professionals can't accept anything of value in exchange for patient referrals. The Stark law also bans doctors from referring Medicare or Medicaid patients to services where they have a financial interest. If you violate either, your claims can automatically become False Claims Act violations.

Whistleblowers are usually the first to uncover these false or fraudulent claims. They are an individual that reports evidence of wrongdoing in an organization. This can be an employee, someone in management, or even someone outside of the company. They can file a qui tam lawsuit and if the government recovers money, they get a cut of the settlement, which can sometimes be in the millions.

So how do you stay compliant? Number one. Appoint a compliance officer. Number two. Train employees on FCA risks. Number three. Conduct internal audits. Number four. Keep billing practices 100% transparent. And number five. Never cut corners. Even small errors can cost millions.

Remember the FCA applies to more than just healthcare. Any federal funding, reimbursement or contract is fair game. If your business touches any federal money through Medicare, defense, education or beyond, you need to take the False Claims Act seriously.

metadata.title: How Qui Tam Lawsuits Actually Work
metadata.author: Stephen Teller - Teller Law
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode Summary:
In this episode of False Claims, Real Consequences, host Lisa Mosbey sits down with Stephen Teller, an experienced employment and whistleblower attorney, to demystify the intricacies of qui tam lawsuits under the False Claims Act. Stephen explains how individuals can step into the shoes of the federal government to report fraud against it, and the types of fraud commonly pursued, such as healthcare and COVID relief fraud. The discussion covers the process from initial whistleblower contact to government investigation, emphasizing confidentiality and the unique aspect of cases being filed under seal. Stephen also sheds light on the government's role and decision-making in these lawsuits, and what whistleblowers can expect throughout the process. This episode is essential for anyone interested in understanding whistleblower rights and the legal mechanisms available to combat fraud against the government.

Key Timestamps:
00:01 – Introduction
00:55 – What is a qui tam Lawsuit?
02:04 – Common Types of Fraud Pursued
04:03 – Initial Steps for Whistleblowers
05:00 – Behind-the-Scenes Work Before Filing
06:04 – Concerns About Confidentiality
07:11 – Cases Filed Under Seal
08:54 – Government's Role in qui tam Lawsuits
10:34 – Government Intervention and Declination
11:46 – Duration and Expectations for Whistleblowers
12:30 – Notable qui tam Cases
13:22 – Closing Thoughts and Insights

About the Show:
False Claims, Real Consequences is a podcast dedicated to exploring the complexities of whistleblower law and the False Claims Act. Hosted by experienced legal professionals, the show provides listeners with insights into the legal processes and strategies involved in exposing fraud against the government. Each episode features in-depth discussions with experts who share their knowledge on various aspects of whistleblower cases, from initial claims to government investigations. The podcast aims to educate and empower potential whistleblowers, legal practitioners, and anyone interested in understanding the legal landscape of fraud and accountability.

For more information, visit our website:
www.stellerlaw.com

#FalseClaimsAct #Whistleblower #QuiTam #FraudPrevention #StephenTeller

videos.full_text: Welcome to False Claims, Real Consequences. Welcome to False Claims, [music] Real Consequences with Steven Teller. Steve is an employment and whistleblower attorney with more than 25 years of experience representing individuals in discrimination, retaliation, and false claims act cases. He has helped clients take on some of the largest companies in the country and has secured significant recoveries in cases involving fraud against the federal government. I'm Lisa Mosby and today we're discussing how kam lawsuits actually work. Welcome, Steve. Thanks so much for joining me today. >> Thanks a lot, Lisa. Good to talk about this stuff. People should know. >> They should, especially me because this is actually not in my scope of knowledge. So, it's a funny thing, right? Most of the time a lawsuit, you know, one person sues another person or a company, mostly one corporation sues another corporation for the most part. Um, in in a false claims act case, a kam case, there's a Latin phrase I don't know the whole of that starts kam and it means he who sues on behalf of the king. So you sort of step into the shoes of the federal government. You file this lawsuit and you give it to the government's lawyers, the department of justice, and you say, "Here's a fraud happening. The government is getting ripped off. Department of Justice, go look at this." and they will go to the agency that's getting ripped off. They'll talk to that client agency and they'll, you know, look at the situation and they will, you know, often find indeed the federal government was being ripped off and if so, they try to get the money back and then they share it with the whistleblower with a small percentage that goes to the whistleblower to incentivize this kind of lawsuit. >> Very interesting. So, what kinds of fraud are most commonly pursued through the False Claims Act? >> Well, right now there's a whole lot of the uh you remember the COVID era relief money, the PPP loans. >> I do. the Small Business Administration was so busy, you know, keeping the economy afloat when we all had to stop working uh that uh you know, they gave out they didn't check a lot of those loans, but they we still can ask for that money back, right? Uh from from the companies that weren't actually eligible. So, there's a lot of those. The most common is the Medicare and Medicaid type of of fraud. Um up coding by doctors and billing people at hospitals who you know figure out a smarter way to charge a little bit more and you know there's a lot of healthcare fraud out there. Um which kind of I think is about our broken system. There's um there's uh you know tariffs, imports, right? Customs when you bring stuff into the country. Now we've had all this turmoil about tariffs. Um the whole time there were people undervaluing the imports uh and you know pretending to uh to uh that the that the thing was something else. So it's a different um charge a different tariff duty amount um or country of origin issues um gosh mortgages. I mean it just goes on and on. Military procurement right so the government this is kind of interesting the government backs mortgages right first-time home buyers veterans etc. there's some level of governmentbacked mortgages. Is that just like it goes to the government and all that stuff happens behind the scenes >> in well so yeah I mean in a way my uh my role is to take the information from my client and turn it into a format that fits the false claims act which is a complaint in a lawsuit. The document that starts a lawsuit and a description of the facts and all the documents we have. We give that to the department of justice and then yes they they investigate. >> Okay. So, it comes about it and say, "Hey, we're curious. You know, will you please look at these documents or your client has a little more information we'd like to rein, >> but for the most part, you know, the the Federal Investigation Service is u you know, paying attention to, you know, uh how the taxpayers have been ripped off and they're trying to get our money back. It's a pretty cool system really. And when someone first comes forward, are there concerns about confidentiality or agreements they sign that need to be addressed right away? >> Um, I mean, there can be, you know, oftentimes this happens in employment, right? So, I'm at my job and I realize there's a fraud going on and I might say, "Hey, boss, we shouldn't do this." And I might get retaliated against for that. So, I've got, you know, a couple of problems. If I settle that retaliation case carelessly, I might accidentally settle the false claims that case out from under the government essentially in a way. So there's a little bit of a trick there, but it's it's rare that we have to worry about that. Other agreements, I mean, it's not a good idea for people to take all their documents and run them through AI and, you know, try to do the work themselves or do the lawyering um or even make a summary. it's um there's some concerns about whether that maintains confidentiality. So uh we could end up having to having some some problems um with discovery if people run their data through AI first that call the lawyer first. >> And one unique aspect that you mentioned is that these cases are filed under seal. What does that mean and why does that process work that way? >> Yeah, it's a funny one. I mean, you know, for the most part, um, the things that happen in the courts are public. So, whoever their client is, the government agency, um the Department of Justice is going to talk to that person um those responsible parties and um find out what's going on as best they can on the inside um of the government. They have the power to issue essentially subpoenas. Um they call them civil investigative demands. Um and it's, you know, like a discovery request in a in a lawsuit. It's a list of documents that the government wants the company to produce, maybe answer some questions either in writing or have somebody show up uh to for a deposition. Um, you know, the all the normal investigative tools of law enforcement uh get used. Um, you know, they occasionally, you know, have my clients wear recording devices. Uh, very rarely, but sometimes um or take other investigative steps, you know, getting uh um you know, sort of wiretap subpoenas and things like that occasionally happens. Um, you know, I'm I'm quite impressed with the Department of Justice attorneys. Frequently, what happens is they've negotiated a settlement by then. They intervene, the case is settled and dismissed. That's not uncommon. Um, when the case is successful, that it's successful early that way. I mean those couple of years while the government is doing its job uh means that the lawyers involved uh and the and the government u um client uh believe that the case is worth the additional effort. Yeah. >> You see it but they don't necessarily say kam or you don't necessarily know that that's I mean we never know that it's happening because it's under seal but um it's really fascinating. It's as an an aspect of the law that has not really come across my purview. But I really want to thank you for your time and walking us through the process. Um, I'm sure that there are many people in my shoes that are not even aware of this. Uh, so it's been enlightening. Thank you for your insights. >> Yeah, for sure. metadata.title: Can a Contract Award Survive When Competitors’ Prices Are Leaked? The FAR is Lava Ep. 9
metadata.author: ASI Education
metadata.shortDescription:
Every episode we help train on the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO) and the FAR through Federal Procurement News! 

In Episode 9 of The FAR is Lava, Ben and Will  break down a remarkable GAO bid protest involving the Air Force, leaked contractor pricing, and a contract award that GAO ultimately challenged.

We're also following a federal contracting fraud crackdown, new whistleblower cash rewards, and growing questions about whether the Pentagon's push toward Other Transactions is sacrificing oversight for speed.

GAO Protest of the Week: The Air Force accidentally disclosed competitors' pricing during an acquisition. One bidder cut its proposed price by $72 million. Did the agency's attempt to level the playing field actually make things worse?

GSA's Fraud Crackdown: GSA and SBA are reviewing contracts involving 689 suspended 8(a) contractors, with a combined contract ceiling of $5.5 billion.

Does Whistleblowing Pay? DOJ introduces WHIP, a new program offering $10,000–$30,000 for qualifying fraud tips.

CMMC Watch: Still paused! After nearly 1,000 industry responses, the Pentagon faces questions about compliance costs, certification requirements, and when Phase 2 might restart.

Are Other Transactions Going Too Far? Critics question whether OTs actually deliver capabilities faster while warning about weakened competition, pricing transparency, and oversight.

Pentagon Pricing Transparency: Senators demand answers about contractors' cost and pricing information and the government's ability to negotiate fair prices.

DHS's $2.7 Billion BPA: Why establish a new agencywide Blanket Purchase Agreement with Carahsoft when DHS can already buy through GSA's Multiple Award Schedule?

GSA's AI Contract Requirements: New safeguards for government data and AI systems are officially in effect.

Free Acquisition Tool: The LAB at Commerce introduces the Pro-Tested Tool, helping acquisition professionals find actual GAO and Court of Federal Claims decisions supporting innovative contracting practices.

Plus, This Day in Contract History takes us back to the Anti-Kickback Act of 1986, and we respond to comments from our viewers.

Resources & Links

Get Your Daily Dose of Federal Acquisition News (Free Newsletter):
https://elink.io/p/dailydose-9ffda63

Earn CLPs and Build Your Acquisition Skills with ASI Education Pro:
https://educationpro.asigovernment.com/

Schedule a Meeting or Learn More About ASI Government:
AskASI@asigovt.com


About The FAR is Lava

The FAR is Lava breaks down federal procurement news to help contracting professionals understand the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO), and the real-world decisions shaping government acquisition.

Whether you're a contracting officer, contract specialist, COR, program manager, or government contractor, we cover the news, protests, policies, and occasional absurdities of federal contracting.

Join the conversation! Subscribe, leave a comment or question for a future episode, and share the show with someone in the acquisition community.

Also available on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

Produced by: ASI Government


#TheFARisLava #GovernmentContracting #GovCon #GAOProtest #FederalAcquisition #ContractingOfficer #FAR #CMMC #Procurement #AcquisitionReform

metadata.title: DOJ Cyber Fraud Initiative - Cyber Faces the FCA Hammer
metadata.author: Thompson Coburn LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
In late 2021, the Department of Justice announced a new initiative to combat misrepresentations about cybersecurity preparedness and control measures by federal contractors. As part of the Cyber Initiative, DOJ has brought actions under the False Claims Act (FCA). The use of FCA creates the possibility of whistleblower actions and the potential for significant liability. Join us to examine the Cyber Initiative, discuss actions under FCA, including qui tam actions, look at FCA actions in the government contracting and healthcare contexts, and consider ways to mitigate risks of being in the DOJ's crosshairs.

Presenters:
Claire Schenk
James Shreve
Elizabeth Casale
Christine Couvillon

Disclaimer: The information provided herein is intended for general purposes only and is not intended to be legal advice. The ethical rules of some states require us to identify this as attorney advertising material. The choice of a lawyer is an important decision and should not be based solely upon advertisements. Past results obtained on behalf of current firm clients afford no guarantee of future results. Every case is different and must be judged on its own merits.

metadata.title: What is the Department of Justice's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative?
metadata.author: Jones Day
metadata.shortDescription: Launched by the U.S. Department of Justice in October 2021, the Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative utilizes the False Claims Act to pursue cybersecurity-related fraud by government contractors. Notably, the Initiative includes a "whistleblower" provision, which allows private parties who provide information relevant to an investigation to share in any assets recovered.  Jones Day partner Jimmy Kitchen explains the Initiative's risks to companies, and talks about how it could change the DOJ's position in the federal cyber-enforcement landscape.

segments.text: - The new Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative
that has been rolled out by the Department of Justice
is really the latest step following an executive order
that President Biden issued ordering the entire government
to use the whole of its authority
to strengthen the government's cybersecurity.
Following that, we had the deputy attorney general
of the United States order the Department of Justice
to conduct a review to determine how the DOJ
could enhance and expand its role in fighting cyber threats.
And so, this is one of the outgrowths of that review.
And so, what this initiative specifically does
is order the DOJ's Fraud unit
to work with US attorney's offices
and utilize the False Claims Act,
which is a pre-existing statute
that is used in other contexts,
against government contracting companies
in relation to their cybersecurity.
The initiative specifically states
that they're going to use the False Claims Act
in three ways against companies.
The first is against companies
who knowingly fail to comply with cybersecurity standards.
These standards are presumably going to exist
in the contracts between the government and these companies,
and so companies need to make sure
that they understand what those standards are
and how vague they might be interpreted.
Second, the FCA is also going to be used
for knowing misrepresentations
of a company's internal controls or practices.
So, for example, if a company,
in trying to procure a contract from the government,
represents that it encrypts
certain types of data, for example,
or if it tells the government
that it has an incident response plan that it follows
in the wake of a cyber breach,
those are things that the government
is going to hold those companies to under the FCA.
And thirdly, they are also gonna use the FCA
against companies for knowingly failing
to timely report cyber incidents.
And so, again, this is presumably going to rely
upon the terms of the contract,
which companies should take a look at
and understand whether or not those terms
provide for vague timeframes,
such as notification within a reasonable time
or without undue delay,
or something that's more akin to the GDPR's hard deadline
of like a 72-hour window.
The False Claims Act provides for statutory penalties
that actually are adjusted for inflation.
So, currently they are standing at a max penalty
of about $23,000 for each false claim.
And what a company needs to understand
is that in a particular enforcement action,
there are, in many cases, many discrete false claims
that are put into an enforcement action.
So, that number can grow quite exponentially,
even when the government hasn't shown
that they have suffered any losses at all.
In cases where the government has suffered losses,
in addition to those penalties,
a company can face treble damages
of up to three times the government's losses,
and so the monetary penalties can be substantial.
In addition to that, though, the False Claims Act
also provides a whistleblower provision,
which allows for private citizens
who report False Claims Act violations to the government
to share in whatever recovery
that the government is able to get.
And so, if you think about it in this context,
think of an information security officer
who's overstressed and overworked
and is always complaining about the fact
that he or she doesn't get the resources they need
to adequately protect a network
and feels like they're being set up to fail.
This is a somebody who could legitimately
turn out to be a whistleblower.
The DOJ has always been the one entity
that was focused on the true bad guys, meaning the hackers,
the criminals that were actually breaking the law
and breaking into companies' networks and stealing data.
And so, they've gone to great lengths
to try to get cooperation from companies
in their criminal investigations
by telling these companies that they view them as victims,
which they generally are.
But now, with this new initiative,
the DOJ is kind of throwing its lot in
with the other state attorneys general and regulators,
who are using their cyber enforcement authority
to turn it against those same companies
who are victims or potential victims of cyber crime.

metadata.title: Speaking of Litigation® - DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division: Early Seizures and Data Mining
metadata.author: Epstein Becker Green
metadata.shortDescription:
What General Counsel and Business Leaders Need to Know:

• Centralized Oversight and Pre-Indictment Asset Seizures: Two October 2026 directives from the U.S. Department of Justice’s (DOJ’s) National Fraud Enforcement Division (NFED) tell prosecutors to report ongoing corporate investigations to a central corporate enforcement section and to seize or freeze assets before anyone is charged. Companies may want to consider forfeiture risk when deciding whether to self-disclose.
• Data Mining and Whistleblowers: DOJ says it is using large-scale data mining to generate leads, and it reports that data miners have filed more than 45 percent of qui tam actions since fiscal year 2024. Companies are advised to conduct internal audits, maintain compliance procedures, and consider voluntary self-disclosure with counsel.
• Civil Rights Fraud Initiative: Federal contractors and funding recipients that certify civil rights compliance while maintaining diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs the government views as unlawful can face False Claims Act (FCA) investigations into conduct dating back to 2017. Companies should perform a risk analysis with counsel rather than rush to settle.

In this episode of Speaking of Litigation, Epstein Becker Green attorneys Zachary S. Taylor, Erica Sibley Bahnsen, and Leah Brownlee Taylor discuss how NFED is organized and what it prioritizes, how the October directives reshape corporate enforcement, and how data analytics and whistleblowers are driving case generation. They also examine where FCA, civil rights fraud, and DEI enforcement fit in and explain what companies should be doing now.

Read more on the topic: https://www.ebglaw.com/commercial-litigation-update/doj-creates-national-fraud-enforcement-division-what-it-means-for-fraud-enforcement-in-america
