videos.full_text: Today on Speaking of Litigation, we're discussing how DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division is organized, what it prioritizes, and how the October directives reshape corporate enforcement from centralized oversight to pre-indictment asset seizures, how data analytics, the new National Fraud Detection Center, and whistleblowers are driving case generation, and where False Claims Act, civil rights fraud, and DI enforcement fit into this new landscape, and what companies should be doing now. Hello everyone. I'm your host today, Zachary Taylor. I'm an attorney in Epstein Becker and Green's healthcare and life sciences practice, specializing in white-collar defense and government investigations based out of our Newark, New Jersey office. In January, the president announced a new Justice Department division with a single mission, fighting fraud. Since then, the National Fraud Enforcement Division, or N FED, has moved fast. It has created sections for healthcare, tax, trade, and corporate enforcement, set a target goal of roughly 500 attorneys and staff in 2026 with continued growth over the next two years, and launched a National Fraud Detection Center. In the span of a week, it also issued two directives. On October 1st, prosecutors were told to report their ongoing corporate investigations to a central corporate enforcement section. In October 7th, they were told to seize and freeze assets early, including before anyone is charged. Meanwhile, the civil division is separately using the False Claims Act to pursue multi-million dollar DEI settlements with companies like Accenture. Yet, we have seen relatively little independent N FED corporate enforcement so far. So the question for companies is what all of this infrastructure actually means for their risk and what GCs and compliance officers should be doing now. Joining our discussion today is Erica Sibley Bondson, member of the firm in our Washington DC office. Erica defends healthcare and life sciences companies in False Claims investigations and litigation, key TAM actions, and white collar internal investigations at both the state and federal level. Hi Erica, great to see you and thank you for being here. >> Hi Zach. >> Also with us is Leah Brownlee Taylor, member of the firm, also in our Washington DC office. Leah is the former acting general counsel of the US Marshal Service and a former senior trial attorney in DOJ's civil division. She now counsels and defends employers in employment, civil rights, and DEI compliance matters. Hi Leah, so glad you could join us. >> Hi Zach, great to be with you today. >> All right, so let's get right into it. The April 7th acting attorney general memo created the N-FED and the August 13th memo set its priorities. DOJ site now lists a healthcare fraud section, a corporate enforcement section, a national fraud detection center, and a district fraud council section embedded in the United States attorney's offices. Erica, I know that's a lot, it's a mouthful, but can you give us a quick background? What is N-FED? What moved into it and what does it mean now that every United States attorney's office has a designated prosecutor? >> So what N-FED really represents is this consolidation and reorganization of existing federal enforcement resources within DOJ. So in April, N-FED assumed operational control over a few different existing litigation components within the criminal division. They now own the tax section, the healthcare fraud unit of the fraud section, and the market, government, and consumer fraud unit of the fraud section. So all on the criminal side and they've left open for now whether there are any divisions, including the civil divisions that will come under the umbrella. There may be civil frauds, maybe civil tax in the future. For now, we're just looking at the criminal side. In many ways, this is an effort to centralize many prosecution decisions going through DOJ. It requires coordination among several different divisions. Like you said Zach, each US attorney's office is required to designate an experienced prosecutor to be detailed in place to the ENFD. ENFD also encourages state and local level participation and cooperation. So as part of their expansion and development nationwide, um ENFD is granted the authority to establish and or refocus grant programs to quote unquote enable state and local prosecutors to join the mission of ENFD. We also see that there's a hierarchy forming within ENFD now that we're 6 months on um starting in October, early October of this year, fraud division prosecutors, including those in healthcare fraud and tax fraud and others now report their caseloads directly up through the corporate enforcement division. The corporate enforcement section has primary responsibility as well for um evaluating corporate compliance with any sort of criminal resolution that that um that corporations may have when this new sort of ENFD schema. >> Very comprehensive and thank you so much. And you know, Leah, Erica raises this good this point about this centralization that's occurring as a result of ENFD. And you know, from your experience in DOJ, what does this centralizing of priority setting in Main Justice mean for how and uh matters actually going to be open and how it's handled in any given district? >> Yes, Zach. From my experience working with AAG McDonald, um it will likely mean a very centralized approach where the most important and impactful investigations and enforcement activity will likely be run through Main Justice with the support and collaboration through the various US Attorneys' Office and districts throughout the country. When I worked with him on other DOJ enforcement priorities, the approach was really to bring all leaders and stakeholders from various DOJ components, districts, divisions, and departments together with a laser focused vision on implementing DOJ priorities. So like Erica said, I suspect it will be a very top-down, centralized but hands-on approach at Main Justice. >> And I think that's really important to see with your past experience and understanding kind of that leadership structure and how you think it's going to impact this. And Erica, you mentioned, you know, we're six months in, right? We see all this kind of centralization, all these efforts to develop an infrastructure to allow NFA to to do its job to fight fraud. But are we seeing any kind of independent NFA enforcement yet? Or is this really a rebranding of the work that's already been occurring? >> I think rebranding is a good a good word for what we've seen so far. I mean, there have been a lot of splashy press releases for several months promoting NFA successes, things like takedowns. There was one in June of this year with 455 defendants in healthcare fraud allegations and opioid abuse allegations. But again, those types of investigations take years of labor by investigators and DOJ attorneys. And NFA has only been around as far back as March of this year. So that's a lot of what we're seeing out of NFA so far. But what I do expect to start seeing soon are some of the non-qui tam, non-whistleblower work emanating from the fraud detection center or some of the focused data mining work that is highly reliant on independent whistleblowers. We'll talk about that a little bit more later. And recent press releases seem to to indicate that some of that data mining, fraud detection work is really ramping up within NFA. >> Yeah, I think you raise a good point, right? Because we've seen that ramp up in in this month, right? We've seen these new directives come out. We've seen all these different press releases occur. And so let let's talk about those and kind of the impact that it's going to have moving forward as you said, as we start to accelerate. So let's start with the first one. October 1st, Colin McDonald, as we said, the assistant AG, he issues directive 2612. It's the corporate enforcement and fight against fraud, which applies to fraud division prosecutors. And so Erica, can can you walk us through this particular directive's priorities? And in particular for you, I know in your clients, what stands out for healthcare entities? >> It emphasizes priorities that have been pretty consistent across the En-Fed memos. We see healthcare, internal revenue, global trade and commerce, and public trust and financial integrity, so sort of grant procurement and grant fraud, and corporate enforcement. Those have been really En-Fed's wheelhouse since the very beginning. When we're talking about healthcare, they did call out certain very specific priorities. Um telemedicine fraud, home health and hospice scams, kickback schemes, opioid distribution, and Medicare and Medicaid fraud. That all really ties in with, like I said before, the use of data miners and the fraud detection center. The memo also places some emphasis on state-level enforcement. This administration in particular is encouraging activity by state MFCUs and offering assistance to state enforcement agencies through En-Fed to try to ramp up additional enforcement activity. >> So obviously a a pretty comprehensive and expanding memo on October 1st. And I know another thing that it mentions is that prosecutors must now work with the corporate enforcement section at all phases, right? From intake through resolution and report these ongoing corporate investigations. And Leah, you know, from your experience, is this an added hurdle for corporate enforcement or do you think this is just to create some consistency in what's occurring in these activities? >> So Zach, I think it's really just consistency and uniformity and again a top-down approach using subject matter experts in corporate enforcement who may have more decision-making authority to ensure that the president's and the AG's priorities are accomplished government-wide. >> So raises a good point. So we're we're talking about this consistency, focusing on these priorities, right? And the October 1st directive listed these factors. There's 10 factors that they give they're going to give great weight when they're making these charging decisions. How should companies read these factors, Erica? >> So there are a lot of factors. I think it's worth taking a look at them on EBG's website. We've got a list of them on there, but amongst several factors, there are things like knowledge or involvement by corporate management, conduct affecting multiple taxpayer funded programs, so Medicare and Medicaid uh are causing substantial financial harm to those programs, or we've got a threshold of of 25 million or more in losses or 25 or more victims. So one that seems to raise the threshold for DOJ to investigate corporate misconduct in comparison to what we see for example in the justice manual. Companies shouldn't necessarily see misconduct that doesn't reach these factors or doesn't hit on all of these factors to be safe from prosecution, but the emphasis right now is on conduct that hits on one or more of these factors. This also may be a reason for companies to consider voluntary self-disclosure. So we've got a couple of self-disclosure options out there. DOJ's department-wide corporate enforcement policy issued in March offers declination to companies that voluntarily self-disclose with um a a few other factors and there's already been one public declination based on voluntary self-disclosure. We also have as recently as yesterday on the the civil side a False Claims Act self-disclosure protocol pilot program that's running for the next 6 months. So we've got options for self-disclosure on both civil and criminal side coming out of of this DOJ. >> So 2 weeks ago AAG McDonald issued a second directive 2613 a comprehensive approach in the fight against fraud. Among other things, it tells prosecutors to prioritize early seizure of fraud proceeds including warrants and forfeiture proceedings to seize funds and accounts, cryptocurrency wallets and securities before initiating criminal charges along with civil restraint orders and injunctions. And Leah, you know, you served as acting general counsel of the US Marshal Service, the agency that takes custody of seized assets, manages them and sells them. If DOJ is seizing earlier including cryptocurrency, what should companies do? >> I think companies really need to be working in close partnership with their council. I mean, they have to stay vigilant. During my time with the US Marshal Service, you know, we went so far as to seizing a Russian oligarch ship. Um but I know that um you know, companies have defenses, have available defenses. And you know, there's the innocent owner defense. They have litigation tools available to them including TROs and PIs. And so that's why companies really need to be working in close partnership with their council to ensure that if there are any legal challenges to an asset seizure or early forfeiture, that they can mount those legal challenges to protect the interests of the company. >> I think that's really great, you know, uh seek the advice of council if you're dealing with this because it's a very complex area. And without diving too much into this, you know, Eric, I just want to get your take on this. So one side, Leah is saying you're defending against a seizure. On the other hand, how does this freeze factor go into decision making regarding a company's self-disclosure of potential problematic conduct? >> This is a big change and it can be scary for healthcare companies that think they might be subject to uh prosecution or or um investigation by Enfat and it it can change the calculation of how you proceed. When you receive a contact from Enfat and like Leah said, aside from challenging seizures, you may also want to consider the risk of asset forfeiture when you're deciding whether to self-disclose. I think that is a particularly important piece of this, especially now that Enfat is emphasizing it. >> You know, you know, you raise a good point with the self-disclosure is understanding kind of what's at risk. And you know, part of that is understanding what's going on in your company, internal compliance investigations, internally understand what your company is at risk for. And the other side though and what this Enfat problem brings up and you mentioned it earlier Erica was how does data analytics and data miners factor into all of this and how is that outside influence also potentially impacting a company's decision making. And we know the division is proactively generating leads and opening new investigations at a rapid pace through this National Fraud Detection Center. And on the civil side, DOJ has announced the Focus Initiative on April 30th inviting data miners to meet with the civil fraud section. So Erica, how is data mining moving front and center at NFD? >> So we've got this uh real push to use data mining and other sources to increase sort of the NFD's reach. And so earlier this year they established the National Fraud Detection Center as you said Zach. We're just learning more details about it now, but it's sort of a prosecutor led center that coordinates just a dozen different entities. We've got FBI, Homeland Security, IRS Criminal, FinCEN, and a dozen others who are coming together for the stated purpose of identifying fraud across various taxpayer funded programs and to generate investigative leads. And one of the ways they say they are generating those leads is through really large scale data mining. There's also a new program called the Fraud Oversight through Careful Use of Statistics or Focus Initiative as you mentioned Zach. It is intended to improve the department's ability to prioritize working with successful data miners as DOJ says. So Deputy Assistant Attorney General Brenna Jenny said in a press release a few months ago that um DOJ is particularly interested in hearing from data miners who believe that they have developed particularly effective tools for detecting fraud against the government. As you know, CMS releases large tranches of data every year on many, many, many different points. And so DOJ is inviting data miners to meet with the civil fraud section to explain their approaches, explains what makes them high quality data miners, how they validate their findings, and why their particular methodology is a reliable basis for identifying actionable False Claims Act matters. >> And I think that's driven large in part by what's happened before Enforcet. So right, on the whistleblower side, DOJ reports data miners have filed more than 45% of key tams since fiscal year 2024, right? So there's just been huge uptick in data miners going out there and bringing these these key tam actions. So what does a data-driven playbook look like when the data is workforce demographics rather than billing, Leah? >> I think from a defense perspective, you know, federal contractors, private employers, publicly held companies, particularly those in healthcare need to be extra vigilant and mindful and proactive as the data miners and government analysts from the whole alphabet soup of agencies that Erica referenced are really scrutinizing available workplace public data. Call this an October surprise, but just this Tuesday, the government is now set up this really robust whistleblower program called the Wip where they're offering 10 to $30,000 for tips related to government fraud. Um companies and organizations need to be actively auditing and reviewing their workplace data and their practices with counsel under a privilege review. They should not be caught flat-footed here. They may even want to consider having their own robust kind of whistleblowing reporting system and platform to get out ahead of these whistleblowers and our authorities. >> It kind of adds this extra layer that I don't think many companies would anticipate of having to worry about these outside, you know, data miners looking at publicly available data and trying to figure out things and weasel their way into a key tam action. You know, and the the real question is, is there a limit here on these data miner relators? You know, Erica, maybe you could talk about that and maybe the Integra case gives a little insight to our audience. >> So there have been some limits on independent data miner relators in the civil False Claims Act setting. So, where there is precedent, we've got this case, US Xarel Integramed Analytics versus Baylor Scott and White Health in 2020. This was a fifth circuit case. It affirmed a district court decision to dismiss for failure to state a claim. So, right at the motion to dismiss phase, a False Claims Act complaint that alleged that Baylor Scott and White and its affiliates had used inflated codes to bill Medicare. So, this relator was a purely independent third party, had looked at available, publicly available data for Baylor Scott and White and had made a claim that the defendant was inappropriately inflating certain codes. The fifth circuit took a look at it. District court dismissed it on motion to dismiss. Fifth circuit took a look at it and found that the relator who was totally unconnected to the defendant health system had failed to plead that there was a false statement or a fraudulent course of action, which in the fifth circuit at least is required to build the basis of a well-pleaded False Claims Act case. So, Integramed had analyzed some inpatient claims data that CMS had released publicly and without knowledge of the actual practices happening inside Baylor Scott and White, both the district court and the fifth circuit determined that statistical data can of course be the basis of a False Claims Act case and it can meet the pleading requirements and particularity requirements of the federal rules. Integramed had failed to meet both because the data was not sufficient to show that claims were actually false. There were obvious alternative explanations for the statistical data and besides Baylor submitting potentially false Medicare reimbursement claims, Integramed couldn't show that there were any guidelines that it was actually violating. So, there's a real hurdle here for data miners, especially totally independent third-party data miners who can see data and find outliers or find patterns, but don't have any insight into what a company is actually practicing and what its actual conduct is. >> Yeah, it would seem having the internal knowledge helps with the explanations, right? The age-old example is a physician being an outlier on heart stents, but they're a cardiac surgeon and that's what they're known for. Of course, they're the outlier, they do more, but someone just looking at data specifically will just see someone who's billing a thousand times more than the next physician. So what should companies do about this? I mean, there's you have these this risk and this push from DOJ to increase the use of data mining relators, but you also on the other hand have a high bar under the federal rules and particularity pleading requirements. How can companies insulate themselves? >> So and I think Leah and I will say this a thousand times. If we say it once, be proactive, audit, have your compliance policies and procedures in place for how to proceed if there is any sort of overpayment or compliance concern, and consider voluntary self-disclosure if that is appropriate in conjunction with counsel. >> Excellent. I want to shift gears here cuz again, there's so much to cover on this topic, but I think it's important to get to some of the the new initiatives that have been pushed and you know, one of them is this the civil rights fraud initiative. So DOJ has used False Claims Act against federal contractors and funding recipients that certify civil rights compliance while allegedly taking race or sex into account in employment decisions. This year has announced three different settlements including the Accenture settlement in September. The Civil Division, the United States Attorney's Offices have handled these cases, not Enned, but DOJ has placed those cases alongside the task force to eliminate fraud and Enned as part of the administration's broader anti-fraud effort. And Leah, I know this is an area you have particular expertise and interest in, but DIAS fraud is a relatively novel concept. I mean, can you walk us through this theory and what companies should be looking for? >> It's unprecedented. We know that it is the administration's priority to either eliminate or curb DEI programs and initiatives for minorities and women. You know, since the Student for Fair Admissions versus Harvard decision in 2023 banning race conscious admissions in higher education, there's been a real push, anti-DEI push. The president issued like five executive orders between 2025 and 2026 with a whole of government approach to really eliminate any programs perceived to provide preferential treatment based on race or sex in violation of Title VI and Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act. So companies that are federal contractors or organizations receiving federal funds that have to certify to federal civil rights compliance with those specific laws, if they certify but they maintain what the government perceives as DEI initiatives or programs that are unlawful, they now find themselves in the crosshairs of a government investigation, subject to fraud investigations under the False Claims Act pursuant to Executive Order 14398. And Zach, these investigations go back years. So they can go back to 2017, 2020 during a time period where these programs were considered lawful and the prior administration. As you've just noted, there have been multi-million dollar settlements, Accenture, but there have also been legal challenges as well. There's been some district court cases and circuit court cases, but no specific DEI rulings by the Supreme Court in the employment context. So what is unlawful DEI or the constitutional contours of what lawful DEI is will remain an open question and will continue to be litigated. >> You raised an interesting point, Leah, that this is this is novel. We're still understanding. Courts haven't made all of these decisions and in the in the workplace context, right? Workforce management context it's one thing, but and I know this is separate from N Fed, but the way DOJ is presenting it kind of is commingling these ideas and Erica, you know, how does this intersect with healthcare if at all in your opinion? And you know, is this really an N Fed issue or is this just a framing by the administration? >> So look, healthcare players are not outside of the purview of the kinds of DEI related activity that we're seeing in settlements so far. So whether N Fed will be involved remains to be seen. So recall that N Fed is criminal enforcement and these are settlements based on civil claims, civil false that claims. But of course, going back to the October 1st directive, we're seeing this instruction from the N Fed AAG to investigate all fraud claims that can fall under the umbrella of conduct by a bad actor. So DEI is not specifically called out as an area of interest in that memo, but given the government's focus on it, I think that it is certainly possible it'll be considered among the various claims brought against certain defendants. >> Basically with all these things, you can't just rely on one grouping of press releases or directives. You kind of have to look at the holistic conversation of the administration to really see where your priority areas are. And Leah, I want to I want to loop back to what you said is, you know, these investigations can go back into a time period where the now problematic initiatives were pushed and encouraged. And so what should organizations do now in response to this where maybe five years ago they were engaged in these activities, but as the administration has changed and their priorities have shifted, they've moved away from that type of practice. >> I think to Erica's point, I mean, companies and organizations really need to conduct a risk analysis. I mean, there's always the opportunity for voluntary disclosure, uh remediation with the government. But honestly, you know, companies and organizations can do an analysis to determine whether or not there are potential defenses to an FCA investigation. You know, whether really there is scienter um or materiality with respect to the government's investigation and prosecution under FCA. Honestly, if five years ago uh they were running DEI programs and initiatives that are compliant with Title VI, that are compliant with Title VII, just because the government has this new interpretation of those statutory laws doesn't mean that uh companies and organizations need to rush to settlement um just because there's a threat of an investigation or there's an investigative inquiry. I think companies and organizations really need to be working closely with counsel, do an audit review, going back in time, conduct a risk analysis, and maybe determine whether or not, you know, litigation or pushing back um on an investigation or a uh threat of prosecution is the best way to move forward in terms of available options. I think that um bringing in all relevant stakeholders is also important to determine whether or not to push back against the government when there's an FCA investigation or whether to move forward with defending a legal challenge. >> I think you uh did a great summary there of kind of the concepts to consider as a an organization, you know, and I I know it's probably going to be repetitive as Erica noted, but you know, Erica, kind of as we wrap this up and thinking about all the things we've discussed today, if, you know, general counsel, a compliance officer, a legal professional at a company has to think about one thing they should be focusing on as a result of NFI's work that over the past six months and in particular these new October directives, what should it be? >> I'll give you two things, Zach. Number one, audit. Number two, contact your counsel if you think that there is a concern that you need addressed, whether it's setting up your compliance program, thinking about what particular conduct at your at your company might need, might be within the crosshairs of NFAD or otherwise, uh audit and contact your counsel. >> And the answer may be exactly the same, but you know, Leah, for for federal contractors and federal funding recipients, is there any other additional steps they should take or is it the same? Should they they audit what they've got going on, contact counsel and be prepared? >> To Erica's point, I mean, I'll just underscore again, yes, audit, conduct those legal reviews, but honestly, you know, it's the real purpose of the legal reviews and the audit is it's really to stay one step ahead of the government, right? And it's so important, I can't emphasize this more, to look beyond the HR enterprise when really evaluating these um decisions around whether or not should we keep these DEI initiatives and programs? Can we retool them and restructure them? I think that it's important to bring in all the stakeholders, CEOs, HR, government affairs officials that are working with companies and organizations. Everyone needs to be singing from like the same sheet of music and think beyond the HR enterprise and how it can impact customers, employees. So DEI is just such a broad concept. It's beyond the HR enterprise. It really can go to the heart of the mission of the organization and the company. So bringing everyone together is my my one piece of advice. >> Great piece of advice. Well, Erica, Leah, thank you all so much for your time and insights and thank you to our listeners. We hope you found this to be informative. Be sure to subscribe to Speaking of Litigation on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts. Have a great day, everyone. >> This podcast is presented by Epstein Becker and Green PC. metadata.title: Preventing Healthcare Fraud: Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute & How to Stay Compliant
metadata.author: nurselyf
metadata.shortDescription:
Understanding the difference between legitimate referrals and potential legal violations is essential in today’s healthcare environment. In this video, we break down the key components of Stark Law and the Anti-Kickback Statute, explain how fraud investigations happen, and outline steps providers and care teams can take to stay compliant and avoid costly penalties.

📌 In This Video, You’ll Learn:
✅ What counts as healthcare fraud vs. abuse
✅ The purpose and scope of the Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute
✅ How federal agencies investigate suspicious billing and referrals
✅ Best practices for documentation, financial arrangements, and compliance training
✅ How to protect your organization—and your license—by doing the right thing

Find more in-depth nursing insights in my books on Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/author/ramrengel

📌 #HealthcareFraud #StarkLaw #AntiKickbackStatute #MedicalBillingCompliance #NursingEducation #PatientReferrals #HealthcareCompliance #JASlyf #HealthAdvocatesOfAmerica

segments.text: Hey health warriors, preventing fraud
and abuse in healthcare is crucial. In
health care, doing the right thing isn't
just about patient care. It's also about
how care is build and referred. Today,
we're breaking down two key laws every
provider should know, the Stark law and
the anti- kickback statute, and how
avoiding these legal pitfalls protects
both your license and your organization.
Understanding healthcare fraud and abuse
is vital for maintaining integrity in
the healthcare system. Fraudulent
activities can lead to severe
consequences including legal actions and
loss of trust. Healthcare fraud is the
intentional deception for financial
gain. Think billing for services not
provided or falsifying records. Abuse
refers to practices that may not be
fraudulent but result in unnecessary
costs like overuse of services, improper
coding, or questionable referrals.
Combined, fraud and abuse cost the
United States tens of billions every
year. and they're monitored closely by
CMS, the Office of Inspector General,
and the Department of Justice. Now,
let's dive into the differences between
the Stark law and the anti- kickback
statute. The Stark law prohibits
physician referrals for certain health
services payable by Medicare if the
physician has a financial relationship
with the entity. On the other hand, the
anti- kickback statute is a criminal law
that prohibits the exchange of anything
of value to induce or reward referrals
of federal health care program business.
Both laws aim to prevent conflicts of
interest and ensure that patient care
decisions are based on the best
interests of the patient. The Stark law,
also known as the physician
self-referral law, prohibits physicians
from referring patients to a medical
facility in which they or an immediate
family member have a financial interest
for certain designated health services
like labs, imaging, and therapy. This
law applies even if there is no intent
to defraud. Violations can result in
denied payments, fines, or even
exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid.
The anti- kickback statute, often
referred to as AKS, prohibits offering,
paying, soliciting, or receiving
anything of value to induce referrals or
generate business reimbursed by federal
health care programs. This statute
covers physicians, hospitals, marketers,
and vendors. It's a criminal statute,
meaning violations can lead to fines,
jail time, and exclusion from federal
healthcare programs. Both laws aim to
keep care based on need, not on profit.
Fraud investigations and compliance are
crucial aspects of maintaining integrity
within the health care system. How fraud
investigations happen. Data analysis
flags unusual billing patterns.
Whistleblowers report suspicious
practices under the False Claims Act.
Audits and subpoenas gather
documentation and interview staff. The
OIG or DOJ may issue civil monetary
penalties or press criminal charges. How
providers stay compliant? Avoid
financial relationships that influence
referrals. Ensure fair market value for
leases, contracts, or services. Keep
detailed documentation for every
referral, service, and payment. Train
staff on compliance policies and
reporting procedures. Conduct internal
audits and seek legal review when
unsure. Use caution with gifts,
incentives, and free services, even for
good intentions. As we wrap up, remember
that staying informed and vigilant is
key to maintaining integrity in
healthcare. Fraud and abuse can derail
careers and damage patient trust. But
with the right knowledge and policies,
we can deliver care that's not just
compassionate, but compliant. Does your
team include fraud awareness in your
annual training? Drop your best tips in
the comments. Like, subscribe, and
follow for more healthcare compliance
tools that protect your practice and
your patients. And remember, do the
right thing the right way every

segments.text: In today’s video, we return to the topic of Stark Law to discuss the differences between
Stark and the Anti-Kickback Statute, because many of our clients have asked us about how
these two features of the regulatory landscape relate to one another.
I’m Michael H. Cohen, founding attorney of the Cohen Healthcare Law Group.
We’ve advised over a thousand healthcare industry clients on healthcare and FDA legal
issues. Today, I’m going to explain some of the key differences between Stark Law and
the Anti-Kickback Statute. By the end of this video, you’ll have a much clearer understanding
of what exactly each one does and how they relate to one another.
To begin, we have to keep in mind that Stark Law prohibits making referrals where the referring
physician has a financial interest, so that’s something you can violate all on your own.
The Anti-Kickback Statute prohibits making referrals in exchange for anything of value,
so a violation would be in the form of an arrangement with another person or entity.
Beyond that most general distinction, there are also others to be aware of. The Anti-Kickback
Statute covers many types of healthcare providers, including nurses. Stark Law just applies to
those practitioners who have advanced education such as physicians, chiropractors, and dentists.
Another difference is whether the violation was done knowingly.
The Anti-Kickback Statute requires that the physician intend to violate the law. Stark
Law applies even if the medical practitioner just should have known they were violating
the law.
The two also diverge when it comes to exceptions. If you’ve watched some of our other videos,
you’ll know that Stark Law has several areas of exceptions, and if they apply, a referral
is exempted.
The Anti-Kickback Statute doesn’t have specific exceptions the way Stark Law does. It does,
however, use the phrase “safe harbor” to cover many types of referral actions that
are protected.
Finally, the Anti-Kickback Statute is a criminal law and it gives prosecutors the discretion
to decide if they will bring charges. Stark Law, on the other hand, is civil law. However,
medical practices can be civilly charged for violating either one.
Thanks for watching. We hope this video has answered some of your questions about the
differences between Stark Law and the Anti-Kickback Statute. Of course, there is so much more
detail that we didn’t cover in this overview video, like the “safe harbor” language
in the Anti-Kickback Statute.
If you still have questions about Stark or Anti-Kickback, click on the link below,
cohenhealthcarelaw.com/contact-us,
to send us a message or book an appointment.
Here’s to the success of your healthcare venture,
we look forward to speaking with you soon.

metadata.author: KLGatesLaw
metadata.shortDescription: In this episode, Norman Acker, Nora Becerra, and Katherine Rippey discuss the False Claims Act as it relates to Stark Law and the Anti-Kickback Statute. They analyze the Wheeling Hospital case and the Catholic Medical Center case and discuss key takeaways from the cases as they relate to the False Claims Act.

metadata.title: Overview of the Anti-Kickback Statute
metadata.author: Group Practice with Neal Goldstein
metadata.shortDescription:
Most doctors think their referral fees are legal consulting work. Under the Anti-Kickback Statute, if even 1% of the intent is wrong, it’s a felony.
Neal Goldstein breaks down the Anti-Kickback Statute (AKS), a broad fraud and abuse law that carries far heavier criminal penalties than the Stark Law. This episode is a must-watch for healthcare providers and group practice managers who need to distinguish legitimate business relationships from illegal "quid pro quo" arrangements.

What you will learn
● Why the "One Purpose" test means your arrangement is illegal if even a fraction of the intent is to induce referrals.
● The critical "Pitcher vs. Catcher" dynamic: why both the giver and receiver of remuneration are equally liable for a felony.
● The primary differences between the Stark Law and the Anti-Kickback Statute regarding federal healthcare programs.
● How to navigate the 27+ Safe Harbors, including small entity investments and ambulatory surgery center (ASC) requirements.
● The cautionary tale of Dr. Grieber and how "interpretation fees" can be legally classified as a criminal ruse.
● How to use OIG Advisory Opinions to get a "hall pass" for complex healthcare transactions.

Timestamps
00:00 — Overview of the Anti-Kickback Statute vs. Stark Law
01:54 — The General Prohibition: Remuneration and Federal Programs
03:36 — Pitchers and Catchers: Who is liable for AKS felonies?
05:12 — The One Purpose Test: United States vs. Grieber
09:12 — Safe Harbor Regulations: Your protection from prosecution
12:54 — Specific Safe Harbors: ASCs, EHR subsidies, and Recruitment
16:46 — OIG Advisory Opinions: How to request official guidance
20:09 — Quid Pro Quo: The Little League analogy for illegal kickbacks

Host bio and links
Neal Goldstein is a seasoned legal expert specializing in healthcare law and the complexities of group practice management. He provides strategic counsel to physicians and medical organizations navigating the treacherous waters of federal fraud and abuse statutes. His expertise helps providers build compliant, thriving practices without risking their licenses or liberty.
Website: https://www.pfs-law.com/
Website: https://www.goldsteingrouppractice.com/
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/neal-t-goldstein-841aa652/

Show subscribe and platform links
New episodes every week — subscribe so you never miss a conversation on the business of medicine.
Spotify | Apple Podcasts | YouTube

Disclaimer
This episode is for informational and educational purposes only and does not constitute legal, financial, or medical advice.

metadata.title: Final Stark and Anti-Kickback Statute Rules: What You Need to Know
metadata.author: Dorsey & Whitney LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Recorded January 6, 2021 

On January 19, 2021, a sweeping set of changes to the federal physician self-referral law (or “Stark Law”) and anti-kickback statute (“AKS”) regulations go into effect.  These changes, which are part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS”) “Regulatory Sprint to Coordinated Care,” are the most significant changes to the Stark Law and AKS in a decade.  Primary aspects of the changes include:
• New exceptions and safe harbors for value-based arrangements that are intended to remove regulatory barriers to entering into care coordination arrangements.  
• Clarifications to fundamental terminology and requirements.
• Added flexibility for non-abusive practices that may alleviate some of the traditional burdens of complying with the Stark Law, in particular.    
• For physician practices, changes to the Stark Law’s “group practice” definition that go into effect on January 1, 2022, which may necessitate modifications to common physician compensation methodologies within group practices.
However, the core requirements and prohibitions of the Stark Law and AKS have not changed, nor have the penalties for violating these laws. As a result, the final rules create new complications from added regulations, changed definitions, and a fresh overlay of agency interpretation of existing rules. This means added risks for organizations in understanding the regulatory changes and ensuring compliance with them.  
Join us for an overview explaining what you need to know about these final rules, including a breakdown of the changes under each of the regulations and examples illustrating how they will impact healthcare organizations and how to address related new compliance challenges.    

Presenters: 
Ross D’Emanuele, Partner, Dorsey & Whitney LLP
Laura Morgan, Partner, Dorsey & Whitney LLP
Alissa Smith, Partner, Dorsey & Whitney LLP

metadata.title: Federal Anti-Kickback Statute
metadata.author: OIGatHHS
metadata.shortDescription:
The Office of Inspector General for The US Department of Health and Human Services discusses the Federal Anti-kickback Statute.

- - -


More info at
http://oig.hhs.gov

U.S. Department of Health & Human Services (HHS)
http://www.hhs.gov

segments.text: My name is Meredith Williams.
I am an attorney with the Office of Inspector General.
Many people ask us what is the Federal Anti-Kickback Statute and how could it affect me?
Here are the four most important things you need to know about the kickback statute.
Number One: You should know what the Anti-kickback Statute prohibits.
Number Two: You should know the penalties under the law.
Number Three: You should know the types of programs the law covers.
And Number Four: You should know that the law has numerous safe harbors.
Let’s start with Number One: What does the law prohibit?
Under the Federal Anti-kickback Statute you may not knowingly and willfully offer, pay,
solicit or receive anything of value to induce or reward for referrals of Federal health
care program business.
In some industries, it is acceptable to reward those who refer business to you.
In health care however, it’s a crime.
The prohibition against kickbacks applies to those who pay for referrals and to those
who receive them.
Kickbacks can take various forms, for example, they can be bribes or rebates.
They can be given in cash or in kind.
Here is an example of an arrangement that would be problematic under the Federal Anti-kickback
Statute.
If a medical device manufacturer gives lavish vacations, gifts, or sham “consulting fees”
to an orthopedic surgeon to reward the physician for using its devices during surgery, now
that, would be suspect under the kickback statute.
In schemes like this, the Government may prosecute the physician who received the kickbacks as
well as the manufacturer who paid them.
Number Two: What are the penalties?
There are criminal and civil penalties for violating the law.
Let’s start with the criminal penalties.
Violating the Anti-Kickback Statute is a felony, which means violators can go to jail.
Conviction can result in fines up to $25,000 per violation, up to a 5-year prison term,
or both.
Now let’s go over the civil and administrative penalties.
Kickback violations can lead to False Claims Act liability.
The False Claims Act is a civil statute.
It provides a way for the government to recover money, through a lawsuit in Federal court,
when someone submits false or fraudulent claims to the government.
A provider can be penalized up to three times the government program’s loss, plus $11,000
per claim.
That’s a lot of money and the penalties can add up quickly.
Kickbacks can also lead to program exclusion.
OIG may exclude violators of the kickback statute from participating in Federal health
care programs under our exclusion authorities.
Lastly, kickbacks can lead to penalties under the Civil Monetary Penalties Law.
Under the law, OIG may subject party, through administrative proceedings, to a $50,000 civil
monetary penalty per violation and an assessment of up to 3 times the total amount of the kickback
payment, even if some part of the payment was for a legitimate purpose.
Number Three: Does the law apply to all referrals?
No.
The Federal Anti-kickback Statute prohibits rewarding referrals or generating Federal
health care program business.
This means that the law only applies to Federal health care programs.
These programs are defined in the law.
Two examples are Medicare and Medicaid.
Therefore, a referral from anyone for items and services covered by Medicare or Medicaid
would implicate the Federal Anti-kickback Statute.
Number Four: Are there any exceptions?
Yes.
We call them safe harbors rather than exceptions.
There are a number of “safe harbors” to the law.
When you structure your arrangement to fit in a safe harbor you are protected from liability.
Some examples of common business practices that may fit in a safe harbor are employment
arrangements or space and equipment leases.
Compliance with a safe harbor is purely voluntary.
But doing so provides assurance that your business practices will not be subject to
liability.
Now you’ve learned four important things every health care provider should know about
the Federal Anti-kickback Statute.
What’s often a common practice in other industries can be a crime when you are talking
about the Medicare and Medicaid programs.
Save yourself from potentially severe penalties.
Review the statute and regulations or consult with your health care counsel for more information.

metadata.title: Anti-Kickback and Stark Law: What Compliance Leaders Need to Know
metadata.author: PYA, PC
metadata.shortDescription:
PYA Takeaways: How the Anti-Kickback Statute and Stark Law apply to physician arrangements, and why fair market value alone does not always establish compliance.

Watch the full webinar: https://youtu.be/Bl2GObjX0Q0

In this clip, PYA's Erin Walker explains that neither fair market value nor an executed agreement always establishes compliance on its own. She outlines the focus of the Anti-Kickback Statute and the potential consequences of violations, then contrasts its intent-based standard with Stark Law, which she describes as a strict liability statute. She notes that Stark Law issues often stem from operational failures, such as unsigned agreements, missing time logs, and arrangements that are not reassessed over their lifecycle, and that reviews often evaluate both frameworks at the same time. She closes with other requirements to consider, including state self-referral and anti-kickback laws, tax-exempt requirements, corporate practice of medicine, and internal approval policies.

0:00 Fair market value and compliance
0:47 Anti-Kickback Statute
2:22 Intent-based vs. strict liability
2:57 Stark Law operational failures
4:11 Where Anti-Kickback and Stark overlap
5:17 State, tax-exempt, and policy requirements

This clip is from PYA's Healthcare Regulatory Roundup webinar, Physician Arrangements Under the Microscope: Regulatory Risk and Compliance, presented October 28, 2026.

Review the webinar page, presentation slides, key takeaways, FAQs, and transcript: https://www.pyapc.com/insights/hcrr-120-webinar-physician-arrangements-under-the-microscope-regulatory-risk-and-compliance/

Healthcare laws, regulatory guidance, and enforcement priorities may change. Confirm current legal requirements for the specific arrangement.

#StarkLaw #AntiKickbackStatute #HealthcareCompliance

What is Anti-Kickback? A kickback is the practice whereby a person or business pays someone to find new clients or referrals and/or pays that person a percentage of the increased transactions resulting from those referrals. The objective of federal anti-kickback statutes is to prohibit illegal “patient referrals between health care providers and entities providing health care services” for financial reasons (i.e. kick-back). Federal anti-kickback laws apply to all healthcare service providers including, but not limited to, physicians, dentists, pharmacists, pharmacies, nursing homes, and hospitals. Stark Laws address situations in which the healthcare provider has a business interest in the facility to which he/she makes referrals.

metadata.title: Anti-Money Laundering Whistleblower Reward Program | 2021 SEC AML Whistleblower Program Summary
metadata.author: Mahany Law
metadata.shortDescription:
Whistleblower lawyer Brian Mahany looks at New legislation that will soon give anti-money laundering whistleblowers their own program: The Anti  Money Laundering Act of 2020 that dramatically strengthens anti-retaliation provisions and allows the US Justice Department to pay rewards of up to 30% of whatever is collected from wrongdoers. In recent years we have seen some billion dollar AML penalties so we should soon see huge rewards.

This video covers what you need to know.

The new program is modeled on the SEC Whistleblower Program. Maximum rewards are capped at 30%. 

Several existing federal laws already protect whistleblowers against retaliation and the new Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 has its own protections. We especially like that it allows whistleblowers to report Bank Secrecy and AML violations anonymously.

Like all the existing whistleblower reward programs, earning an anti-money laundering whistleblower reward requires the person to be the original source of the information - meaning having inside information that the government isn’t already aware of.

Almost anyone with inside information is eligible including auditors and compliance officers. 

AML (Anti Money Laundering) Whistleblower Lawyer Brian Mahany   brian@brianmahany.com.

metadata.title: Rewarding Whistleblowers Regarding Money Laundering
metadata.author: Robert Eckard Law
metadata.shortDescription:
How whistleblowers can get awards for reporting money laundering or sanctions violations: a whistleblower lawyer’s guide to the anti-money laundering whistleblower program
To strengthen the enforcement of anti-money laundering (AML) laws and Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) regulations, Congress included in the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA) 
Anti-Money Laundering Whistleblower Improvement Act
1) establishes a minimum award of 10% of collected monetary sanctions
2) creates an AML and counter-terrorism financing fund from which whistleblower awards can be paid (from sanctions collected in successful enforcement actions stemming from whistleblower disclosures)
To qualify for an award, the whistleblower must voluntarily provide original information to their employer, Treasury, or the Department of Justice.
The AMLA whistleblower reward program is modeled on the highly successful SEC whistleblower program. 
Who is Eligible for an AMLA Whistleblower Reward?
In contrast to the SEC whistleblower program eligibility rules, the AMLA whistleblower reward program does not impose limitations on award eligibility for whistleblowers who gain information through the performance of compliance or audit job duties. 
Non-U.S. citizens are eligible for AMLA whistleblower awards.
Can a Whistleblower Report Money Laundering or Sanctions Violations Anonymously?
If represented by an attorney, an AMLA whistleblower may submit a tip anonymously to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).  
To determine the amount of an AMLA whistleblower award, Treasury will consider:
• the significance of the information provided by the whistleblower to the success of the covered money laundering judicial or administrative action;
• the degree of assistance provided by the whistleblower and any legal representative;
• the programmatic interest of Treasury in deterring the particular violations that the whistleblower disclosed; and
• additional relevant factors that Treasury will promulgate, which will likely echo the factors that the SEC employs to determine the amount of an SEC whistleblower award.

metadata.author: Phillips & Cohen LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
In part 3 of Berkeley Law Executive Education’s “Berkeley Boosts” three-part webinar series, “Speaking Up: Whistleblowers, Whistleblowing and the US’s Unique Approach to Fraud Enforcement,” Phillips & Cohen partner Erika Kelton moderates a discussion about the success and impact of government whistleblower reward programs under the False Claims Act and the Dodd-Frank Act.

The panel features DOJ civil fraud section Director Jamie Yavelberg, CFTC whistleblower program director Chris Ehrman, and Phillips & Cohen partner and former chief of the SEC Office of the Whistleblower Sean McKessy. 

Sean McKessy was the first Chief of the SEC Office of the Whistleblower and a principal architect of the whistleblower program. During his tenure, the SEC whistleblower program achieved unprecedented success in record time and the SEC established itself as an aggressive advocate for whistleblowers. He now represents whistleblowers in his practice at Phillips & Cohen.

Erika Kelton is an internationally recognized whistleblower lawyer whose cases have recovered billions. She has represented whistleblowers in record qui tam cases and won for a client one of the largest SEC whistleblower rewards. 

Watch Part 1, “Speaking Up: Whistleblowers, Whistleblowing and the US’s Unique Approach to Fraud Enforcement,” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hJOl_KwCHEw) and Part 2, “The False Claims Act: Why that whistleblower law is so powerful against fraud,” of the Berkeley Law Executive Education’s “Berkeley Boosts” three-part webinar series, “Speaking Up: Whistleblowers, Whistleblowing and the US’s Unique Approach to Fraud Enforcement.”

Learn about Berkeley Law Executive Education’s free “Berkeley Boosts” webinar series here: https://executive.law.berkeley.edu/be... 

Learn more about US whistleblower laws and programs and how they protect and reward whistleblowers at https://www.phillipsandcohen.com

metadata.title: Can You Be a Whistleblower If You Participated in the Fraud? #whistleblower
metadata.author: Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
Can you still be a whistleblower if you participated in the fraud or scheme? In many cases, the answer may be yes, but your legal strategy needs to change immediately.

In this video, Brown LLC explains what happens when a potential whistleblower has “unclean hands,” why participation does not always eliminate award eligibility, and why protection must come before reporting. The video discusses whistleblower eligibility under programs including the False Claims Act, SEC, IRS, CFTC, and AML/FinCEN whistleblower programs.

You’ll learn how different levels of involvement can affect your exposure, your potential award, and your reporting strategy. A billing clerk, coder, salesperson, compliance employee, manager, approver, or executive may all face very different risks depending on what they did, what they knew, when they knew it, and whether they personally benefited from the fraud.

Whistleblower submissions are not immunity agreements. If your own conduct could be questioned, speak with an experienced whistleblower attorney before contacting regulators, confronting your employer, filing a claim, or moving records.

Contact Brown LLC for a free confidential consultation- https://ifightforyourrights.com/contact-us/

segments.text: Can I be a whistleblower if I
participated in the scheme and or fraud?
A lot of whistleblowers may have
somewhat unclean hands. At the FBI, we
used to say big sources, big problems,
mid sources, mid problems, no sources,
no problems. However, without sources,
you can't make big cases. And when
there's fraud going on, to make a big
case, you sometimes need someone whose
hands are a little dirty or at minimum
know where the dirt is. That's why you
need an objective whistleblower lawyer
right away who can tell you if the dirt
just won't wash off or with a little
rinse and refresh, whether you'll be
eligible for a whistleblower award. The
dirt could be anywhere and everywhere.
Some dirt involves people who process
claims. Some entered diagnosis codes,
signed off on reports. Some prepared
invoices, helped with tax schedules,
helped with invoices for customs,
cleared compliance alerts. Some were
just following orders from a supervisor.
And a lot of people are just following
orders and only later realized that the
company may be committing fraud. So, the
question is, can I still be a
whistleblower if I participated in the
fraud? The answer is, most of the time,
yes, but you got to watch out. Once your
own conduct could be questioned, the
strategy has to change immediately, not
to advancing the ball for an award, but
to protection. It's not a situation
where you just fill out a form, call a
regulator, or confront your employer.
What you really need to know is, number
one, what's the upside for you, but
before that, what's the exposure for
you. And here are four questions to ask.
First, what did you actually do? Second,
what did you know? Third, when did you
know it? Fourth, what whistleblower
program applies? And as always, follow
the dough. The government will want to
know, did you receive money as a result
of the fraud? If so, how much? The False
Claims Act, SEC, IRS, CFTC, and AML
programs do not treat participation in
the same way. Let's start with the False
Claims Act. The False Claims Act is used
to remedy fraud against the government,
whether it's Medicare fraud, Medicaid
fraud, defense contractor fraud,
government procurement fraud,
cybersecurity certification fraud, PPP
fraud, grant fraud, customs fraud, or
other false claims involving federal
government money. Under the FCA, being
involved does not automatically prohibit
you from obtaining a whistleblower
award, but the statute does address
people who planned and initiated the
fraud. If the court and/or the DOJ find
that the relator planned and initiated
the violation, you may have a
whistleblower reward reduced if the
relator/whistleblower is convicted of
criminal conduct arising from the
violation, the relator is dismissed from
the civil action and receives nothing.
That means participation is not just one
thing. Participation may have multiple
meanings and you need to sort that out
early. For example, a billing clerk who
followed instructions is not the same as
an executive who designed and profited
handsomely from the scheme. A coder who
later realized diagnoses were
unsupported is not the same as person
who ordered the manipulation and was
paid per claim. A salesperson pressured
to follow a script is not the same as
the person who wrote the fraudulent
script and directly economically
benefits from it. The key is to separate
casual, passive, or even active
involvement from leadership and direct
profit per scheme under the False Claims
Act. Now, let's look to see whether
you're eligible for an SEC whistleblower
award if you're part of the scheme. SEC
cases can involve public company fraud,
accounting manipulation, misleading
investor disclosures, insider trading,
market manipulation, crypto fraud, FCPA
issues, Ponzi schemes, and investment
adviser misconduct. The SEC rules
culpability when determining awards.
Culpability can reduce the award. So can
unreasonable delays and interference
with internal compliance systems. And
SEC whistleblower status is not
immunity. If you violated the securities
law, becoming a whistleblower does not
automatically protect you from SEC
action. This is a critical point. A
whistleblower submission is not an
immunity agreement. Now, we're going to
look at whether or not you're eligible
for an IRS whistleblower award if you
participated in that scheme. IRS cases
are submitted through form 211. They may
involve offshore accounts, hidden
income, sham deductions, abusive tax
shelters, payroll tax fraud, transfer
pricing manipulation, crypto
concealment, tax underpayments, or any
of the thousand ways people deprive the
federal government of money wrongfully
when they're owed taxes. The IRS has its
own version of the same issue. Did the
whistleblower plan and initiate the
action that led to the underpayment? If
so, the award can be reduced. If the
person is convicted of criminal conduct
arising from their role, the award can
be denied. That's a common theme in all
these programs. But IRS guidance also
draws a meaningful line. A junior
employee acting under the direction and
control of a senior employee is not the
same as someone who designed or launched
the tax scheme. So, the extent of the
role in the tax scheme is very important
to flush out to determine number one
eligibility for award and number two,
whether or not there's criminal
exposure. CFTC and AML cases have
similar themes to see if people are
eligible for awards if they're
committing some of the conduct. The CFTC
rules consider culpability, scienter,
financial benefit delay, and
interference with compliance systems.
FinCEN and AML cases can involve
transaction monitoring, sanction
steering, KYC, SAR decisions, suspicious
transfers, shell companies, and money
laundering. If you participated in
clearing alerts or approving the
transactions, that does not
automatically mean you don't have a
whistleblower path, but it does mean
your role must be evaluated before you
report. Now, I want to talk about
something that applies to all the
programs, immunity. A lot of people
think if I blow the whistle, I receive
immunity. That's just wrong. A
whistleblower reward track and a
criminal cooperation agreement and track
are just two different things. The
reward track is about voluntarily
providing original useful information
that leads to a successful enforcement
action. The Protection Act may involve a
proffer, cooperation presentation,
voluntary self-disclosure,
non-prosecution discussion, or some sort
of criminal defense strategy that you're
providing information so you won't go to
jail. These tracks can overlap, but
they're definitely not the same. And
sometimes they conflict. If you're
seeking immunity or leniency because
you're afraid of prosecution, the
government may view your testimony as
cooperation motivated by avoiding
criminal consequences. That does not
make your information useless. In fact,
it may make it integral to the
investigation, but it may not look like
a clean voluntary whistleblower
submission cuz the objective is not to
obtain award. The objective is stay out
of jail. That's why the first legal
question you should ask is not how much
money can I receive by blowing the
whistle. The first question you should
ask and your whistleblower attorney
should ask is, "How do I protect myself
while potentially preserving an award
path?" So, protection is first. Always
use protection and a good whistleblower
attorney will go over your protection.
Here's the practical involvement ladder.
Level one, minimal involvement. You
processed records or followed routine
instructions without even understanding
the fraud. Level two, a concerned, more
conscious employee. You suspected
something was wrong but continued under
pressure or direction. Level three,
knowing participant. You understood key
facts, but you still helped carry out
part of the scheme. Level four, manager
or approver. You signed off, supervised,
certified, coded, billed, approved, or
directed parts of the conduct. Level
five, planner or initiator. You helped
design the fraud, launched the
misconduct. Level six, obstruction. This
is a big one for the eyes of the
government. You destroyed evidence,
altered records, lied, concealed
documents, or interfered with
investigators. And on all levels, they
want to see how much and how often you
directly benefited from the fraud. As
you move up that ladder, your exposure
increases. It's not a ladder you want to
climb. That doesn't always eliminate
whistleblower options, but makes your
legal strategy critical. So, what should
you do? Build a timeline. Separate what
you know from what you suspect. Identify
who directed the conduct, identify what
documents exist, preserve lawful
evidence in your possession. Do not, and
I repeat, do not destroy, alter, or hide
anything. Do not lie. Do not take
privileged or unauthorized documents.
Don't call the regulators alone because
if you have exposure, you may be the one
who this is hung on. Do not assume
internal reporting is safe. A lot of
times they're going to blame you for the
conduct and fire you. Do not wait until
someone blames you first and do not
assume that participation automatically
ends your option. A serious
whistleblower matter is not just about
reporting fraud, it's also about
protecting the whistleblower. A focused
whistleblower law firm should evaluate
five things before anything is filed.
Front and center, first, your exposure.
Next, the correct program to file it in.
Then evaluate the evidence, the
disclosure strategy, and the award and
cooperation issues to plot the case in
its entirety. If your own conduct could
be questioned, obtain advice before
making the next move. The right strategy
can protect you, the wrong first move
can make a bad situation worse and damn
you. If you have credible information
about fraud but are worried you were
involved, contact Brown LLC for a free
confidential case evaluation before
reporting, filing, or moving records, or
destroying anything. That may be the
difference between obtaining an award or
going to jail.

And when there's fraud going on, to make a big case, you sometimes need someone whose hands are a little dirty or at minimum know where the dirt is. That's why you need an objective whistleblower lawyer right away who can tell you if the dirt just won't wash off or with a little rinse and refresh, whether you'll be eligible for a whistleblower award. The dirt could be anywhere and everywhere. Some dirt involves people who process claims. Some entered diagnosis codes, signed off on reports. Some prepared invoices, helped with tax schedules, helped with invoices for customs, cleared compliance alerts. Some were just following orders from a supervisor. And a lot of people are just following orders and only later realized that the company may be committing fraud. So, the question is, can I still be a whistleblower if I participated in the fraud? The answer is, most of the time, yes, but you got to watch out. Once your own conduct could be questioned, the strategy has to change immediately, not to advancing the ball for an award, but to protection. It's not a situation where you just fill out a form, call a regulator, or confront your employer. What you really need to know is, number one, what's the upside for you, but before that, what's the exposure for you. And here are four questions to ask. First, what did you actually do? Second, what did you know? Third, when did you know it? Fourth, what whistleblower program applies? And as always, follow the dough. The government will want to know, did you receive money as a result of the fraud? If so, how much? The False Claims Act, SEC, IRS, CFTC, and AML programs do not treat participation in the same way. Let's start with the False Claims Act. The False Claims Act is used to remedy fraud against the government, whether it's Medicare fraud, Medicaid fraud, defense contractor fraud, government procurement fraud, cybersecurity certification fraud, PPP fraud, grant fraud, customs fraud, or other false claims involving federal government money. Under the FCA, being involved does not automatically prohibit you from obtaining a whistleblower award, but the statute does address people who planned and initiated the fraud. If the court and/or the DOJ find that the relator planned and initiated the violation, you may have a whistleblower reward reduced if the relator/whistleblower is convicted of criminal conduct arising from the violation, the relator is dismissed from the civil action and receives nothing. That means participation is not just one thing. Participation may have multiple meanings and you need to sort that out early. For example, a billing clerk who followed instructions is not the same as an executive who designed and profited handsomely from the scheme. A coder who later realized diagnoses were unsupported is not the same as person who ordered the manipulation and was paid per claim. A salesperson pressured to follow a script is not the same as the person who wrote the fraudulent script and directly economically benefits from it. The key is to separate casual, passive, or even active involvement from leadership and direct profit per scheme under the False Claims Act. Now, let's look to see whether you're eligible for an SEC whistleblower award if you're part of the scheme. SEC cases can involve public company fraud, accounting manipulation, misleading investor disclosures, insider trading, market manipulation, crypto fraud, FCPA issues, Ponzi schemes, and investment adviser misconduct. The SEC rules culpability when determining awards. Culpability can reduce the award. So can unreasonable delays and interference with internal compliance systems. And SEC whistleblower status is not immunity. If you violated the securities law, becoming a whistleblower does not automatically protect you from SEC action. This is a critical point. A whistleblower submission is not an immunity agreement. Now, we're going to look at whether or not you're eligible for an IRS whistleblower award if you participated in that scheme. IRS cases are submitted through form 211. They may involve offshore accounts, hidden income, sham deductions, abusive tax shelters, payroll tax fraud, transfer pricing manipulation, crypto concealment, tax underpayments, or any of the thousand ways people deprive the federal government of money wrongfully when they're owed taxes. The IRS has its own version of the same issue. Did the whistleblower plan and initiate the action that led to the underpayment? If so, the award can be reduced. If the person is convicted of criminal conduct arising from their role, the award can be denied. That's a common theme in all these programs. But IRS guidance also draws a meaningful line. A junior employee acting under the direction and control of a senior employee is not the same as someone who designed or launched the tax scheme. So, the extent of the role in the tax scheme is very important to flush out to determine number one eligibility for award and number two, whether or not there's criminal exposure. CFTC and AML cases have similar themes to see if people are eligible for awards if they're committing some of the conduct. The CFTC rules consider culpability, scienter, financial benefit delay, and interference with compliance systems. FinCEN and AML cases can involve transaction monitoring, sanction steering, KYC, SAR decisions, suspicious transfers, shell companies, and money laundering. If you participated in clearing alerts or approving the transactions, that does not automatically mean you don't have a whistleblower path, but it does mean your role must be evaluated before you report. Now, I want to talk about something that applies to all the programs, immunity. A lot of people think if I blow the whistle, I receive immunity. That's just wrong. A whistleblower reward track and a criminal cooperation agreement and track are just two different things. The reward track is about voluntarily providing original useful information that leads to a successful enforcement action. The Protection Act may involve a proffer, cooperation presentation, voluntary self-disclosure, non-prosecution discussion, or some sort of criminal defense strategy that you're providing information so you won't go to jail. These tracks can overlap, but they're definitely not the same. And sometimes they conflict. If you're seeking immunity or leniency because you're afraid of prosecution, the government may view your testimony as cooperation motivated by avoiding criminal consequences. That does not make your information useless. In fact, it may make it integral to the investigation, but it may not look like a clean voluntary whistleblower submission cuz the objective is not to obtain award. The objective is stay out of jail. That's why the first legal question you should ask is not how much money can I receive by blowing the whistle. The first question you should ask and your whistleblower attorney should ask is, "How do I protect myself while potentially preserving an award path?" So, protection is first. Always use protection and a good whistleblower attorney will go over your protection. Here's the practical involvement ladder. Level one, minimal involvement. You processed records or followed routine instructions without even understanding the fraud. Level two, a concerned, more conscious employee. You suspected something was wrong but continued under pressure or direction. Level three, knowing participant. You understood key facts, but you still helped carry out part of the scheme. Level four, manager or approver. You signed off, supervised, certified, coded, billed, approved, or directed parts of the conduct. Level five, planner or initiator. You helped design the fraud, launched the misconduct. Level six, obstruction. This is a big one for the eyes of the government. You destroyed evidence, altered records, lied, concealed documents, or interfered with investigators. And on all levels, they want to see how much and how often you directly benefited from the fraud. As you move up that ladder, your exposure increases. It's not a ladder you want to climb. That doesn't always eliminate whistleblower options, but makes your legal strategy critical. So, what should you do? Build a timeline. Separate what you know from what you suspect. Identify who directed the conduct, identify what documents exist, preserve lawful evidence in your possession. Do not, and I repeat, do not destroy, alter, or hide anything. Do not lie. Do not take privileged or unauthorized documents. Don't call the regulators alone because if you have exposure, you may be the one who this is hung on. Do not assume internal reporting is safe. A lot of times they're going to blame you for the conduct and fire you. Do not wait until someone blames you first and do not assume that participation automatically ends your option. A serious whistleblower matter is not just about reporting fraud, it's also about protecting the whistleblower. A focused whistleblower law firm should evaluate five things before anything is filed. Front and center, first, your exposure. Next, the correct program to file it in. Then evaluate the evidence, the disclosure strategy, and the award and cooperation issues to plot the case in its entirety. If your own conduct could be questioned, obtain advice before making the next move. The right strategy can protect you, the wrong first move can make a bad situation worse and damn you. If you have credible information about fraud but are worried you were involved, contact Brown LLC for a free confidential case evaluation before reporting, filing, or moving records, or destroying anything. That may be the difference between obtaining an award or going to jail.

metadata.title: Qui Tam Basics: What is a Qui Tam Lawsuit
metadata.author: Lockaby PLLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Tune in as Amanda guides you through the basics of a whistleblower lawsuit to recover funds fraudulently obtained from the government, also known as a Qui Tam lawsuit. 

She’ll explain how these cases work and why they matter. Using her personal experiences with these cases, Amanda offers insights into the real-world application of these lawsuits.

Whether you're new to the topic or want to learn more, this video is a great primer. 

Follow us on socials!

Instagram: www.instagram.com/lockaby_pllc   
LinkedIn: www.linkedin.com/lockaby-pllc   
Website: www.LockabyLaw.com 

Subscribe to our newsletter!
http://eepurl.com/hOJJNz
