metadata.title: What Makes a Strong Whistleblower Case? Brown, LLC Explains
metadata.author: Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
If you've witnessed fraud against the government, one of the hardest questions is whether your case is strong enough to actually move forward. In this video, Brown, LLC managing partner Jason T. Brown, walks through the framework the firm uses to evaluate whistleblower and qui tam cases, so you can understand what makes a case strong before you ever pick up the phone.

Brown, LLC is built on former Department of Justice alumni, including a former senior trial counsel from the DOJ unit that prosecutes False Claims Act cases nationwide. The firm has been ranked by Lex Machina as one of the most prolific False Claims Act firms, its cases have helped the government recover over a billion dollars, and it represents whistleblowers coast to coast and worldwide.

You'll learn the six factors that shape a strong case: whether you're an insider or an outsider, how the scale of the damages trades off against the strength of the proof, why facts beat theories under Rule 9(b), why your own credibility as a whistleblower matters so much, how geography and jurisdiction come into play, and which whistleblower programs the firm focuses on.

Chapters:
00:00 - What we look for in a whistleblower case
00:41 - Who we are: former FBI and DOJ insiders
01:45 - Factor 1: Insider vs. outsider knowledge
02:52 - Factor 2: Damages and the sliding scale
04:10 - Factor 3: Facts over theories (Rule 9(b))
05:18 - Factor 4: You, the whistleblower
06:53 - Factor 5: Geography and jurisdiction
07:47 - Factor 6: The type of whistleblower case
09:00 - The framework in a nutshell
09:20 - First-to-file and free confidential consultation

Have information about fraud against the government? Whistleblower laws generally follow a first-to-file rule. The first relator to file can block everyone behind them, so timing matters. Contact Brown, LLC for a free, confidential consultation:
Website: https://ifightforyourrights.com/
Phone: (877) 561-0000

Disclaimer: This video is attorney advertising and is for informational purposes only. It does not constitute legal advice, and viewing it does not create an attorney-client relationship. Past results do not guarantee future outcomes. Every case depends on its own facts.

#Whistleblower #QuiTam #FalseClaimsAct #WhistleblowerRights #FraudAgainstGovernment #BrownLLC

segments.text: How a whistleblower firm selects what
whistleblower cases to litigate. Over
the years, people have offered millions
of dollars in potential fees up front
and on the back end to take potential
whistleblower cases, and we've said no.
We turn down the overwhelming majority
of cases that come through our door. Not
because they aren't real problems, a lot
of times they are, but because a
whistleblower case is a years-long war,
and we only like to go to war when we
think we're going to win it, and with a
client who is worthy. But, just because
we take it, it doesn't guarantee any
result because more fail than succeed,
unfortunately. But, today, I'm going to
walk you through a little about how we
decide what whistleblower cases we are
going to litigate. I'm Jason T. Brown.
I'm the founding partner of Brown LLC.
Before I had the privilege and honor of
representing individuals in private
practice, I also had the great privilege
and honor of serving the country as an
FBI special agent and a legal adviser.
And I did some great work, and the teams
did great back work back then. Our
current firm, Brown LLC, is built on
former Department of Justice alumni,
including another partner who spent
years as a senior trial counsel in the
Department of Justice unit that
prosecutes False Claims Act cases
nationwide. We've been ranked by Lex
Machina as one of the most prolific
False Claims Act firms in the world, if
not the country, and our cases have
helped the government recover over a
billion dollars. But again, past results
do not guarantee future success. But, we
love to succeed. We handle these cases,
these whistleblower cases, coast to
coast and worldwide on contingency,
which means we only are paid if we
succeed, which is why we're extremely
selective. Every case we take, we're
invested in it with our own money, our
time, our years, and we are aligned with
your interest. So, here's the framework
we look at. First question we ask is,
are you an insider or an outsider? An
insider is an employee, an executive, a
billing manager, a compliance officer,
someone who has personal knowledge about
the scheme and the scam the wrongdoing.
You saw the meetings, you have the
emails, you know where the bodies are
buried, and more importantly, you can
point to where those bodies are buried,
and you could help prove it. You don't
need to prove it right away, but you
need to show the government that you
can. The False Claims Act has what's
called a public disclosure bar. If the
fraud is already out there in the public
domain, your case can get dismissed
unless you qualify as an original source
with independent material knowledge.
Insiders usually clear that bar. They
also help us develop the case and let us
plead it properly. Outsiders often do
not. Now, outsider cases certainly can
work. Analysts who reverse engineer
fraud from data, data miners,
competitors who see rigged bidding or
customs fraud. We've evaluated cases
like that, we've taken them, and even
settled them, but the burden is much
heavier, and we underwrite them much
more skeptically unless you have insight
and visibility to the scheme in its
entirety. The second thing we look at is
damages, and let me be candid with you.
Our firm fortunately is in extremely
high stratospheric demand, and as a
general rule, we're looking for cases
where the fraud against the government
exceeds $10 million.
Under the False Claims Act, damages are
trebled and penalties attached to each
false claim, so a $10 million fraud is a
serious case for the government and a
potential meaningful recovery for the
whistleblower. We also look to make sure
the defendant is solvent, but here's the
nuance. And when I say 10 million,
that's 10 million pre-trebling,
pre-doubling of the damages, 10 million
in actual damages. But it's very
nuanced. Damages and liability sit for
us on a sliding scale. The bigger the
damages, the more extensive the possible
damages are, the more challenging the
liability picture we can accept. A
billion-dollar fraud may be worth
fighting through a hard proof problems,
but on the flip side, the tighter the
liability, the crisper the proof, the
inside visibility, and the ease of
making the case, the lower the damages
we'll consider. So, a smaller case with
a smoking gun document can beat a giant
case on inference for our evaluation.
However, a giant case with a good theory
with an insider we'll look at pretty
hard. Don't self-reject cuz you think
your number's too small. Tell us the
number, tell us how you got there, show
us the proof, and we'll do the math.
Third, and this is where most cases die.
Facts versus theories. People call us
all the time saying, "I think my
company's defrauding Medicare." And it's
worthy of a call. But when they say it's
just a theory versus here are the
patient files, here are the billing
codes, here are the dates, and here's
the email where the director told us to
upcode, well, we know that's the case.
I'm not saying for you to go ahead and
gather documents on your own. You should
make sure you consult with an attorney
and make sure you're legally, ethically,
and lawfully have access to documents
before you forward them to us. Federal
fraud cases are pled under Rule 9B,
which requires particularity. The five
W's, who, what, when, where, and fifth W
has a W at the end, how. Courts dismiss
whistleblower complaints every week
because the relator had a just a strong
suspicion, but is weak on the specifics.
Details, details, details, details. I
said that a lot because details are
important. When you contact us, the
single most valuable thing you can do is
name things specifically. Names, dates,
amounts, documents you lawfully possess.
As a former FBI agent, I'll tell you
what every investigator knows. Cases
aren't just built on outrage, not based
on just theory, they're built on
evidence. Fourth criteria we evaluate is
you, the whistleblower. We only work
with people who we generally want to
work with. That's not a slogan. Over the
years, we've walked away from probably
hundreds of millions of dollars in
potential fees because the client wasn't
someone we could stand next to for 5
years. No amount of money will make us
deliberately take on a difficult
plaintiff. People offer us money up
front, we will not do that if we don't
want to work with you. We deal with
challenging adversaries every single
day. Fortune 500 defense teams, top 10
defense teams, or armies of billable
attorneys and hours who constantly
multiply. We have to confront and combat
them. We don't want problems from the
inside, too. And here's an uncomfortable
truth. In litigation, the
whistleblower's credibility is the case
at times. The government will vet you
before it vets the defendant. If your
story shifts, if you can't take
counsel's advice, if you're pursuing in
vendetta instead of the truth, a jury
will feel it and so will the Department
of Justice. They'll evaluate whether
they're going to intervene or not. And
if you don't come across as unlikable
and inconsistent, they probably won't
take the case. Nobody ever calls us
thinking they're a difficult client. We
do the assessment for both of us
honestly at the start. The
whistleblowers we represent are people
of integrity who saw something wrong and
want it fixed. That's who typically
wins, somebody with a noble heart. I'll
tell you outright, if you're mean to our
intake staff, which some people are for
some reason, we just won't take your
case. If you demand that you only speak
with me, we won't take your case. We're
a firm. The firm is an extension of me.
If you follow the golden rule and treat
others like you want to be treated, we
will consider your case. A fifth factor
is geography. While we do litigate all
over the country and the world,
sometimes in conjunction with local
counsel at no additional expense to you,
not every courthouse and district is
created equally. Circuits split on key
False Claims Act doctrines. Judges
differ in how they apply Rule 9B, how
they treat the public disclosure bar,
how they handle motions to dismiss, how
they handle customs fraud, how they
handle PPP loan fraud. From an outsider
perspective, all those are important to
us. Some United States Attorneys Offices
are very aggressive on fraud, others are
stretched thin. Where a case can be
filed and where it should be filed is a
strategic decision we make with decades
of federal experience, including from
the inside, including me. I have 30
years experience and we have people like
such as Tom Morris with even more. So,
if you're in a smaller state or a
tougher circuit, that's not
disqualifying, it's just a variable we
are going to factor in. Six, the type of
whistleblower case. We primarily
concentrate on bounty programs, the
False Claims Act, the SEC whistleblower
program, IRS, CFTC, and the newer

that reward the whistleblower with a

recovers. And there where our federal
experience creates the most leverage and

the government. We unfortunately rarely

harm, you may have a case. But if your
case includes retaliation on top of
fraud, which often does, we factor it
in. But an individual retaliation case,
based upon high demand we are, it's rare
for us to handle. But if it's an
individual retaliation case, based on
how busy we are, it's rare for us to
handle, but not unheard of. But if you
call us, we may have some ideas and we
may also be able to evaluate whether you

program. If you listen this far and if
some of your situation, you're trying to

Whistleblower laws generally have a

metadata.title: What’s the #1 Thing a Whistleblower Should Do? #whistleblower
metadata.author: Brown, LLC - A Premier Whistleblower Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
If you’re thinking about blowing the whistle on fraud against the government—whether it’s Medicare fraud, procurement fraud, PPP loan fraud, tax fraud, securities fraud or another scheme—the most important decision you make can determine whether your case succeeds or fails—and if it succeeds, just how successful it will be.
In this video, former FBI Special Agent Jason T. Brown of the nationally recognized whistleblower law firm Brown, LLC reveals the single most important step every whistleblower must take to protect themselves and maximize their chances of success under the False Claims Act and other whistleblower laws.
With a proven track record in high-stakes litigation and hundreds of millions recovered through whistleblower programs, Brown, LLC is one of the nation’s premier law firms for those ready to speak up and fight fraud. Contact Brown, LLC for a free and confidential consultation at (877) 561-0000 or visit https://ifightforyourrights.com/whistleblower-lawyer/

Disclaimer: No attorney-client relationship is established by watching this video. This video is for informational purposes only and should not be taken as legal advice. This may be considered attorney advertising.

metadata.title: False Claims Act and Other Risks of Non Compliance
metadata.author: CMMC LaunchPad
metadata.shortDescription:
This session examines the legal, financial, and operational risks associated with CMMC non-compliance, with particular focus on exposure under the False Claims Act (FCA).

As CMMC requirements become embedded in DoD solicitations and contracts, inaccurate certifications, unsupported self-assessments, or misrepresentation of compliance status can create significant liability. This briefing explains how cybersecurity attestations intersect with FCA enforcement, recent enforcement trends, and how seemingly minor documentation or scoping errors can escalate into material risk.

Topics include:

How CMMC and DFARS representations can trigger FCA liability
Common compliance failures that lead to enforcement action
The role of documentation, evidence, and internal controls in risk mitigation
Practical steps to reduce exposure while maintaining contract eligibility

This session is designed for executives, compliance leaders, and risk owners who need a clear-eyed understanding of what is at stake—and how disciplined compliance programs protect not only contracts, but the organization itself.

metadata.title: The Secret Law That Pays You 30% to Expose Corporate Fraud (False Claims Act Deep Dive)
metadata.author: Against The Fraud
metadata.shortDescription:
💰 $6.8 BILLION recovered. One law. Everyday people as the weapon.

What if you could legally pocket up to $30 million just for reporting fraud you already know about at work? That's not clickbait. That's the False Claims Act, and it's one of the most powerful anti-fraud tools in U.S. history.

In this video, we break down exactly how whistleblowing works, why the government needs ordinary citizens to protect taxpayer money, and what happens when someone decides to speak up.

📌 WHAT YOU WILL LEARN:
- What the False Claims Act actually is and why fraudsters are terrified of it
- Who qualifies as a whistleblower (hint: you do not need to be a lawyer)
- The most common healthcare fraud schemes: upcoding, unbundling, and illegal kickbacks
- How the secret court docket works and why cases stay hidden for years
- The first-to-file rule and why timing is everything
- How whistleblowers legally earn 15 to 30% of billions recovered

🔗 RESOURCES:
DOJ False Claims Act Info: justice.gov/civil/false-claims-act
Find a Qui Tam Attorney: search "FCA whistleblower attorney" in your state

🔔 Subscribe for more explainers on the legal systems that shape your money and your rights.

powerful law called the False Claims
Act. This is the government's absolute
primary anti-fraud weapon, and frankly,

here's why. It doesn't just politely ask

treble damages. That means if you get
caught, you have to pay back triple the

plus some extremely heavy penalties for
every single false claim. It's basically

system.

that brings us to part one, the inside
man, and decoding qui tam
whistleblowers. Let's look at how the

Act has its roots all the way back in
1863. Right in the middle of the Civil
War, they passed this to stop corrupt
military suppliers from ripping off the
Union Army. And baked into it is this
ancient legal concept known as qui tam.
It's Latin and it roughly translates to
he who brings a case on behalf of our
Lord the King as well as for himself.
Basically, it means a completely private
citizen is legally allowed to step
directly into the shoes of the
government to sue these fraudsters.
In the legal world, this insider is
officially known as a relator. And the
wild thing is, they are usually just
everyday ordinary employees. We're
talking about the accountant crunching

unsecured servers. They don't even need

the secret spreadsheets. They are the

Okay, so what exactly are these relators
uncovering? Let's move right into part
two, the ultimate scams and follow the
stolen tax dollars. Healthcare fraud is
by far the biggest offender we see here.
Out of that record $6.8 billion
recovered in 2025, over 5.7 billion of
it was related to the healthcare
industry. And that brings us to one of
the absolute most common schemes out
there, which is called upcoding.
Here's how it works in practice. A
patient might be given a completely
standard, cheap, manual wheelchair. But
on the books, the provider turns around
and bills Medicare for a vastly more
expensive, top-of-the-line
power-assisted wheelchair. They just
pocket the massive difference and the
taxpayer completely foots the bill.
Then, we have something called
unbundling. Normally, certain medical
procedures are supposed to be billed
together as a single cheaper package,
like a bundle. But unbundling is this

into staggered, piecemeal bills. It's
kind of like a dealership charging you
separately for the steering wheel, the
tires, and the engine when you're just
trying to buy a single car. The end
result? A much, much higher, totally
fraudulent payout from Medicare. And
guys, it gets even wilder. There are
laws, specifically the Anti-Kickback
Statute and the Stark Law, that strictly
prohibit medical providers from paying
or receiving anything of value in
exchange for patient referrals. But
companies get incredibly creative to get
around this. For instance, a spinal
device company called Innovasis recently
settled for $12 million after they
allegedly bribed orthopedic surgeons
with luxury ski trips. Another
pharmaceutical company, US WorldMed,
paid $17.5 million for a kickback scheme
that actually included handing out
Kentucky Derby tickets. I mean, it's
crazy. These lavish bribes totally
clouded doctors' medical judgment, and
they drive up costs for all of us. But
hey, it isn't just doctors and hospitals
gaming the system. Contractor fraud is a
massive drain on our resources, and
honestly, a huge threat to national
security. Prime defense contractors have
literally been caught billing the
government for ghost services, work that
never happened. They've been caught
cross-charging expenses from their
commercial clients onto government
contracts, and critically, failing to
comply with really strict cybersecurity
and security clearance requirements.
Because of a contractor lies to the
government about securing sensitive data
in the cloud, yep, that is officially
submitting a false claim. So now that we
know what these crimes actually look
like, how do we go about catching them?
Welcome to part three, the covert
operation. Let's take a peek inside the
secret docket. Whenever a
whistleblower's attorney files a qui tam
lawsuit, it does not go on the public
record, not at all. On day one, the
complaint is filed under seal on a
secret court docket that's kept locked
down by the clerk of the court. The
paperwork is only given to the
Department of Justice and the specific
judge assigned to the case. The
defendant, they have absolutely no idea
they're even being sued. By law, it has
to stay completely hidden for at least
60 days. But in reality, this stretches
into months or even years as the
government requests ongoing extensions.
Actually, most successful cases stay
completely dark for at least 2 years
while the trap is being set. During
those years in the shadows, this
incredible covert operation takes place.

the FBI or postal inspectors,
meticulously investigates the relator's
claims. They issue subpoenas, they
review all the whistleblower's
disclosure statements, and they slowly
build the case.
Then, at the end of this whole process,
the government has to make a big choice.
They either intervene, which means they
officially step in and take over the
prosecution, or they decline.
And here's a fun fact for you.
The DOJ actually intervenes in fewer
than 25% of all filed qui tam actions.
And the reason for that is the
government strictly gatekeeps this
entire process. There's an internal DOJ
document known as the Granston memo, and
it outlines their unfettered authority
to just dismiss qui tam actions
entirely. If they look at a
whistleblower's lawsuit and decide it's
frivolous, lacks merit, or maybe it's
just a parasitic claim trying to ride
the coattails of an ongoing government
investigation, the DOJ will kill it
right there to preserve their limited
investigative resources. They absolutely
do not want opportunists draining the
public purse.
Okay, but what happens when the evidence
is rock solid, the fraud is proven, and
the government actually recovers
millions or even billions of dollars?
That brings us to part four, the big
payoff, and the reality of the
whistleblower financial reward.
So, the absolutely crucial point here is
the math. Congress knew they had to
highly incentivize people to take the
immense personal and professional risks
required to actually blow the whistle.
It's a scary thing to do. So, when a qui
tam action is successful, the
whistleblower gets to take home a slice
of the pie, ranging anywhere between 15
to 30% of the total government recovery.
And remember that massive $6.8 billion
number? well, in fiscal year 2025, over
$5.3 billion of that came directly from
these qui tam suits. So, to put that in
perspective, if a company settles for
$100 million,
the insider who brought that case could
legally walk away with up to $30
million. But, before you go running off
to the courthouse, there is a catch, and
it is a really big one. The False Claims
Act has a very strict first-to-file
rule. This means that literally no other

on those same underlying facts. Only the

the fraud to the government is legally
entitled to recover that monetary award.
It is a literal race to the DOJ. If your
coworker figures it out and beats you to
the punch by even a single day, they get
the millions and you get absolutely
nothing. So, absolute urgency is
required. Which brings us to the final
and perhaps the most important question
for all of us. Look at the organizations
around you. Pay attention to the billing
practices, the quiet kickbacks, the

contracts. The reality is the government

protect our tax dollars. So, I'll leave
you with this. Are you sitting on a
billion-dollar secret?
Thanks so much for joining me for this
explainer. Until next time, keep your
eyes open and keep learning.

Let's move right into part two, the ultimate scams and follow the stolen tax dollars. Healthcare fraud is by far the biggest offender we see here. Out of that record $6.8 billion recovered in 2025, over 5.7 billion of it was related to the healthcare industry. And that brings us to one of the absolute most common schemes out there, which is called upcoding. Here's how it works in practice. A patient might be given a completely standard, cheap, manual wheelchair. But on the books, the provider turns around and bills Medicare for a vastly more expensive, top-of-the-line power-assisted wheelchair. They just pocket the massive difference and the taxpayer completely foots the bill. Then, we have something called unbundling. Normally, certain medical procedures are supposed to be billed together as a single cheaper package, like a bundle. But unbundling is this really sneaky manipulation where a provider breaks that one service down into staggered, piecemeal bills. It's kind of like a dealership charging you separately for the steering wheel, the tires, and the engine when you're just trying to buy a single car. The end result? A much, much higher, totally fraudulent payout from Medicare. And guys, it gets even wilder. There are laws, specifically the Anti-Kickback Statute and the Stark Law, that strictly prohibit medical providers from paying or receiving anything of value in exchange for patient referrals. But companies get incredibly creative to get around this. For instance, a spinal device company called Innovasis recently settled for $12 million after they allegedly bribed orthopedic surgeons with luxury ski trips. Another pharmaceutical company, US WorldMed, paid $17.5 million for a kickback scheme that actually included handing out Kentucky Derby tickets. I mean, it's crazy. These lavish bribes totally clouded doctors' medical judgment, and they drive up costs for all of us. But hey, it isn't just doctors and hospitals gaming the system. Contractor fraud is a massive drain on our resources, and honestly, a huge threat to national security. Prime defense contractors have literally been caught billing the government for ghost services, work that never happened. They've been caught cross-charging expenses from their commercial clients onto government contracts, and critically, failing to comply with really strict cybersecurity and security clearance requirements. Because of a contractor lies to the government about securing sensitive data in the cloud, yep, that is officially submitting a false claim. So now that we know what these crimes actually look like, how do we go about catching them? Welcome to part three, the covert operation. Let's take a peek inside the secret docket. Whenever a whistleblower's attorney files a qui tam lawsuit, it does not go on the public record, not at all. On day one, the complaint is filed under seal on a secret court docket that's kept locked down by the clerk of the court. The paperwork is only given to the Department of Justice and the specific judge assigned to the case. The defendant, they have absolutely no idea they're even being sued. By law, it has to stay completely hidden for at least 60 days. But in reality, this stretches into months or even years as the government requests ongoing extensions. Actually, most successful cases stay completely dark for at least 2 years while the trap is being set. During those years in the shadows, this incredible covert operation takes place. The DOJ, working alongside agencies like the FBI or postal inspectors, meticulously investigates the relator's claims. They issue subpoenas, they review all the whistleblower's disclosure statements, and they slowly build the case. Then, at the end of this whole process, the government has to make a big choice. They either intervene, which means they officially step in and take over the prosecution, or they decline. And here's a fun fact for you. The DOJ actually intervenes in fewer than 25% of all filed qui tam actions. And the reason for that is the government strictly gatekeeps this entire process. There's an internal DOJ document known as the Granston memo, and it outlines their unfettered authority to just dismiss qui tam actions entirely. If they look at a whistleblower's lawsuit and decide it's frivolous, lacks merit, or maybe it's just a parasitic claim trying to ride the coattails of an ongoing government investigation, the DOJ will kill it right there to preserve their limited investigative resources. They absolutely do not want opportunists draining the public purse. Okay, but what happens when the evidence is rock solid, the fraud is proven, and the government actually recovers millions or even billions of dollars? That brings us to part four, the big payoff, and the reality of the whistleblower financial reward. So, the absolutely crucial point here is the math. Congress knew they had to highly incentivize people to take the immense personal and professional risks required to actually blow the whistle. It's a scary thing to do. So, when a qui tam action is successful, the whistleblower gets to take home a slice of the pie, ranging anywhere between 15 to 30% of the total government recovery. And remember that massive $6.8 billion number? well, in fiscal year 2025, over $5.3 billion of that came directly from these qui tam suits. So, to put that in perspective, if a company settles for $100 million, the insider who brought that case could legally walk away with up to $30 million. But, before you go running off to the courthouse, there is a catch, and it is a really big one. The False Claims Act has a very strict first-to-file rule. This means that literally no other person can bring a related action based on those same underlying facts. Only the absolute first whistleblower to report the fraud to the government is legally entitled to recover that monetary award. It is a literal race to the DOJ. If your coworker figures it out and beats you to the punch by even a single day, they get the millions and you get absolutely nothing. So, absolute urgency is required. Which brings us to the final and perhaps the most important question for all of us. Look at the organizations around you. Pay attention to the billing practices, the quiet kickbacks, the corners being cut on major government contracts. The reality is the government relies entirely on the courage and the insider knowledge of everyday people to protect our tax dollars. So, I'll leave you with this. Are you sitting on a billion-dollar secret? Thanks so much for joining me for this explainer. Until next time, keep your eyes open and keep learning.

metadata.title: How the False Claims Act transforms CyberSecurity Non-compliance Risks into Fraud against the US Gov
metadata.author: Blue Ocean Law Group. innovative Counsel [iC]
metadata.shortDescription:
This video provides a timely warning to all US Federal Government Contractors who have not met cybersecurity requirements under US Federal Government contracts since 2017.

It also addresses some US State Government Contractors and any merger or acquisition parties that have purchased a US Government Contractor with existing or historical cyber gaps or breaches that have not been identified, or if identified, no safe harbor protections have been invoked.

Under the Federal False Claims Act (FCA), each potential false claim can result in a civil penalty of up to $28,619 in 2025, plus three times the amount of damages (treble damages) the government sustains.

The Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative Catalyst

"While the 2017 deadline created the legal baseline, it was the 2021 launch of the Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative that began aggressively prosecuting gaps that had existed since that 2017 window. 

For example, a 2025 settlement involving Health Net Federal Services for $11.25 million specifically targeted false certifications made between 2015 and 2018, capturing the period immediately surrounding the 2017 implementation deadline.

In summary, 2017 is the "trigger year" because it was the moment the government stopped asking for progress and started demanding verified implementation of the NIST controls. Any invoice submitted since then by a non-compliant contractor potentially constitutes a false claim."

This post is also a call to action for whistleblowers. If you are aware of any cyber gaps, false cyber certifications, or failures to report cyber breaches that can be prosecuted as fraud against the US Federal Government (or US State Government where a state False Claims Act applies), we encourage you to privately contact us. Financial rewards under one of the False Claims Acts may be available for those who come forward.

The cover infographic and the video were generated using Google's NotebookLM.

#cybersecurity  #Mergers #Acquisitions #whistleblowers #falseclaims #quitam #fraud #usa #legal #law #riskmanagement #corporategovernance

What are ways companies can violate the FCA with regard to cybersecurity?
What are some examples of FCA matters involving cybersecurity?
What can companies do to avoid cybersecurity FCA liability?

metadata.shortDescription:
With its chaotic rollout, conflicting regulations, and breakneck disbursements, the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) is primed to create a wave of litigation. This includes actions taken under the False Claims Act (FCA), which sets penalties for anyone who knowingly submits a false claim for money to the federal government. Small business borrowers face potential FCA liability exposure during the PPP application and forgiveness process, so it is imperative that they learn to manage this risk.

This webinar covers key information on avoiding FCA liability under the PPP, including:

• top avenues for FCA liability exposure in the PPP;
• tips for mitigating risk; and
• steps for forming a contingency plan in case there is an allegation of fraud.

Disclaimer: This communication does not provide legal advice, nor does it create an attorney-client relationship with you or any other viewer. If you require legal guidance in any specific situation, you should engage a qualified lawyer for that purpose. Prior results do not guarantee a similar outcome. 

Attorney Advertising: It is possible that under the laws, rules, or regulations of certain jurisdictions, this may be construed as an advertisement or solicitation.

metadata.title: Trump administration looks to False Claims Act to curb cybersecurity violations
metadata.author: Federal News Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Over the past year, there’s been a major uptick in the government’s use of the False Claims Act to take companies to task for cybersecurity violations. The Trump administration has announced six separate False Claims Act settlements. And enforcement has been especially aggressive for companies who do business with the Defense Department. Sara McLean is a former assistant director of the fraud section in the Justice Department’s Commercial Litigation Branch. She talked with Federal News Network’s Jason Miller about the enforcement trend.

October was a big month in this space. So within basically one week um in October DOJ and HHS gave healthcare companies a clear way to come forward um in two different you know environments. The first is this criminal path where a company disclosing possible criminal healthcare conduct um can now go straight to this uh National Fraud Enforcement Division um that Jennifer was just speaking to. And that one disclosure now if you go straight to the NFED for potential criminal conduct can give uh a company kind of credit under both the corporate enforcement policy and for DOJ as well as HHS OIG self-disclosure protocol because I think um for a while companies were trying to do both or not knowing which one to go to first or feeling like oh I have a pending OIG SDP but now there's a criminal case. Um so this now gives kind of a clearer path forward for criminal disclosure um and you know OIG has also updated its protocol to say that's where criminal matters go when you're disclosing. Um the other announcement that followed about a week later was this civil pilot. Um it's the first kind of False Claims Act disclosure program that has now really set kind of clear um parameters around what to expect for for what your repayments going to look like. Um this is a pilot program. So right now we're about a little less than a month into it. Submissions though are due by April 22nd, 2027 and they can't be kind of incomplete or pending. They're treating that at least right now as a hard deadline. Um but what's most interesting about this pilot is that they're saying that repayment is going to be kind of set at the 1.25 to 1.6 times you know the the base amount. So a 1.25 to 1.6 x or multiplier. Um and you might be wondering well how do I know you know that's still a pretty big range. Um they're saying that kind of the factors considered will be timeliness duration and scope of you know the misconduct um senior leadership involvement the extent to which there was kind of a an actual financial benefit to the company and um whether the company is an acquirer that inherited the conduct and then promptly remediated. So it's kind of thinking about this in the transaction or something that was identified in a diligence um period. And uh another benefit of this pilot program is that there will be no factual admissions. So it's not like kind of in your when you're typically settling directly with the US attorney's office and there's kind of a scope of facts. Um so they're not requiring factual admissions uh and also there will be no CIA agreement requirement and no CMPs civil monetary penalties or um revocations sought. So this does actually really coordinate also with with OIG on that front um whereas in the past you sometimes had to to kind of manage both DOJ and OIG for that purpose. Um and the release then would cover the FCA plus Medicare revocation and OIG's permissive exclusive exclusion authorities. Um next slide please. So one thing to think about, um because um I think this particularly arises in the anti-kickback statute um environment and considering that is kind of the basis for the potential False Claims Act um is that they are going to be using um uh remuneration as the um kind of basis for the calculation for an AKS violation, which I think typically is not the case, right? Like normally you're you have all of the um dollars paid, the claims paid, you know, at risk um in in the AKS False Claims Act um setting, but here for purposes of the self-disclosure and this pathway, they're saying that they um will skip kind of claims paid damages and set the base on the remuneration um and the revenue from the conduct and then as long as there's not kind of other factors, like if there's aggravating factors like patient harm, I think then then it might be um a different situation. Um the example that's given, if you look at kind of some of the the documents associated with the pilot program include um you know, private equity buyers and what they're identifying when they kind of take over a company or um and any legacy kickback conduct that um are is being disclosed post-closing. Uh you know, if the government already knows about it, there might still be some opportunity for cooperation credit, but you're no longer kind of getting to be a participant in the pilot program. Um just one other point kind of on on why particularly as it relates to if you have an anti-kickback statute violation, that's the basis for False Claims Act, why this pilot program might be beneficial to you. If look at some of kind of the recent um you know settlements and and cases out there, typically the settlements have been settling it looks like close to about the 2x mark. Um and you know we're also seeing that self-disclosures outside of the pilot program have included some pretty huge dollars. metadata.title: False Claims Act Defense Lawyers for Government Contractors
metadata.author: Theodore Watson
metadata.shortDescription:
How To Avoid Criminal Penalties? What is the Federal False Claims Act and How to Minimize Criminal Liability In Federal Government Contracts. Watson Federal False Claims Act Defense Lawyers. 

If you are a federal government contractor that is facing a potential or actual false claims act whistleblower charge, you want to quickly assess the reality of what the government is really going after. There is no doubt that in recent years false claims charges have escalated and the DOJ is more actively involved than ever before. You could be facing potential jail time and harsh financial false claims penalties.
This short video covers the three most important points when dealing with a federal false claims act whistleblower charge:

1. Dealing with imminent charges under the criminal false claims act
• Whether you are a contractor or an individual, you want to immediately assess the facts of your case to find out the strengths and weaknesses of the government’s case. 
• This step can save you tens of thousands in unnecessary attorney fees
Most Qui Tam Lawsuit defendants miss this part and then find themselves playing from behind  and thus giving the government a clear advantages

2. Do the Government’s Qui Tam Lawsuit Attorneys Really Understand the Underlying Rules?
• This is very important when companies are charged for violating SBA and small business program rules
• If you are charged with a government contract or procurement violations, do you have an attorney that really understands the landmines that can blow your case wide open?
(Narrative- Rules under the federal small business program are very complex and have a variety of nuances that even the federal prosecutors are not fully aware of? There are many cases where defendants have been convicted without the detailed representation they needed.

• Develop Internal Policies and Controls to Help Avoid Federal False Claims Penalties When you take the time to develop meaningful internal policies and controls, it says a lot about your company when a criminal case comes about
• Having these policies in place can mitigate the outcome of your case
• Having internal policies in place can certainly help if there are suspension and debarment proceedings
3. Be Transparent With the Government
During the performance of the contract and you find something that can lead to potential false claims act charges or liability under criminal law, you want to immediately bring it up to the government. This goes over and beyond any mandatory disclosure requirements. Even if your company has to spend money and resources retaining counsel to help you with these issues or avoid criminal penalties, it certainly beats your having your reputation being tarnished or even going through embarrassing criminal lawsuits that can impact the company’s future. For help defending a federal false claims case or implementing policies and controls to avoid criminal charges, contact Watson & Associates, LLC False Claims Act lawyers at 1-866-601-5518 for FREE Initial Consultation.

metadata.title: Qui Tam Dismissals Are Spiking: What That Means for FCA Enforcement
metadata.author: Husch Blackwell
metadata.shortDescription:
Host Jonathan Porter (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/jonathan-porter)  welcomes Husch Blackwell’s Tanner Cook (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/tanner-cook)  back to the podcast to discuss the recent spike of DOJ dismissals of improper qui tams under 31 U.S.C. § 3730(c)(2)(A). This episode is a follow-up of our last podcast (https://www.huschblackwell.com/newsandinsights/false-claims-act-insights-doj-announces-record-number-of-qui-tams-and-qui-tam-dismissals) , in which Husch Blackwell partner Cormac Conner (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/cormac-connor)  discussed how qui tam dismissals increased by around 400% in 2025. 



We begin by addressing common misconceptions about how DOJ views its dismissal power, with its focus on process abuse rather than merit disputes. Next, we examine the Granston Memo, which outlines the Department of Justice's protocols for considering dismissal of qui tam actions on various grounds. 



Tanner then walks listeners through the details of considerations DOJ uses to assess qui tams for dismissal potential, with examples of the types of instances where DOJ has exercised its (c)(2)(A) dismissal power in the past. We end the discussion by examining what those who defend False Claims Act investigations and qui tams can learn from these recent developments and how to structure dismissal requests to maximize changes of DOJ action.



Jonathan Porter | Full Biography (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/jonathan-porter) 



Jonathan focuses on white collar criminal defense, federal investigations brought under the False Claims Act, and litigation against the government and whistleblowers. He draws on his experience as a former federal prosecutor to guide clients in sensitive and enterprise-threatening litigation. At the Department of Justice, Jonathan earned a reputation as a top white-collar prosecutor and trial lawyer and was a key member of multiple international healthcare fraud takedowns and high-profile financial crime prosecution teams. He serves as a vice chair of the American Health Law Association’s Fraud and Abuse Practice Group and teaches white collar crime as an adjunct professor of law at Mercer University School of Law.



Tanner Cook | Full Biography (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/tanner-cook) 



Based in St. Louis, Tanner is a member of Husch Blackwell’s Commercial Litigation group, focusing on consumer class actions, antitrust litigation, and multidistrict litigation. He frequently takes the lead in drafting critical pretrial briefs, including dispositive motions and evidentiary challenges. In addition to his commercial litigation practice, Tanner regularly assists on white collar defense matters, especially in the False Claims Act context. He has significant experience defending companies from qui tam whistleblower suits at every stage of the litigation process, combining his deep substantive knowledge of the law with creative defense strategies. Tanner served as law clerk at the U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Missouri, for Judge Sarah E. Pitlyk.

>> Thanks, Tanner. So, I previewed in the

Tanner, why don't you start us off by
giving us the big picture of what DOJ
looks for in dismissals. Yeah. So, at a
high level, DOJ will intervene in and
dismiss keys that somehow abuse the

little different than what us lawyers
typically mean when we say abuse the
process. Right? Ordinarily, when we
think of an abusive process, we think of
someone bringing a lawsuit for an

things like that. In the KAM dismissal
context, abuse of process seems
something more like undermining the

further the government's interests. So,

Now, one thing that I want to clarify is

likely just dispose of it at the

anyways. On the other hand, if it turns
out that the case actually does have
support, the government stands to
benefit. So when we're looking at key
dismissals by DOJ, we're looking at
certain defined criteria that focus on
whether the suit is undermining the
government's interests or initiatives.
And those criteria, you know, as we're
going to discuss, are laid out in what's
called the Granston memo, which is a
2018 memorandum from former Deputy
Assistant Attorney General Michael
Granston. Those criteria can be kind of
categorized as follows. So, first you've
got curbing meritless key TAMs. And that
might sound like its intention with what
I just said about questionable suits not
being candidates for dismissal, but
we'll explain actually why those aren't
intention. Second, the DOJ focuses on
preventing opportunistic or parasitic
keys. Third, it focuses on preventing
interference with agency policies and
programs. Fourth, it focuses on
controlling litigation brought on behalf
of the government. Fifth, it focuses on
safeguarding classified information or
national security interests. Sixth, it
focuses on preserving government
resources. And seventh, it focuses on
addressing egregious procedural errors.
So that's kind of the universe of
criteria for key dismissals. The memo
indicates that that's not an exhaustive
list, but in practice, those are the
ones that really come into play.
>> Thanks, Tanner. Any great lawyer knows
how to road map stuff, and you just gave
us an excellent road map, so thanks for
that. The big point that I want people
to understand upfront, Tanner, is you
don't go to DOJ and say, "Look, we think
our facts are better than their facts."
At least under the Grandstston memo,
DOJ's not going to dismiss a key just
because you think that your facts are a
little bit better than their facts.
DOJ's their policy is to look for some
actual impropriety, something wrong with
the kam itself that the courts might not

There's something different about DOJ
saying, "No, we're going to we're going
to do something that the courts aren't
designed to do. We're going to step in
and look at the process." And so that's
the big thing that I people mess that up
all the time. I can't tell you when I
was at DOJ how many times people came to
me asking, "Hey, we want you to dismiss
this kit because, you know, we think
that we're right." That's really not
what it's designed for. You got to fit
your request into one of these

by talking about some examples of these
categories that you just excellently
roadmap for us. And so, again, we're
taking these directly from the Grand
memo. And the first one that we want to
talk about is allegations that facially
lack merit. So Tanner, you talked about
the tension between these two things.
Why don't you explain this category for
us?
>> Yeah, absolutely. So I'll try to break
this down in a way that makes sense
because they do appear to be at odds
with each other, right? If the
government, you know, wants to curb
meritless key TAMs, but it's saying it
won't dismiss just because the case is
meritless. So we'll try to make sense of
that. So, this category is not for cases
where the relator fails to satisfy the
rule 9b heightened pleading standard or
cases where there's a good chance that
the relator's claims are barred by the
public disclosure bar. It's not any of
the cases where the defendant simply has
a good merits defense. These are cases
that on their face don't allege
something that fits within the FCA. So
in philosophical terms, it's what we
would call a category error, which is
when you assign something to a category
to which it does not belong. And the
best example of this is when a relator
names a government agency or official as
a defendant, right? DOJ has dismissed
kams against the Federal Reserve, for
example. And and that's because we're
looking for fraud on the government,
right? Not fraud by the government. The
government is not a proper defendant in
FCA cases. Another example that's
somewhat related is when the relators
allegations do not involve any federal
funds. Right? The misuse of federal
funds is an essential ingredient of FCA
claims. So if that's lacking, this it's
just it's simply not an FCA suit.
Finally, DOJ will occasionally dismiss
KAMS when its own investigation finds
conclusive evidence that the KAMS
allegations were factually incorrect.
That's exceedingly rare and it's
different than just telling DOJ, hey,
we're going to be able to prove that our
facts are right and we didn't do
anything wrong. DOJ is not going to take
that assurance, right? But if DOJ
conducts its own investigation, right?
If there's a a parallel investigation
that's ongoing and they find conclusive
evidence, sometimes they might step in
to intervene. So hopefully that resolves
any confusion over what is meant by
curbing meritless keys.
>> Thanks, Tener. And you mentioned the
philosophical approach. I appreciate
that. you're way ahead of me when it
comes to those types of things. But no,
I think what our listeners should know
here is this is for just a really
obvious glaring problem. There have been
keys that have named presidents before.
That's really not what kams are designed
to do. So that's what we're talking
about here is something that's super
obvious or something where when DOJ

DOJ's going to the relator and saying

they're not going to that's where DOJ
would step in because it is super clear
this is not something that should
proceed as a key tab. That's what that
means. And then Tener, thanks for
resolving the tension because I think
some people may read that and say,
"Okay, well, if I can convince DOJ that

then that's something." But it's very
different. It's very different from what
we may think of as as not meritorious.
So Sam, the next category is what the
Grandston memo calls parasitic kams.
What are those? So parasitic keams are
those that simply duplicate a
pre-existing government investigation
and that provide no useful information
beyond what the government already
knows. So an example of this would be
there was one where DOJ dismissed a
kitam against a financial institution
where the government had been
investigating this institution for
years. It was already pretty far into

rationale here makes sense, right?
government does not want to share its
recovery with the relator who really

lawsuit. To that end, you'll also see

the same defendant. And so what the

Branson memo refers to as parasitic
kabams. Thanks, Tanner. And this really
does happen. So, when agents are
investigating kams or false claims act
allegations that weren't started by kam,
they'll go out and they'll interview

They didn't really advance the

Gransson memo talks about. And so
Tanner, moving on. The Gransson memo

interfere with agency policies and
programs. Tanner, tell us about that
category. So this is an interesting

Similar example is the Wolf Creek case.

>> Yeah, like you said, T, this is probably
the one that we see the most and it's
because this one is a really fascinating
concept within the False Claims Act.
There are a lot of situations where
there are government actors who know
what's going on and the question is what

keys, a lot of false claims at cases

done something differently in response
to all of this? And it gets really
sticky when essentially you're using the
ketaman process to make a big change

And this I'll tell you this is the one
that is most interesting to me because
it's a really big deal for a lot of our
clients. So Tan, moving right along, the
next category that we want to talk about
is controlling litigation. So what does
that mean? Oftent times relators will

multitude of doctors or hospital

Let's roll with that. I think relators

for obvious reasons here, but I think

almost 20 years ago now against a major

in national security really depends on
this contractor, the risk of losing that

just too much compared to the benefit of
a recovery there. So, this one makes a
lot of sense, right? The government is
obviously interested in safeguarding
confidential information and ensuring
national security. So whenever that gets
put at risk, DOJ is going to look
closely at that costbenefit analysis of
what are we likely to recover if the
relator suit goes forward versus what
are the downsides here. Are we going to
be putting an essential national
security contractor out of business and
then we suddenly don't have what we need
to defend the nation. So that's going to
be the analysis there at DOJ.
>> Yeah. And the analysis is a super simple
balancing act here. I mean, it really
DOJ's not going to just let egregious
fraud go just because there's some
national security interest, but the
juice has got to be worth the squeeze.
If DOJ looks at this and says, "This is

not going to do it. But if it's

But you don't see this very often. This
would require a borderline case
involving a lot of effort. DOJ we need
to go through in order to preserve the
confidential information. So Tanner,
next we've got preserving government
resources. This one fascinates me. Tell

>> Yeah, so this is one that's often

So the idea here is that even when DOJ

are still some potentially tremendous
resources that either DOJ or the
affected agency need to invest while the
KAMs go forward. So when you have kams
that depend on actions or decisions by
government actors you know perhaps in
the context of materiality discovery can
be a real burden for the government
right the agencies often have to respond
to requests for documents occasionally
they have to provide a representative
who's going to sit for deposition so DOJ
according to the grandston memo should
dismiss kams when the burden of
monitoring or participating in the
litigation outweighs the expected gain
and we talked about one of those cases
already the sequoia orange case where
the USDA citrus industry regulations
were involved and there DOJ said that
the burden of seeking discovery into
USDA officials mindsets in terms of how
they set regulations over the citrus
industry DOJ characterized that burden
as enormous. Similarly, in the Wolf
Creek case that we talked about, the
discovery into the NASA contracting
officers knowledge or intention when
they were entering proving these
contracts and entering into these
agreements, it was going to be
incredibly timeconuming and it was going
to distract those officials from their
more pressing duties of carrying out
their jobs there. So, like I said, this
is one it's tough to invoke at the
outset of a a case, right? Because DOJ
doesn't really know how much of a burden
that there's going to be. But as the
case goes on and it becomes more and
more burdensome for DOJ or the affected
agency, you know, that might be an
avenue for kind of reopening these
discussions with DOJ and saying, "Look,
as you can see, this is taking a lot of
time away from the agency and doing what
the agency is supposed to do. We think
that the burdens are clearly outweigh
the benefits here and you should
consider dismissing."
>> Yeah, that's exactly right, Tanner. I
think what DOJ is looking for on this
one is something really, really, really
egregious. I mean, the fact that a
couple of witnesses are going to need to
be deposed or that they'll need to
respond to some discovery is really not
enough. That's really not what DOJ is
looking for. I'll tell you DOJ really
doesn't want to be seen as not willing
to put in the work when the work is
needed to rectify knowing fraud. They'll
do the work. This is getting to a level
where there's an entire agency and their
entire decision-m up to the highest
levels are being scrutinized. And that's
where I think this would kick. And I
think this is a pretty rare one, but
it's still one that could be a big deal
to some agencies. I think DOJ's time is
really they're going to be willing to
put in the work. The question is, are
you going to have to like shut down an
agency in order to litigate this case?
That's where this comes into play. And
so Tanner, we got one more. And the
final one, again, this is a rare one.
This is egregious procedural errors. So
Tanner, tell us about that and then
close us out by offering your thoughts
on what we should know about this
process as a whole. Yeah. So, egregious
procedural errors, right? The focus here
is really on that that word egregious.
So, as I mentioned at the outset,
failing to satisfy 9B, naming the wrong
defendant, that sort of stuff is not
going to be a procedural error that DOJ
is going to care about. But the ones
that DOJ will care about are the

And so when DOJ can't do that

in those instances actually even the

that's really going to get in the way of
the government doing their job. And
Jonathan, to your question about closing
us out here, the big thing that I think
is the takeaway here is that DOJ isn't
looking to dismiss weak cases. They're
looking to dismiss flawed cases, right?
Cases that for one reason or another
have a fundamental flaw. That means they
either don't fit into the FCA. They're
actually going to frustrate the purposes
of the FCA or they're actually going to
make it harder for the government,
whether it's DOJ or affected agencies,
to do their jobs. That's really what DOJ
is looking for. And it's going to be
interesting, you know, going forward. As
you mentioned, dismissals are up for the

interesting because that coincides with

it's possible we'll see more key
dismissals because the government is

prosecution. So, it's interesting, you
know, how those work in tandem and we'll

>> Thanks, Tanner. That's excellent wisdom
both on this one and throughout the
episode. And so Tanner, thanks for
coming on the podcast and telling our
listeners about this growing and very
important issue for a lot of people who

>> Absolutely. Thanks for having me.
>> To close, this is a big deal because as

Record number of kams filed last year
and that means a lot of companies are

themselves under investigation. And so

Flawed in a way that meets the

And so we're going to continue to talk
