videos.full_text: Welcome to another episode of Hush Blackwell's False Claims [music] Act Insights podcast. I'm your host, Jonathan Porter. On our last episode, Cormick [music] Connor told us about an announcement from DOJ leadership about False Claims Act dismissals. That's a big deal. So, for those who missed it, DOJ dismissals last year went from around six per year up to around 25, I think 25 dismissals last year. [music] And that may not seem like a big jump, but it's a really important jump because as our regular listeners know, declined KAMs can be a bear to litigate. And so [music] if DOJ is going to step in and start dismissing more declined keys, that's something that we need [music] to know about. And so today on the podcast, we're going to unpack dismissed keys a little bit more than the last episode. Talk about [music] what goes into a good pitch to ask DOJ to dismiss declined keys. why DOJ dismisses decline key TAMs, [music] everything like that, because this is a really big deal for False Claims Act enforcement. And little spoiler alert, it doesn't go the way a lot of people think it goes. A lot of people have a misperception about how and why declined [music] Kams are dismissed by DOJ. So, we're going to unpack all of that today on the podcast. Joining me to talk about dismissed [music] kams is my Hush Blackwell colleague, Tanner Cook. Tanner's been on the podcast a ton and I've introduced him every single time and so hopefully our listeners know him very well by now, but Tanner is one of my favorites in the firm. He's a senior associate in our St. Louis um office and a very valuable member of our False Claims Act working group. And so Tanner, I'm thrilled that you're coming back on the podcast today [music] to talk to our listeners about DOJ dismissing kams. >> Yeah, thanks Jonathan as always. It's a pleasure to be on this podcast. It's always great collaborating with you whether on our our cases or on thought leadership like this. So, I'm really looking forward to the discussion. >> Thanks, Tanner. So, I previewed in the open that these things don't go the way some people think they go. And so, Tanner, why don't you start us off by giving us the big picture of what DOJ looks for in dismissals. Yeah. So, at a high level, DOJ will intervene in and dismiss keys that somehow abuse the process. But that means something a little different than what us lawyers typically mean when we say abuse the process. Right? Ordinarily, when we think of an abusive process, we think of someone bringing a lawsuit for an improper purpose or disregarding important procedural requirements, things like that. In the KAM dismissal context, abuse of process seems something more like undermining the purpose of the FCA. So, uh, KAMS that are candidates for DOJ dismissals are typically those that actively work against the government's interests in one way or another. And that makes sense when you think about it, considering that the entire purpose of the FCA's KAM provisions are for private relators to further the government's interests. So, if they're hurting the government's interest, that's all the more reason for the government to step in and intervene. Now, one thing that I want to clarify is that when we're talking about undermining the government's interests, it's not so much that the the lawsuit is bad or has bad facts or is poorly pleaded. That's the typically not enough to get DOJ interested in intervening to dismiss the case. In fact, the prevailing wisdom is that DOJ will typically let questionable facts proceed as declined KAMS because the case is truly without support, the court will likely just dispose of it at the pleading stage or at summary judgement anyways. On the other hand, if it turns out that the case actually does have support, the government stands to benefit. So when we're looking at key dismissals by DOJ, we're looking at certain defined criteria that focus on whether the suit is undermining the government's interests or initiatives. And those criteria, you know, as we're going to discuss, are laid out in what's called the Granston memo, which is a 2018 memorandum from former Deputy Assistant Attorney General Michael Granston. Those criteria can be kind of categorized as follows. So, first you've got curbing meritless key TAMs. And that might sound like its intention with what I just said about questionable suits not being candidates for dismissal, but we'll explain actually why those aren't intention. Second, the DOJ focuses on preventing opportunistic or parasitic keys. Third, it focuses on preventing interference with agency policies and programs. Fourth, it focuses on controlling litigation brought on behalf of the government. Fifth, it focuses on safeguarding classified information or national security interests. Sixth, it focuses on preserving government resources. And seventh, it focuses on addressing egregious procedural errors. So that's kind of the universe of criteria for key dismissals. The memo indicates that that's not an exhaustive list, but in practice, those are the ones that really come into play. >> Thanks, Tanner. Any great lawyer knows how to road map stuff, and you just gave us an excellent road map, so thanks for that. The big point that I want people to understand upfront, Tanner, is you don't go to DOJ and say, "Look, we think our facts are better than their facts." At least under the Grandstston memo, DOJ's not going to dismiss a key just because you think that your facts are a little bit better than their facts. DOJ's their policy is to look for some actual impropriety, something wrong with the kam itself that the courts might not necessarily pick up on because the way DOJ thinks, if you think you're going to win on the merits, okay, then go to the courts and have and win on the merits. There's something different about DOJ saying, "No, we're going to we're going to do something that the courts aren't designed to do. We're going to step in and look at the process." And so that's the big thing that I people mess that up all the time. I can't tell you when I was at DOJ how many times people came to me asking, "Hey, we want you to dismiss this kit because, you know, we think that we're right." That's really not what it's designed for. You got to fit your request into one of these categories. And so, Tanner, let's start by talking about some examples of these categories that you just excellently roadmap for us. And so, again, we're taking these directly from the Grand memo. And the first one that we want to talk about is allegations that facially lack merit. So Tanner, you talked about the tension between these two things. Why don't you explain this category for us? >> Yeah, absolutely. So I'll try to break this down in a way that makes sense because they do appear to be at odds with each other, right? If the government, you know, wants to curb meritless key TAMs, but it's saying it won't dismiss just because the case is meritless. So we'll try to make sense of that. So, this category is not for cases where the relator fails to satisfy the rule 9b heightened pleading standard or cases where there's a good chance that the relator's claims are barred by the public disclosure bar. It's not any of the cases where the defendant simply has a good merits defense. These are cases that on their face don't allege something that fits within the FCA. So in philosophical terms, it's what we would call a category error, which is when you assign something to a category to which it does not belong. And the best example of this is when a relator names a government agency or official as a defendant, right? DOJ has dismissed kams against the Federal Reserve, for example. And and that's because we're looking for fraud on the government, right? Not fraud by the government. The government is not a proper defendant in FCA cases. Another example that's somewhat related is when the relators allegations do not involve any federal funds. Right? The misuse of federal funds is an essential ingredient of FCA claims. So if that's lacking, this it's just it's simply not an FCA suit. Finally, DOJ will occasionally dismiss KAMS when its own investigation finds conclusive evidence that the KAMS allegations were factually incorrect. That's exceedingly rare and it's different than just telling DOJ, hey, we're going to be able to prove that our facts are right and we didn't do anything wrong. DOJ is not going to take that assurance, right? But if DOJ conducts its own investigation, right? If there's a a parallel investigation that's ongoing and they find conclusive evidence, sometimes they might step in to intervene. So hopefully that resolves any confusion over what is meant by curbing meritless keys. >> Thanks, Tener. And you mentioned the philosophical approach. I appreciate that. you're way ahead of me when it comes to those types of things. But no, I think what our listeners should know here is this is for just a really obvious glaring problem. There have been keys that have named presidents before. That's really not what kams are designed to do. So that's what we're talking about here is something that's super obvious or something where when DOJ looks at it, it is like an ex or not X situation. If you're going to bring a kam and say this person was never licensed as a physician and they're there doing all this stuff and you run an investigation, find well okay well they've always been licensed so they're just wrong for some reason. That's the type of thing first of all hopefully the DOJ's going to the relator and saying you missed this why don't you just dismiss this on on your own? But if they're not going to that's where DOJ would step in because it is super clear this is not something that should proceed as a key tab. That's what that means. And then Tener, thanks for resolving the tension because I think some people may read that and say, "Okay, well, if I can convince DOJ that there's no merit in them proceeding, then that's something." But it's very different. It's very different from what we may think of as as not meritorious. So Sam, the next category is what the Grandston memo calls parasitic kams. What are those? So parasitic keams are those that simply duplicate a pre-existing government investigation and that provide no useful information beyond what the government already knows. So an example of this would be there was one where DOJ dismissed a kitam against a financial institution where the government had been investigating this institution for years. It was already pretty far into settlement negotiations. And the rationale here makes sense, right? government does not want to share its recovery with the relator who really contributes nothing besides filing the lawsuit. To that end, you'll also see DOJ dismisses claims as parasitic when relators file a bunch of kits against the same defendant. And so what the government is trying to do here is limit its obligation to share its recovery with the relators. For our listeners out there, as you recall, right, relators get up to a third of the government's recovery in non-intervened key tabs. And so, you know, the government doesn't want to share a third of its recovery when the relator is really doing nothing besides filing a lawsuit. So, that's the rationale behind dismissing what the Branson memo refers to as parasitic kabams. Thanks, Tanner. And this really does happen. So, when agents are investigating kams or false claims act allegations that weren't started by kam, they'll go out and they'll interview people. And it's not unusual for someone who gets interviewed to turn around and contact a lawyer and file a key stamp saying I'm going to get a piece of this myself. And a lot of times they really are successful. What's going on here I think Tanner is that what the grants and memo is saying is look if they're in advanced negotiations if we're like about to sign and someone files a key and it's not really right for them to go and just grab 15% of all of those funds when they didn't really do anything. They didn't really advance the investigation beyond what was already agreed to. So that's what this is. But I'll tell you, it does still happen where people will file a KAM after they get wind of an investigation and they'll still get to share in it. But that's our job is to try to figure out does this cross some sort of line that the Gransson memo talks about. And so Tanner, moving on. The Gransson memo also counsels DOJ to dismiss keys that interfere with agency policies and programs. Tanner, tell us about that category. So this is an interesting category and it's the one that I see invoked most often in in briefing on this issue here. DOJ looks for key TAMs that essentially try to seconduess what government agencies have done. Government agencies often get second guessed. That's not uncommon. But DOJ is sensitive to relators using the key process to do that, right? Especially when it puts the agencies in a position of having to defend the propriety of their actions. In short, DOJ doesn't want judges or even worse jurors running rough shot over agency decision-m. An example of this is the Sequoia Orange case in which a relator tried to file a kitam that sought to force the department of agriculture to change its regulations in the citrus industry. Similar example is the Wolf Creek case. The Sequoia Orange one is mentioned in the Grandon memo. The Wolf Creek one is a fairly recent and kind of highly talked about case. But in Wolf Creek, the relator alleged that NASA contracting officers didn't vet proposals from contractors before approving them. And DOJ dismissed this because the key provisions are not meant to make sure that government officers are doing their jobs properly, right? They don't want outsiders really having a say on that. And so there are other more tangible examples besides these. Sometimes a relator suit does not just second guessess an agency's decision, but actively interferes with the agency's efforts to fulfill its functions. And obviously in those cases, DOJ is highly incentivized to intervene in and dismiss those cases. So, I think that's why we see this category talked about so much in briefing because it does seem to be the most compelling, right? If a relator is getting in the way of an agency's functions and at the same time purporting to act in that agency's interests, that's a problem and DOJ will want to correct that. >> Yeah, like you said, T, this is probably the one that we see the most and it's because this one is a really fascinating concept within the False Claims Act. There are a lot of situations where there are government actors who know what's going on and the question is what do we do with that? You see it a lot in the contracting space where you've got contracting officers and they're making determinations in real time. What do we do with this? And there's a lot a lot of keys, a lot of false claims at cases that really come down to what do the government know? Why did they know it? And should this government person have done something differently in response to all of this? And it gets really sticky when essentially you're using the ketaman process to make a big change within the government. And so that's where this comes in trying to figure out, okay, are NASA contracting officers doing enough to vet something. That's a really hard thing because you're saying that the contractor committed fraud. Remember the False Claims Act is for knowing fraud. How in the world did the contractor commit fraud because the NASA contracting officer didn't do his or her job? So that's what this is getting at. And this I'll tell you this is the one that is most interesting to me because it's a really big deal for a lot of our clients. So Tan, moving right along, the next category that we want to talk about is controlling litigation. So what does that mean? Oftent times relators will name a ton of defendants, right? We've seen this in in keys where there's multitude of doctors or hospital systems, things like that. And everyone who has litigated cases knows that it's very difficult, sometimes impossible to try a case with hundreds of separate defendants. So when DOJ identifies fraud that is more limited than the relator thinks, DOJ will sometimes dismiss the defendants who are on the periphery of the fraud. And that's to make it easier for DOJ to focus on the main players. So an example of this is in 2002, a relator brought a case against companies involved in purported natural gas royalties fraud involving natural gas produced from federal lands. But the relator named 300 defendants. So what DOJ did was intervene as to some of those but not others. And then when the relator wanted to proceed against the rest, DOJ realized it would be impossible to actually litigate the case with all of these defendants. Some of which it had intervened on, some of which it did not. So it dismissed the ones where it had not intervened, and that was to make it more manageable, right? To really focus on the defendants that DOJ thought it had a solid case against and that it could streamline its pre-trial efforts. >> Thanks, Tanner. And this is one that I don't think is invoked very often because I think relators by now understand if you're going to litigate this, you absolutely can go to trial against 300 defendants. That's a really hard hard thing to do. Even if you're going to bifrocate and all that stuff, that's a hard that's a hard thing. Relators now I think understand if you're going to name 50 defendants and DOJ is going to cut it to four, good. Let's roll with that. I think relators understand that that's the way to go. So Tanner, the Grant memo also says to dismiss key TAMs that risk classified information and national security interests. This one sounds interesting. Tell us about this one. >> Yeah, so this is one that I don't see come up that often, you know, kind of for obvious reasons here, but I think it's intuitively the most compelling reason. So sometimes key TAMs involve government contractors who engaged in highly confidential matters or whose work was vital to national security and prosecuting FCA cases involving these issues brings a lot of challenges for the government. Right? There are certain tools that make it easier in criminal cases. But with civil FCA cases with relators and with the public right of access, the analysis is quite a bit different. So DOJ will weigh the risks and rewards of key tams involving national security or classified information and it's going to dismiss the ones that it thinks are too risky. Right? So there was a case you know almost 20 years ago now against a major defense contractor where DOJ dismissed after determining that the national security interests outweighed the relators right to go forward with the case. And so, right to put it at a high level, if a government agency involved in national security really depends on this contractor, the risk of losing that contractor because of an FCA judgment is just too much compared to the benefit of a recovery there. So, this one makes a lot of sense, right? The government is obviously interested in safeguarding confidential information and ensuring national security. So whenever that gets put at risk, DOJ is going to look closely at that costbenefit analysis of what are we likely to recover if the relator suit goes forward versus what are the downsides here. Are we going to be putting an essential national security contractor out of business and then we suddenly don't have what we need to defend the nation. So that's going to be the analysis there at DOJ. >> Yeah. And the analysis is a super simple balancing act here. I mean, it really DOJ's not going to just let egregious fraud go just because there's some national security interest, but the juice has got to be worth the squeeze. If DOJ looks at this and says, "This is really not a very good KAM, and we would have to do a lot in order to preserve our national security interest and and all this confidential stuff," they're not going to do it. But if it's egregious, they will do it. They just want to make sure that it's worth it. But you don't see this very often. This would require a borderline case involving a lot of effort. DOJ we need to go through in order to preserve the confidential information. So Tanner, next we've got preserving government resources. This one fascinates me. Tell us about this one. >> Yeah, so this is one that's often invoked and it doesn't really gain much traction until the case goes on. Right. So the idea here is that even when DOJ declines to intervene in the KAM, there are still some potentially tremendous resources that either DOJ or the affected agency need to invest while the KAMs go forward. So when you have kams that depend on actions or decisions by government actors you know perhaps in the context of materiality discovery can be a real burden for the government right the agencies often have to respond to requests for documents occasionally they have to provide a representative who's going to sit for deposition so DOJ according to the grandston memo should dismiss kams when the burden of monitoring or participating in the litigation outweighs the expected gain and we talked about one of those cases already the sequoia orange case where the USDA citrus industry regulations were involved and there DOJ said that the burden of seeking discovery into USDA officials mindsets in terms of how they set regulations over the citrus industry DOJ characterized that burden as enormous. Similarly, in the Wolf Creek case that we talked about, the discovery into the NASA contracting officers knowledge or intention when they were entering proving these contracts and entering into these agreements, it was going to be incredibly timeconuming and it was going to distract those officials from their more pressing duties of carrying out their jobs there. So, like I said, this is one it's tough to invoke at the outset of a a case, right? Because DOJ doesn't really know how much of a burden that there's going to be. But as the case goes on and it becomes more and more burdensome for DOJ or the affected agency, you know, that might be an avenue for kind of reopening these discussions with DOJ and saying, "Look, as you can see, this is taking a lot of time away from the agency and doing what the agency is supposed to do. We think that the burdens are clearly outweigh the benefits here and you should consider dismissing." >> Yeah, that's exactly right, Tanner. I think what DOJ is looking for on this one is something really, really, really egregious. I mean, the fact that a couple of witnesses are going to need to be deposed or that they'll need to respond to some discovery is really not enough. That's really not what DOJ is looking for. I'll tell you DOJ really doesn't want to be seen as not willing to put in the work when the work is needed to rectify knowing fraud. They'll do the work. This is getting to a level where there's an entire agency and their entire decision-m up to the highest levels are being scrutinized. And that's where I think this would kick. And I think this is a pretty rare one, but it's still one that could be a big deal to some agencies. I think DOJ's time is really they're going to be willing to put in the work. The question is, are you going to have to like shut down an agency in order to litigate this case? That's where this comes into play. And so Tanner, we got one more. And the final one, again, this is a rare one. This is egregious procedural errors. So Tanner, tell us about that and then close us out by offering your thoughts on what we should know about this process as a whole. Yeah. So, egregious procedural errors, right? The focus here is really on that that word egregious. So, as I mentioned at the outset, failing to satisfy 9B, naming the wrong defendant, that sort of stuff is not going to be a procedural error that DOJ is going to care about. But the ones that DOJ will care about are the procedural errors that hinder the government's own efforts to investigate and police fraud. And so, this is, you know, rare because most of the time relators do the proper things and they don't commit these sorts of egregious errors. But that's not always the case, right? So in 2013, there was a case where the relator ignored DOJ's request to have the KAM to served on DOJ or the complaint itself and ignored DOJ's request to have the relator disclose facts to DOJ. All of this is required by the FCA and you know relator for whatever reason just didn't want to comply. And those things matter because if DOJ doesn't have what it needs, it can't perform its investigation during the seal period, right? As our listeners probably recall, a kitam gets filed under seal. DOJ investigates, decides whether or not it wants to intervene. And so when DOJ can't do that investigation, that obviously is going to be a problem and going to lean in favor of dismissal. Other things that you can imagine, sometimes relators violate the seal period, right? they'll serve a complaint that should be under seal and that can really impact DOJ's ability to investigate because then the defendant is on notice of this and the investigation is trickier when the defendant's aware of what's going on. So in those instances actually even the court can theoretically dismiss the case under its power and certainly DOJ can intervene in the case and dismiss as well. So an overall takeaway on this issue it has to be a procedural error that's really going to get in the way of the government doing their job. And Jonathan, to your question about closing us out here, the big thing that I think is the takeaway here is that DOJ isn't looking to dismiss weak cases. They're looking to dismiss flawed cases, right? Cases that for one reason or another have a fundamental flaw. That means they either don't fit into the FCA. They're actually going to frustrate the purposes of the FCA or they're actually going to make it harder for the government, whether it's DOJ or affected agencies, to do their jobs. That's really what DOJ is looking for. And it's going to be interesting, you know, going forward. As you mentioned, dismissals are up for the first time in in recent memory. And it's interesting because that coincides with what appears to be pretty aggressive FCA enforcement from the government. So, it's possible we'll see more key dismissals because the government is taking a more active role in FCA prosecution. So, it's interesting, you know, how those work in tandem and we'll see where things go from there. >> Thanks, Tanner. That's excellent wisdom both on this one and throughout the episode. And so Tanner, thanks for coming on the podcast and telling our listeners about this growing and very important issue for a lot of people who are under investigation. Tanner, thanks for coming on the podcast. >> Absolutely. Thanks for having me. >> To close, this is a big deal because as Tanner said, kams are through the roof. Record number of kams filed last year and that means a lot of companies are now under investigation or about to find themselves under investigation. And so if there's a kam that crosses a line, then that is defense council's job is to go to the government and explain why the kam is [music] flawed. Not weak, flawed. Flawed in a way that meets the strictctures of the of the grand memo. And so we're going to continue to talk about on this podcast all the different things that we need to know as we're defending these. The False Claims Act, I've said this a number of times, is to me the most one of the most fascinating areas in which to practice. And it's a pleasure to practice with such a talented team here at Hush Blackwell. And Tanner, I'm grateful that you're such a critical part of that team. But to our listeners, we hope you'll continue to listen to us and we'll see you next time.

metadata.title: Startup Funding Espresso – Claiming Whistleblower Status
metadata.author: Hall Martin
metadata.shortDescription: Claiming Whistleblower Status Hello, this is Hall T. Martin with the Startup Funding Espresso -- your daily shot of startup funding and investing. There are three Whistleblower programs, False Claims, SEC Whistleblower, and IRS Whistleblower. One can file multiple claims under each of the programs. One must file within a time limit of the act of fraud which in most cases is 10 years. Some IRS and SEC claims require a filing within three years. The False Claims Act requires you to have an attorney. This gives anonymity to the filer. This act covers fraud and waste to the Federal Government. This includes healthcare, tax, defense, pharmaceutical, educational, financial and more. Once filed you cannot discuss the case with anyone. For SEC Whistleblower cases you file a Form TCR. For IRS Whistleblower cases you file a Form 211. The government will determine whether to pursue or not. The filer can make another claim under a different act to gain a higher payout. The Department of Justice or SEC will lead the investigation. The faster you submit the claim, the better the chance of success. The Whistleblower can receive a percent of any rewards collected which can range from 10% to 30% of the funds collected. Consider these steps in filing a whistleblower claim. Thank you for joining us for the Startup Funding Espresso where we help startups and investors connect for funding. Let's go startup something today. _______________________________________________________ For more episodes from Investor Connect, please visit the site at: http://investorconnect.org Check out our other podcasts here: https://investorconnect.org/ For Investors check out: https://tencapital.group/investor-landing/ For Startups check out: https://tencapital.group/company-landing/ For eGuides check out: https://tencapital.group/education/ For upcoming Events, check out https://tencapital.group/events/ For Feedback please contact info@tencapital.group Please follow, share, and leave a review. metadata.title: How Do Attorney Fees Work In a Whistleblower Case? | Tony Munter Attorney at Law
metadata.author: Tony Munter Attorney at Law
metadata.shortDescription:
Visit : http://whistleblower-quitam-attorney.net/how-much-will-whistleblower-case-cos/

DC Whistleblower Attorney Tony Munter discusses how much it would cost an individual to hire an attorney for a whistleblower case. 

Tony explains that Federal False Claims Act cases are handled on a contingency fee basis, which means if we don't win, you don't win. You don't need to have any money to be able to file a case up front. 

If you believe you have a whistleblower case, do not hesitate to contact experienced False Claims Act Attorney Tony Munter on our website http://whistleblower-quitam-attorney.net/ or at (202) 552-1777.

Tony Munter Whistleblower Attorney
409 7th St NW Suite 210
Washington, DC 20004
(202) 552-1777
http://whistleblower-quitam-attorney.net/

We Welcome You to Subscribe to the Tony Munter Whistleblower Attorney Channel 
https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcIw8mTRdECYC44howjm9GA

*Please note that laws change. This information is accurate as of the date this video was published and is not to be construed as legal advice. To find out how your prospective case applies to current law give us a call today.

segments.text: Hi, I'm Tony Munter.
I'm an attorney at Prince Benowitz.
I've been filing cases under the Federal False Claims Act for almost ten years now and we
handle these cases on a contingent fee basis.
People ask about attorney fees, they want to know how we handle it.
A contingent fee is pretty simple, it's basically saying that if we win, we take a share of
whatever your recovery is.
I guess that's the bad news.
But the good news is you don't need any money to file a case up front.
No matter how complicated the case is, maybe you've been fired and you don't have any money,
you can still handle even a very large False Claims Act case on this basis.
That's not unusual, there's a lot of other tort laws that work this way.
But it's especially important in this type of law, because when you first file a False
Claims Act case, you have to file it under seal.
And at that point, you can't tell anyone except your lawyer about it.
You got to marry your lawyer at that point, because they're the only ones you can talk
to about this case and it's hard not to talk about it a case that's this important to you.
You need somebody to call.
And if you're worried about every phone call costing you money, or every inquiry from your
lawyer or email from your lawyer trying to get more details you won't be able to do the
job you need to do to present the case to the government.
So a contingent fee basis is really the only way to handle these types of cases.
It puts you and your lawyer in the same boat.
You can win a large recovery or you can win statutory attorney fees, but you and your
lawyer are in the same boat going in the same direction, working together, almost as partners
in litigation.

metadata.title: The False Claims Act: What makes a whistleblower law so powerful | Berkeley Boosts
metadata.author: Phillips & Cohen LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
In part 2 of Berkeley Law Executive Education’s “Berkeley Boosts” three-part webinar series, “Speaking Up: Whistleblowers, Whistleblowing and the US’s Unique Approach to Fraud Enforcement,” Phillips & Cohen partner Claire Sylvia moderates a discussion about the history and structure of the US federal False Claims Act and its unique whistleblower (“qui tam”) provisions. 

Phillips & Cohen co-founder John Phillips, who was a key architect of the modern-day False Claims Act, and Jeb White, chief executive officer of Taxpayers Against Fraud and the TAF Education Fund, contribute their insights into how the False Claims act became the government’s chief fraud enforcement tool. 

Claire Sylvia is the author of a widely cited treatise on the False Claims Act and a thought leader in the qui tam bar. She has represented a number of whistleblowers in successful qui tam cases against defense contractors and healthcare providers.

Watch Part 1, “Speaking Up: Whistleblowers, Whistleblowing and the US’s Unique Approach to Fraud Enforcement,” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hJOl_KwCHEw) and Part 3, “The SEC and CFTC whistleblower reward programs – their impact and success,” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j2GyHTrfNTE) of the Berkeley Law Executive Education’s “Berkeley Boosts” three-part webinar series, “Speaking Up: Whistleblowers, Whistleblowing and the US’s Unique Approach to Fraud Enforcement.”

Learn about Berkeley Law Executive Education’s free “Berkeley Boosts” webinar series here: https://executive.law.berkeley.edu/be... 

Learn more about US whistleblower laws and programs and how they protect and reward whistleblowers at https://www.phillipsandcohen.com

metadata.title: Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank Whistleblower Protections
metadata.author: Garrison, Levin-Epstein, Fitzgerald & Pirrotti
metadata.shortDescription:
Federal whistleblower laws provide important protections for employees who report suspected fraud and corporate misconduct, including employees who do not work on Wall Street.

In this video, Garrison Law attorneys Amanda DeMatteis and Josh Goodbaum discuss two major federal whistleblower protection laws: the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) and the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act.

The attorneys explain how these laws protect employees from workplace retaliation, including those working for publicly traded companies and certain contractors or subsidiaries.

They also examine the key differences between the two laws, including internal versus SEC reporting requirements, deadlines for filing retaliation complaints, and the potential remedies available to whistleblowers.

Finally, they discuss why employees who suspect workplace fraud should document their concerns and seek legal guidance before making decisions that could affect their legal protections.

Learn more about Amanda DeMatteis:
https://garrisonlaw.com/about-the-firm/amanda-m-dematteis/

Learn more about Josh Goodbaum:
https://garrisonlaw.com/about-the-firm/joshua-r-goodbaum/

Learn more about Garrison Law:
https://garrisonlaw.com/

00:00 - Introduction: Whistleblower Protections Beyond Wall Street
00:20 - Who Is Protected Under Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank?
00:46 - Reporting Fraud and Reasonable Belief
01:02 - How Whistleblower Laws Protect Against Retaliation
01:16 - Sarbanes-Oxley: Internal Reporting and Filing Deadlines
01:47 - Dodd-Frank: Damages, Deadlines, and SEC Reporting
02:16 - What Employees Should Do if They Suspect Workplace Fraud
02:50 - Final Takeaways and Seeking Legal Guidance

#WhistleblowerProtection #EmploymentLaw #SarbanesOxley #DoddFrank #EmployeeRights #GarrisonLaw

segments.text: Hi, Josh.
>> Hi, Amanda. What are we talking about
today?
>> We're going to talk about whistleblowers
today, Josh. People here Sarbanes-Oxley
and Dodd-Frank and they immediately
think of Wall Street. But shouldn't
employees that [clears throat] don't
work on Wall Street care about these two
federal laws and why?
>> Absolutely, Amanda, because these are
two of the main federal laws that
protect whistleblowers. If you work for
a publicly traded company, any company
that's traded for example on the New
York Stock Exchange or the Nasdaq or for
a contractor or a subsidiary of one of
those companies and you report fraud,
these laws can protect your job. Under
Sarbanes-Oxley, that means reporting
things like securities fraud, mail or
wire fraud, bank fraud, or violations of
SEC rules. And importantly, you don't
have to be right about whether there was
fraud occurring. You just need a
reasonable belief that something illegal
is going on in your company.
>> Josh, we hear all the time from
employees who are afraid, sometimes
rightly so, to make these complaints
either in house or to a government
agency. What do you say to them?
>> Both of these laws, Amanda, prohibit
retaliation. And that's a critical part
of both Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank,
but they prohibit retaliation in
different ways. Let's talk about that.
Under Sarbanes-Oxley, you only have to
report your concern internally to your
supervisor or to your compliance
department. And if you're retaliated
against because you reported that
concern even internally, you only have
to prove that your protected conduct was
a contributing factor in the negative
thing that happened to you as a result.
Now, that's a lower standard than under
most employment laws. That's very
employee positive. On the other hand,
you only have 180 days from the time
that you experienced that retaliation to
make a formal complaint of retaliation.
So you have to move very quickly.
Dodd-Frank gives more damages than
Sarbanes-Oxley including potentially
double penalty damages and it has a
longer limitations period. An employee
can file a complaint up to 6 years after
they've experienced retaliation. But to
engage in protected activity under
Dodd-Frank, you have to report that
concern directly to the SEC. Reporting a
concern internally to your employer, to
your manager, to the uh compliance
department isn't enough to implicate the
protections of Dodd-Frank.
>> And Josh, what do we tell an employee
whether they're on Wall Street or not
who thinks that they have witnessed or
been asked to engage in fraud at work?
>> Write down what you saw, Amanda, and
when, and talk to an employment lawyer
as soon as possible, ideally before you
make your whistleblower complaint, but
certainly after you report that fraud,
and especially if anything negative
happens to you. The choices you make at
the beginning, like who to report to and
when to report, can dictate which
protections you have under each of these
laws and can dictate what your
employment lawyer might be able to
accomplish for you if you experience any
retaliation.
>> Thank you so much, Josh. This is really
critical information and frankly
complicated for lawyers let alone
non-lawyers. If you are having issues
with whistleblower protections,
Sarbanes-Oxley, Dodd-Frank, or anything
else at work, please reach out. Thank
you so much for watching and we'll see
you next time.

segments.text: This is an accuser media investigative
[music] case documentary examining the
$279 million whistleblower inside the
largest SEC bounty payout in history.
In modern legal warfare, the boundary
between exercising constitutional free
speech, blowing the whistle on
institutional misconduct, and crossing
into actionable defamation represents
one of the most fiercely litigated
frontiers in American jurisprudence.
When public accusations are leveled
against corporate institutions or
individuals, the judicial system does
not evaluate claims based on viral
headlines, [music] coordinated social
media campaigns, or public sentiment.
Instead, courts demand verified
documentary proof, strict statutory
compliance, and rigorous adherence to
[music] constitutional due process.
In our first act, we examine the
controlling statutory framework that
governs this dispute.
When an accuser asserts formal
allegations of malfeasance, disclosures
must satisfy three foundational legal
hurdles, evidentiary specificity,
procedural compliance with authorized
agency channels, and the total absence
of bad faith fabrication.
Litigants who bypass confidential
statutory reporting mechanisms to
orchestrate [music] sensationalized
media smear campaigns immediately
forfeit statutory safe harbor
protections and expose themselves to
catastrophic civil liability.
Turning to evidentiary standards,
appellate precedent confirms that courts
impose strict burdens [music] of proof
on asserting parties.
Corroborating allegations requires
objective cross-referencing between
contemporaneous digital metadata,
[music]
forensic audit logs, and sworn
depositions.

settlement leverage or inflict
commercial harm, modern statutes provide
powerful countermeasures, including
mandatory anti-SLAPP fee shifting,
severe judicial sanctions, and
multi-million dollar defamation per se
judgments.
In our forensic discovery breakdown,
documentary integrity serves the
decisive battlefield.
Witnesses who contradict contemporaneous
[music] emails or alter physical records
face severe evidentiary exclusions and
criminal referrals under federal perjury
statutes.
For legal teams and investigative
journalists, the mandate is unambiguous.
[music] Independent corroboration must
precede public publication and
constitutional due process must remain
sacrosanct at every procedural [music]
phase.
Explore the primary court dockets, full

metadata.title: Why Workplace Investigations Matter: Avoiding Bias in Employee Claims | California Employment Law
metadata.author: Koegle Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Workplace investigations play a critical role when employers face discrimination, harassment, retaliation, or whistleblower claims, yet they are often overlooked or handled informally until it’s too late.

In this video, Koegle Law Group Partner Lucas Rowe shares insights from a recent employment law panel discussion, drawing on his experience representing California employers in discrimination, harassment, and retaliation matters under FEHA and related statutes. Lucas explains why many employers first learn of a complaint when a lawsuit is filed, and how early investigation decisions can significantly impact risk, credibility, and defense strategy.

This discussion explores:
- Why employees often claim they complained internally, even when no formal complaint was documented
- The importance of conducting prompt, objective, and well-documented investigations
- The challenges HR teams face when investigating internal complaints
- How perceived bias can undermine an investigation, even when conducted in good faith
- When and why engaging an outside investigator may strengthen the process
- The role of documentation, electronic records, and transparency in building a defensible investigation

For California employers, the goal isn’t just responding to complaints, it’s creating a process that supports fairness, clarity, and informed decision-making from the start. A thoughtful investigation can help businesses understand potential exposure, address workplace issues appropriately, and take meaningful steps toward resolution and compliance.

At Koegle Law Group, we partner with business owners and HR professionals to focus on proactive compliance, prevention, and clear communication, helping employers navigate workplace challenges before they escalate into litigation.

This communication may be considered advertising material under the rules of professional conduct governing lawyers in California.

00:00 – Types of Claims Employers Commonly Face
00:22 – Why Workplace Investigations Are So Important
01:00 – When Outside Investigators May Be Appropriate
01:22 – What a Thorough Investigation Should Include
01:44 – Using Investigations to Identify and Address Risk

videos.full_text: I deal mostly with like discrimination, harassment, retaliation claims. Uh those are under the FIHA or under the whistleblower protection act under California law. Sometimes we see federal cases, but very rarely. When someone files a lawsuit, many times it's the first time you're hearing of the complaint because employees don't, in my experience, many times don't actually make complaints, but they claim that they do. when they do make those claims, um, you know, the investigation is really important and and I almost never see this because it it costs money and it takes time, but the best thing you can do is hire an outside company to do your investigations because there is always going to be this shadow of bias if if your HR professionals are doing the investigations on their own. Not saying that's bad. Many times it's perfectly fine. Uh but there's always this element that HR doesn't work for the employees. They don't. I know they love to say so and companies will often tell their employees that HR is there for you. HR is there for the corporation. HR is there to protect the company in whatever way they possibly can. So there's always going to be this shadow of bias in any investigation undertaken by your HR group. Um and so to the extent you can to the extent you can afford it, you should hire an outside company to do the investigation. And that just might mean interviewing the the person who's complaining, the person they're complaining about, other individuals around, pulling emails if there's anything that might be electronic, Teams messages, Slack if you use those, pulling all that data out and providing it to the investigator, even if it is your HR team, so that they can do a robust investigation because what I often deal with is sort of like the after facts. How do I fix this problem? Because you, you know, the the client didn't necessarily do it correctly from the start. When I do the investigation, because I try to approach everything objectively, if my client is wrong, I want to be able to tell them, hey, you've got some serious liability. Here are some steps we can take to try to mitigate against that liability. But I can't do that if you're not honest with me and don't provide me everything I need. So that's important.

metadata.shortDescription:
Most FCA cases settle. An experienced mediator and varied practitioners discuss approaches to settling FCA matters, including DOJ's 2019 directive regarding cooperation and structuring settlements based on ability to pay in the midst of financial uncertainty, among other issues affecting the resolution.

Stephen Altman, Partner, Dispute Resolution Services
Sarah Frazier, Law Office of Sarah Frazier
Kirsten Mayer, Partner, Ropes & Gray
Christen Nedwick, Assistant Attorney General, Texas Office of the Attorney General

metadata.title: Violating the False Claims Act (Case Study 019)
metadata.author: Compliance Mitigation
metadata.shortDescription:
Violating the False Claims Act
Workrite Ergonomics, founded in 1991 and located in California, pioneered the design, manufacture and distribution of innovative ergonomic and space optimization products for the workplace. They produce keyboards with unique designs, adjustable sit-stand desks and specialized monitor arms to provide for a more comfortable and productive office environment. Its parent company, Knape & Vogt Manufacturing, has annual revenues in excess of $100 million and over 500 employees, owned by the private equity company Wind Point Partners.
 
All the information in this background comes from a Department of Justice press release and related articles.
 
Workrite utilizes a team of designers and engineers to incorporate modern techniques, the latest technologies, and high-quality specifications, creating products to serve its worldwide clientele, including the United States government. The company focuses on comfort and safety, believing that comfortable employees will be more productive and less likely to miss workdays due to injury or bad health, benefitting the entire organization. Workrite products may be easily adjusted, making them highly adaptable to meet a company’s specific needs or changing needs as business develops.
 
Workrite additionally takes care to protect the environment and the health and safety of employees, striving to develop products and processes that use recycled materials and environmentally sound manufacturing methods.
 
Workrite, moreover, received recognition as being one of the Healthiest Companies, thanks to its internal employee benefits and programs. The company provided such free benefits as access to OnSite Wellness, a third-party web portal, and offered staff wellness participation bonuses of up to $250 based on earning 1,100 wellness points. These points could be earned by participating in events such as Breast Cancer Awareness Day; Stress Awareness; and a 21-Day Gratitude Mini-Challenge, among others.
“Grateful people tend to have 10 percent fewer stress-related illnesses and 12 percent lower blood pressure,” according to Workrite’s Human Resource Director, in noting the fact that Workrite’s internal policies mirrored its corporate objective of endeavoring to provide a more enjoyable work experience to all employees, including its own. 
It’s the exact kind of company one would expect government to promote, not target as part of a criminal investigation. 
 
Workrite provided office furniture to US government entities from 2009 to 2017 through the GSA’s Multiple Award Schedule (MAS) program. The MAS program provides the government with a streamlined process to procure commonly used commercial goods and services, eliminating the otherwise typical requirement of competitive bidding. 
 
Workrite, like many companies, provides flexible pricing for bulk orders of its products. Prices may at times also be influenced by internal oversupply, the potential for additional business and other factors typically contemplated in conducting commerce.
 
In certain contracts Workrite fulfilled for the government between 2009 and 2017, it charged higher prices than it charged to certain other private clients. This matter was brought to the attention of government regulators under the whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act by a former Workrite sales manager named Michael Franchek.
 
The False Claims Act (FCA), also called the "Lincoln Law", is an American federal law that imposes liability on persons and companies who defraud governmental programs (typically government contractors). It is the federal Government's primary litigation tool in combating fraud against the Government. The law includes a qui tam provision that allows people who are not affiliated with the government, called "relators" under the law, to file actions on behalf of the government (informally called "whistleblowing" especially when the relator is employed by the organization accused in the suit). Persons filing under the Act stand to receive a portion (15-30 percent, depending on certain factors) of any recovered damages. As of 2019, over 71 percent of all FCA actions were initiated by whistleblowers.
 
The case was taken up by the Department of Justice’s Civil Division. The government alleged that Workrite did not fulfill its contractual obligations to provide GSA with accurate information about its commercial sales practices during contract negotiations and did not subsequently extend lower prices to its government agency customers as required by the GSA contract’s price reduction clause. Workrite, faced the prospect of lengthy and expensive litigation, along with the uncertain consequences of potentially losing at trial.  The company therefore elected to settle the matter for $7.1 million, with Franchek receiving approximately $1.27 million from the settlement proceeds.

For more insight, contact Michael@ComplianceMiigation.com or visit our website.

metadata.shortDescription:
What's all the talk about the False Claims Act? What makes it unique? Why is everyone worried about it? During this webinar, Baker Donelson Shareholder Tom Barnard will answer these questions and more on the basics of the False Claims Act.

The False Claims Act casts a long shadow over many health care entities, including long term care providers. This webinar will help you:

-Identify potential risk areas
-Understand the nature of various processes
-Recognize opportunities to expand existing client relationships

As monetary recoveries by the Department of Justice for health care infractions continue to increase, understanding how the statute works, the risks, and what is likely to happen during an investigation will better position your company with your clients.

Visit Baker Donelson's Long Term Care practice at https://www.bakerdonelson.com/long-term-care

Visit Baker Donelson's Health Law practice at https://www.bakerdonelson.com/Health

Visit Baker Donelson at https://www.bakerdonelson.com

metadata.title: Financial Fraud: Qui Tam Lawsuits Explained
metadata.author: Tycko & Zavareei LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Looking to blow the whistle on financial fraud? Qui tam attorney Jon Tycko explains how to file a False Claims case for commodities, banking, lending, and securities fraud.

Contact Us for More information:

https://www.fraudfighters.net 

Tycko & Zavareei LLP
2000 Pennsylvania Avenue NW
Suite 1010
Washington, DC 20006
Tel: (202) 973-0900
Fax: (202) 973-0950

segments.text: In recent years, frauds affecting the country's
financial markets and systems have become a particular focus of
whistleblower reward programs.
A whistleblower in the securities,
commodities, lending or banking industries
is able to turn to government agencies
with their information.
And if those agencies obtain a recovery as a result,
the whistleblower can earn large rewards.
Currently, at least five major avenues
for reporting these types of frauds exist.
One: The False Claims Act.
If the fraud involves the mortgage lending industry
or other areas in which the government provides funding
or guarantees to lenders or insurers,
it may trigger liability
under the False Claims Act.
Two: The SEC Whistleblower Program
covers violations of the securities laws
or of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act,
and those may be reported to the SEC.
Three: Violations of the laws governing commodities futures
and other violations of the Commodities Exchange Act
may be reported directly to the CFTC.
Four: Fraud in the banking industry
may be reported to the Department of Justice.
And finally, violations of anti-money laundering requirements
or other violations of the Bank Secrecy Act
can be reported directly to the Treasury Department.
These programs have a number of factors in common.
Two of the most important being,
first, that rewards in each program are based
on a percentage of the government's recovery.
So the government must actually recover money
based on the whistleblower’s information before any reward is paid.
And second,
each of these programs has its own unique procedures
that a whistleblower must follow to preserve a right to an award.
Now, these agencies receive a large volume of whistleblower reports,
but only a small number result in recoveries and rewards.
So it's crucial that you present your information
to the agency in a way
that's not only correct under the agency's procedures,
but that is compelling enough
so that the agency will devote its limited resources
to pursuing your case.
The attorneys here at Tycko & Zavareei
understand these procedures
and know how to present your case to the agencies in a way
that maximizes the chances
that your case will be pursued to a successful conclusion.

metadata.title: False Claims Act
metadata.author: OIGatHHS
metadata.shortDescription:
The Office of Inspector General (OIG) of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) discusses the False Claims Act.


- - -


More info at
http://oig.hhs.gov

U.S. Department of Health & Human Services (HHS)
http://www.hhs.gov

segments.text: Hello.
My name is Katie Fink.
I am an attorney with the Office of the Inspector General.
I'm here to introduce you to the False Claims Act.
The False Claims Act, or FCA, provides a way for the government to recover money when someone
submits or causes to be submitted false or fraudulent claims for payment to the government,
including the Medicare and Medicaid programs.
Examples of health care claims that may be false include claims where the service is
not actually rendered to the patient, is provided but is already provided under another claim,
is upcoded, or is not supported by the patient's medical record.
Claims also may be false if they result from referrals made in violation of the Federal
Anti-kickback statute or the Stark law.
These laws are addressed in other OIG presentations.
When the government pursues violations of the False Claims Act, it does not target innocent
billing mistakes.
False claims are claims that the provider knew or should have known were false or fraudulent.
Should have known means deliberate ignorance or reckless disregard of the truth.
This means providers cannot avoid liability by ignoring inaccuracies in their claims or
hide their heads in the sand.
Health care providers need to understand the program rules and take proactive measures,
such as conducting internal audits within their organizations, to ensure compliance.
I should point out that even if a provider makes an innocent billing mistake, that provider
still has a duty to repay the money to the government.
The Affordable Care Act included a new requirement that providers must repay identified overpayments
to Medicare and Medicaid within 60 days or be subject to penalties.
What happens if a provider does not comply with the False Claims Act?
For False Claims Act violations, a provider can be penalized up to three times the program's
loss, plus an additional $11,000 per claim.
And penalties add up quickly because each claim for payment can be a separate ground
for liability.
In addition to serving as a powerful tool to recover money from fraudulent providers
and suppliers, the False Claims Act also provides a strong financial incentive to whistleblowers
to report fraud.
Whistleblowers can receive up to 30 percent of any False Claims Act recovery.
And that can be a lot of money.
Who are the most common whistleblowers?
Often whistleblowers turn out to be ex-business partners, current or former employees, competitors,
or even patients.
FCA cases are in the news and many involve large companies, such as drug and device manufacturers
or pharmaceutical companies.
But there also are many cases involving smaller entities and individuals.
For example, a recent FCA case involved a cardiologist who allegedly submitted claims
to the Federal health care programs for services that were not supported by patient medical
records and did not meet the billing criteria.
Additionally, the physician allegedly billed separately for services that the government
had already paid for as part of a bundled payment for a group of services.
To resolve these allegations the doctor paid $435,000 and entered into a 5-year Integrity
Agreement.
Providers must ensure that the claims they submit to Medicare and Medicaid are true and
accurate.
One of the most important steps a provider can take is to have a robust internal audit
program that monitors and reviews claims.
If a provider identifies billing mistakes in the course of those audits, the provider
must repay overpayments to Medicare and Medicaid within 60 days to avoid False Claims Act liability.
Providers also can disclose billing errors to the OIG through the OIG Self-Disclosure
Protocol.
Remember it is a provider's responsibility to consistently submit accurate claims.
It is the easiest way to comply with the law.
For more information, review the False Claims Act or consult with your health care counsel.

metadata.title: How Medicare And Medicaid Fraud Became A $100B Problem In The U.S.
metadata.author: CNBC
metadata.shortDescription:
In an exclusive investigation, CNBC takes you inside how fraudsters are stealing Medicare and Medicaid funds through a wide variety of criminal operations. Special agents from the Office of Inspector General (OIG) show us how brazen these schemes have gotten from burying stolen Medicare funds in PVC pipes under a home to setting up a fraudulent business in the same building as the OIG. A convicted fraudster who served time for health care-related crimes says it’s “very easy” to make millions and stay under law enforcement’s radar because the fraud is so rampant. In a Miami shopping mall that’s been the targeted of OIG investigations, CNBC finds a medical supply company that’s billed Medicare more than $2 million in a small glass-enclosed office with someone sitting at desk, which investigators say is typical about fraudulent operations are set up. Annual Medicare and Medicaid fraud is estimated at more than $100 billion.

metadata.title: Biz Tips: Understanding the new SEC Whistleblower Rules
metadata.author: BizTipsVideos
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn about the new whistleblower rules adopted by the Securities and Exchange Commission. http://ow.ly/VimEh 

These rules reward individuals who provide the agency with high-quality tips that lead to successful enforcement actions. Frank Campagna with CBIZ Risk & Advisory Services explains how these rules are important for your business.

CBIZ Risk & Advisory Services offers leading edge assurance and consulting services to help organizations navigate the perils of controlling a business in turbulent times. As part of CBIZ, the nation's 7th largest financial services provider in the country, CBIZ Risk & Advisory Services provides risk, internal control, internal audit, anti-fraud, and IT audit services to leading businesses across North America. With an internal leadership team from Fortune 1000 companies and Big Four firms, we provide experienced teams of professionals to assist you with your audit and compliance needs.

Visit http://ow.ly/VimEh for more information.
keywords: U.S. Securities And Exchange Commission (Government Agency)

segments.text: Welcome to Biz Tips.
My name is Frank Campagna, and I work for CBIZ in the Risk and Advisory Practice.
Today we're going to cover the new whistle blower rules and how they may impact your
company.
On May 25th, 2011 the SCC approved new whistle blower rules mandated by the Dodd-Frank Act.
These new rules reward whistle blowers who provide regulators with information on security
law violations.
The caveat is they need to lead to successful enforcement.
New rules provide a bounty to any individual who provides the government or self-regulatory
agency with new information, original information, based on independent knowledge or analysis
that is not already known by the commission.
The Investor Protection Fund was created to pay to these bounties.
The reward could be up to 30 percent of the penalties collected.
Prior to this, only insider trading cases paid a bounty, and that was only up to 10
percent.
Keep in mind, certain parties are excluded from being eligible whistle blowers, The most
commonly contested being attorneys, especially in-house counsel.
But there are exceptions to these rules.
There's been a great deal of concern and opposition to the new rules.
Many people, including the SCC Commissioner, feel it will undermine internal compliance
programs at many companies.
Also, they feel it will bring forth a plethora of new complaints, many of which that don't
have basis will still need to be managed and addressed.
The new rules have already brought forth modifications.
The grace period given to companies to investigate a tip internally has gone from 90 days to
120 days in order to be eligible for a bounty.
Another modification to the rules, which is very controversial point, allows whistle blowers
to not notify their company of their submission if they notify regulators.
If you'd like to discuss how these new whistle blower rules affect your company or your internal
audit department, please feel free to contact me at the email on the screen or visit my
LinkedIn profile.
Thank you for your time today in listening to my presentation.
I look forward to hearing from you soon.

metadata.title: Fraud, Healthcare, COVID 19, and the False Claims Act
metadata.author: First Healthcare Compliance
metadata.shortDescription:
First Healthcare Compliance hosts Shauna Itri, Partner at Seeger Weiss LLP, for an interactive discussion on “Fraud, Healthcare, COVID-19, and the False Claims Act.” A whistleblower or qui tam action can provide financial rewards to individuals who have information that a company/individual has committed fraud. The primary statutes under which this relief may be sought are the federal and state False Claims Acts (“FCAs”). In addition to the FCAs, there are other statutes which apply to tax fraud, securities fraud, and in California, fraud on private insurance companies. 

This practical Course will provide an overview of the False Claims Acts, the knowledge and skills to be able to recognize a potential whistleblower case, and understand the unique procedures utilized in filing whistleblower cases/tips. The second half of the Course will go into recent trends in cases brought (or could be brought) under the False Claims Act including cases involving mined data and potential fraud related to COVID-19.

This webinar will cover the following objectives:

1. Develop an understanding of the types of whistleblower laws available to clients to pursue fraud, waste and abuse.
2. Speak knowledgeably about whistleblower laws to potential clients.
3. Understand where government money for COVID-19 relief has been going, potential COVID-19 fraud schemes, and government response to COVID-19 fraud.

Our flexible and scalable solutions allow organizations to share, track, and manage their compliance processes with ease, view compliance in real time across all locations, and have peace of mind that they are current in all federal healthcare regulatory areas.

Administrators using the First Healthcare Compliance platform are able to share, track, and manage their compliance processes with ease, view compliance in real time across all locations, and have peace of mind that they are current in all areas.

metadata.title: Why physicians should care about the False Claims Act
metadata.author: Kevin Pho, MD
metadata.shortDescription:
Our guest, Scott Ellner, a general surgeon, shares insights and real-life stories that shed light on the challenges health care providers face when financial incentives clash with patient-centered care. We'll explore the impact of wasteful spending, the power of the False Claims Act in combatting fraud, and the Department of Justice's evolving focus on value-based payment models.

Scott Ellner has been a general surgeon for over 20 years, and can be reached at PEAK Health.

He discusses the KevinMD article, "In the crosshairs: The False Claims Act’s new targets in health care."

Our presenting sponsor is Nuance, a Microsoft company.

Together, Microsoft and Nuance are leveraging their rich digital technology and advanced AI capabilities to tackle some of health care's biggest challenges. AI-driven technology promises to revolutionize patient and provider experiences with clinical documentation that writes itself.

The Nuance Dragon Ambient eXperience, or DAX for short, is a voice-enabled solution that automatically captures patient encounters securely and accurately at the point of care. DAX Copilot combines proven conversational and ambient AI with the most advanced generative AI in a mobile application that integrates directly with your existing workflows.

Physicians who use DAX have reported a 50 percent decrease in documentation time and a 70 percent reduction in feelings of burnout, and 85 percent of patients say their physician is more personable and conversational.

Discover AI-powered clinical documentation that writes itself. Visit https://nuance.com/daxinaction to see a 12-minute DAX Copilot demo.

metadata.title: The Rise of State False Claims Act Enforcement
metadata.author: Husch Blackwell
metadata.shortDescription:
Host Jonathan Porter (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/jonathan-porter)  welcomes Husch Blackwell partners Rebecca Furdek (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/rebecca-furdek)  and Todd Gee (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/todd-gee)  back to the podcast to discuss the growing amount of enforcement under various state-level False Claims Acts, and the recent Risk Management Magazine article (https://www.rmmagazine.com/articles/article/2025/11/18/the-growing-liability-risk-of-state-false-claims-act-statutes)  that Rebecca and Todd have written on the subject. Our conversation starts with an overview of state False Claims Acts and how the use of FCA varies from state to state. We examine recent settlements in Massachusetts and Minnesota that show the reach of state False Claims Acts and discuss a large District of Columbia False Claims Act settlement for tax liability that could be the next big enforcement area for state-level False Claims Acts.


Our conversation then turns to how states have traditionally focused FCA enforcement on Medicaid claims but are broadening their FCA laws to reach new types of government claims. We discuss how California, for example, is considering a new law that would allow false claims relating to tax to be enforceable under the California False Claims Act. We also talk about how State Attorneys General are likely to play a huge role in using their state FCAs to enforce things that may not gain traction with federal authorities.


We conclude with a discussion of what might happen next, and how those doing business with multiple states should track what is enforceable under each state’s FCA. We look at how a robust compliance program should be every company’s first line of defense against FCA liability by finding and fixing issues before they result in FCA problems.


Jonathan Porter | Full Biography (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/jonathan-porter) 


Jonathan focuses on white collar criminal defense, federal investigations brought under the False Claims Act, and litigation against the government and whistleblowers. He advises clients on sensitive and enterprise-threatening litigation, drawing on his experience as a former federal prosecutor. At the Department of Justice, Jonathan earned a reputation as a top white-collar prosecutor and trial lawyer and was a key member of multiple international healthcare fraud takedowns and high-profile financial crime prosecution teams. He serves as a vice chair of the American Health Law Association’s Fraud and Abuse Practice Group and teaches white collar crime as an adjunct professor of law at Mercer University School of Law.


Rebecca Furdek | Full Biography (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/rebecca-furdek) 


A partner in Husch Blackwell’s Milwaukee office, Rebecca is a member of the firm’s White Collar, Internal Investigations & Compliance team and regularly helps clients navigate today’s regulatory and government enforcement landscape. Before joining Husch, Rebecca served as Counsel to the Solicitor at the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL), where she gained firsthand insight into federal agency rulemaking and administrative enforcement. Prior to her government service, she worked as an associate in the Washington, D.C. office of a global law firm, focusing on litigation and government enforcement, and began her legal career as a judicial law clerk at the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas. During law school, Rebecca served as a law clerk with the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee.


Todd Gee | Full Biography (https://www.huschblackwell.com/professionals/todd-gee) 


Based in Washington, Todd is a former United States Attorney and experienced trial lawyer who represents businesses and individuals in complex criminal defense, corporate fraud investigations, and regulatory compliance matters. With years of experience as a federal prosecutor and counsel to a congressional committee, he is well-positioned to help clients navigate high-stake and sensitive issues. Todd specializes in guiding them through multifaceted investigations involving overlapping risks posed by criminal investigators, civil litigants, regulatory agencies, or congressional inquiries.

metadata.title: UAP Whistleblowers: The False Claims Act
metadata.author: UAP Legion
metadata.shortDescription:
Unauthorized black budget UAP programs implicate federal fraud and abuse law. 

Ever wonder how the Department of Justice prosecutes U.S. defense contractors for fraud?

TOP SECRET classifications and non-disclosure agreements have NOT prevented the DOJ from prosecuting U.S. defense contractors.

The DOJ has used the False Claims Act to recover $78 billion from U.S. contractors since 1986. FCA whistleblower lawsuits, filed on behalf of the government, represent a substantial number of FCA cases. 

Major defense contractors settled more than 15 multi-million-dollar FCA cases over the past 22 years resulting in over $1.3 billion in government recoveries. These settlements were paid by Lockheed Martin, Raytheon, Northrop Grumman, SAIC, and Booz Allen Hamilton.

Under Section D of the FCA, monetary awards from $4 million to $68 million have been awarded to whistleblowers for reporting alleged defense contractor fraud. Section H of the FCA spells out federal laws providing injunctive relief, reinstatement, and damages for retaliation against whistleblowers.
