segments.text: It's been eight years since Leslie Keane's 2017 New York Times story
released footage of U.S. navy pilots chasing UAP. It took the U.S. congress six years to schedule
hearings on the UAP topic during 2023 and 2024. During 2025, we've learned more about the
phenomenon from independent whistleblowers and journalists than we've ever learned from the U.S.
government over the past 78 years. Why has U.A.P. disclosure been so
painfully slow? Until recently, UAP
whistleblowers perceived a lack of benefits for coming forward, as well as a lack of protections.
Many of these would-be whistleblowers have not received any legal advice.
Attorney Danny Sheehan is an admirable leader in the advocacy effort for UAP
disclosure. However, Danny Sheehan is not a False Claims Act whistleblower attorney.
The False Claims Act, or FCA, is a federal law that was enacted in 1863. The False Claims Act was
created to prosecute fraud committed by defense contractors against the United States government
during the Civil War. In recent years the False Claims Act has proven to be a critical tool for
helping the Department of Justice recover tens of billions of dollars from government contractors,
including Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, S.A.I.C., and Booz Allen Hamilton.
The FCA’s qui tam provision allows private individuals, called relators, to file lawsuits,
on behalf of the federal government. Qui tam FCA lawsuits are filed against government
contractors that knowingly submit false claims for payment. Under the requirements
of the FCA, the federal government has paid whistleblowers multi-million dollar rewards.
The FCA also includes federal legal protections against whistleblower retaliation.
Today we’ll discuss the role of the False Claims Act in UAP disclosure. We’ll share recent examples
of successful qui tam whistleblower lawsuits against government defense contractors,
including multiple settlements with Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, S.A.I.C.,
and Booz Allen Hamilton.
What is the False Claims Act? The FCA is a federal legal statute
that imposes liability on individuals or entities that knowingly submit false claims for payment to
the government; use false records in relation to a false claim; or conspire to commit such acts.
In the context of a defense contractor, fraud might involve billing for work not performed,
inflating costs, or misrepresenting the scope of work. For example, if a contractor bills
the government for a hundred million dollars for activities outside the contract’s scope,
this would constitute a false claim under the FCA. The federal FCA statute allows the government to
recover trebled damages (three times the amount of the fraud) plus penalties. As of July of 2025,
these additive penalties range from $14,308 to $28,619 per false claim. If a contractor
submits hundreds or thousands of false claims, the penalties can really add up
in addition to tripled damages on the applicable contract amount.
The qui tam provision of the FCA, derived from the Latin phrase meaning he who sues for the king as
well as himself, empowers whistleblowers to act as private prosecutors, filing lawsuits on behalf of
the government. This provision is particularly relevant for defense contractors' workers,
including both employees and 1099 contractors, with insider knowledge of fraudulent practices.
There are several steps to file a qui tam whistleblower claim under the False Claims Act.
Step One. Identify and Document the Fraud. The first step is for a whistleblower to
identify specific instances of fraud. There are several common types of defense contractor fraud.
Cross Charging involves shifting costs from one government contract to another.
Billing for Unauthorized Work involves charging for activities outside the contract’s scope.
Defective Pricing involves failing to disclose accurate cost or pricing data
during contract negotiations, as seen in the 2025 Lockheed Martin case, where the company
settled with the Department of Justice to pay $29.74 million to resolve FCA allegations.
The whistleblower must gather substantial evidence, such as invoices, contracts,
or purchase orders showing discrepancies; emails, internal memos, or presentations indicating
knowledge of the fraud; and or financial records demonstrating unauthorized expenditures.
In FCA cases, it is common for the relator, or whistleblower, to be someone with direct,
first-hand knowledge of fraud and access to evidentiary documentation.
In real FCA cases, the whistleblowers are commonly the Chief Financial Officer, a finance manager,
a compliance officer, a consultant, former dismissed employees, or others
with direct first-hand knowledge of fraud. Step Two. Consult with an Experienced False
Claims Act Whistleblower Attorney. Filing a qui tam claim is complex and
requires legal expertise. The whistleblower should consult an attorney specializing in FCA
litigation to discuss several key issues. There are two types of False Claims Act
attorneys. There are whistleblower attorneys who represent qui tam relators. There are also
False Claims Act defense attorneys, sometimes referred to as white collar defense attorneys.
First, an FCA whistleblower attorney must assess the strength of the evidence and the credibility
of the whistleblower. FCA whistleblower attorneys commonly work on a contingency basis. Legal fees
for FCA whistleblower attorneys, which may be over $1,000 per hour, will accrue millions of
dollars against the settlement or judgment during the litigation process. If the FCA attorneys do
not win or settle the case, the FCA attorneys will not get paid. FCA attorneys will think
long and hard about the strength of the evidence at hand before taking a whistleblower’s case.
Second, an FCA whistleblower attorney will ensure compliance with FCA procedural requirements. One
such requirement is the first-to-file rule, which bars subsequent lawsuits based on the same facts.
You want to be the first whistleblower to report government contractor fraud. If you are the second
whistleblower reporting the same fraud, and you are not working with the first whistleblower on
the same lawsuit, you may get nothing. Third, an FCA whistleblower attorney
will ensure to protect the whistleblower’s identity and rights during the process. Under
the federal FCA statute, whistleblowers are entitled to injunctive relief, reinstatement,
and or damages if they are retaliated against for being a whistleblower. In the private sector,
while some whistleblowers are terminated, it is not unheard of for a whistleblower
to keep their job during a multi-year case. Additionally, FCA cases are sealed confidential.
Step three. File a Complaint Under Seal. The whistleblower, through their attorney, files a
complaint in federal district court. The complaint must be filed under seal, meaning it remains
confidential to allow the Department of Justice to investigate without alerting the defendant.
FCA complaints include several elements. The whistleblowers complaint is a detailed
description of the fraudulent conduct. The complaint contains
a long list of the plaintiff’s claims. The whistleblower provides evidence supporting the
allegations. This evidence is commonly in the form of documentation, including financial records,
emails, slide presentations, and photographs. The whistleblower and their attorneys will
provide an explanation of how the fraud breaks the law and affects government funds. The fraud
may trigger the False Claims Act directly through outright fraudulent misuse of funds. The fraud may
also trigger the False Claims Act indirectly. If a defense contractor breaks a law other than the
False Claims Act or violates a term of the defense contract, this activity may trigger
the False Claims Act indirectly by triggering a breach of the defense contract. For example,
indirect triggers of the False Claims Act may include falsifying technical results, falsifying
quality performance standards, not adhering to regulatory requirements, or not implementing
mandatory cybersecurity standards. Any breach of a defense contract’s terms is a basis for
triggering a False Claims Act complaint and putting the entire contract’s value in question
as a fraudulent dollar amount, subject to triple damage value plus penalties per each violation.
Step four: Government Investigation. Once filed, the complaint is served
on the government. The government has 60 days to investigate, though extensions are common.
After the Department of Justice reviews the complaint, evidence,
and completes its own initial investigation, the case may be affected in several ways.
First, the Department of Justice may intervene in the case. When the DOJ intervenes in a
whistleblower case, the DOJ takes over the case and leads the prosecution. The DOJ has 93
U.S. attorneys nationwide. The DOJ allocates its resources to cases in which it has high confidence
it will recover funds and be successful. Alternatively, the DOJ may decline to intervene in
a whistleblower’s case. This does not necessarily mean the case does not have merit. The DOJ may
simply not have the resources for the case. Even if the DOJ does not intervene, it will still allow
the whistleblower, and their attorneys, to proceed independently if they choose.
Lastly, the DOJ may move to dismiss the case if the case lacks merit, is frivolous,
or simply represents a nuisance case seeking to shake down the defendant for money.
Step five. Litigation or Settlement. If the government intervenes, it typically
leads the litigation, leveraging its investigative resources to pursue the case. In False Claims Act
whistleblower cases, the DOJ can mobilize the FBI, Defense Criminal Investigative Service,
the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, Defense Contract Audit Agency, the DOD's Joint Program
Office, and Offices of the Inspector General in any department of the federal government.
If the government declines to intervene, the whistleblower can continue the lawsuit,
though this is more challenging. FCA cases take a long time. FCA whistleblower attorneys and
their clients should discuss in advance what they will do if the government declines to intervene.
Whether the DOJ intervenes or not, an FCA case may result in two categorical outcomes.
The first result is a settlement, wherein the defendant agrees to pay damages and penalties,
but likely admits no wrongdoing. The second outcome is a trial,
where a court awards triple damages, plus penalties, if the defendant is found liable.

recovers triple damages plus penalties. For example, if False Claims Act fraud involves
$100 million in improper billing, the recovery could be $300 million (triple or treble damages)
plus additional penalties. Since 1986, the FCA has recovered over $78 billion, with qui tam actions
accounting for a significant portion. There are major monetary awards for
whistleblowers with successful recoveries under the federal False Claims Act statute.
Under the federal False Claims Act, if the qui tam FCA action succeeds, the whistleblower is
entitled to 15% to 30% of the total recovery by law. The whistleblower’s award percentage is
determined by the court based on several factors. According to Section D of the federal FCA statute,
if the government intervenes in the case, the whistleblower shall receive 15 to 25 percent of
the proceeds of the action or settlement. If the government does not intervene in the case,
the whistleblower is entitled to receive 25 to 30 percent of the recovered proceeds.
Within these ranges, the court will consider The significance of the whistleblower’s
information, the extent of their contribution to the case,
the risk undertaken by the whistleblower, and compliance with FCA procedural requirements.
Hypothetically, let us assume a defense contractor is spending one hundred million dollars on
unauthorized activities. If the government recovers $300 million under tripled damages,
the whistleblower’s award could range from $45 million at the 15% minimum rate, up to
$90 million at the maximum 30% rate. As you will hear during real case examples momentarily,
these are not unprecedented awards for whistleblowers.
Protections Against Retaliation Under Section H of the federal False
Claims Act statute, whistleblowers are entitled to relief from retaliation, such as termination,
demotion, or harassment, for reporting fraud. If retaliation occurs, the whistleblower can file a
separate claim for reinstatement to their former position, double back pay for lost wages with
interest, and or compensation for special damages, including litigation costs and attorneys’ fees.
Recent Developments and Risks The FCA remains a robust tool,
with 979 qui tam lawsuits filed in fiscal year 2024, the highest in a single year.
It is worth mentioning that a 2024 Florida district court ruling declared the qui tam
provision unconstitutional. This ruling only creates binding precedent in the
Middle District of Florida for certain specific types of qui tam false claim whistleblower cases
when the government declines to intervene in cases in this district. At the current time,
this ruling is not binding precedent outside the middle district of Florida.
This ruling has no impact on the federal statute. Most major defense contractors are incorporated
in Virginia, Maryland, or Delaware. Would-be whistleblower’s and their attorneys should
be cognizant to avoid choice of law and choice of venue provisions placing their
cases in the Middle District of Florida. At least 15 different multi-million dollar
False Claims Act cases have been settled by major defense contractors during the past 22 years.

involved in these cases include Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, S.A.I.C., Raytheon, and Booz
Allen Hamilton. The total liability, if damages were trebled in court, would have likely been at
least three times this amount, if not more. Among these 15 cases,
several are worth mentioning. In February 2025, Lockheed Martin Corporation
settled FCA allegations for $29.74 million related to defective pricing on F-35 contracts.
The company allegedly failed to disclose accurate cost data, violating the Truth in
Negotiations Act. Under the federal statute, the whistleblower’s award in this case may not be less
than $4.4 million. This represents the minimum whistleblower award at 15% of the total recovery.
During 2023, Booz Allen Hamilton agreed to pay the government over
$377 million to resolve allegations that it violated the False Claims Act by improperly
billing costs to its government contracts over a 10 year period. The whistleblower, former Booz
Allen employee Sara Feinberg, was awarded $69.8 million for her role in pursuing the case.

for $325 million. Northrop Grumman agreed to settle the matter relating to alleged faulty
transistor equipment that its predecessor, TRW, sold to the U.S. government for use in
NRO satellites. The whistleblower in this case was scientist Robert Ferro, Ph.D. Dr.
Ferro alleged that he tested and identified the faulty transistors as a contractor for TRW through
his employer, The Aerospace Corporation. The whistleblower alleged that there was a
coordinated cover-up to conceal his test results and report of the faulty transistors , including
the use of his Non-Disclosure Agreement. Dr. Ferro received $48.75 million as his
whistleblower share of the recovery under the qui tam provision of the False Claims Act.
For this Northrop Grumman case, the Department of Justice constructed three
high-tech secure facilities called Sensitive Compartmented Information Facilities or SKIFs.
Many of the issues of the case could only be discussed in these secure SKIF facilities.
This case proves that neither top secret defense security classifications nor Non-Disclosure
Agreements of government contractors can deter the Department of Justice from
investigating and prosecuting fraud reported by whistleblowers under the False Claims Act.

The qui tam provision of the False Claims Act is intended to target whistleblowers who are
private citizens, and do work for government contractors. The False Claims Act specifically
excludes members of the armed forces. Most government employees are also excluded from
being whistleblowers under the False Claims Act if they obtained the information about
the fraud in the course of their official duties. Apart from the False Claims Act, there are other
federal laws intended to protect whistleblowers inside the federal government. The Intelligence
Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2014 amended the National Security Act to provide statutory
protections for government employees who make lawful disclosures of fraud, waste, or abuse.
PPD-19 is a directive signed by President Barack Obama on October 10, 2012,
titled Protecting Whistleblowers with Access to Classified Information. Its purpose is to ensure
that employees in the Intelligence Community, and those with access to classified information,
can report instances of waste, fraud, abuse, gross mismanagement, violations of law,
or substantial dangers to public health or safety. PPD-19 prohibits retaliation against intelligence
employees for such protected disclosures. Conclusion
Private citizens doing work for government defense contractors, who discover fraud, can use the FCA’s
qui tam provision to file whistleblower claims. By gathering evidence, consulting an attorney, and
filing a sealed complaint, the whistleblower can initiate a process that may lead to significant
government recovery, as well as substantial awards for whistleblowers. The three defense contract
whistleblowers we identified here were awarded from $4 million up to nearly $70 million. This
is a substantial benefit for whistleblowers. The FCA’s protections against retaliation also
ensure whistleblowers have rights to injunctive relief and damages. Despite the recent legal
challenge to the False Claims Act in the Middle District of Florida, the FCA remains a vital tool
for ensuring accountability in government contracting and DOJ enforcement efforts.
Whistleblowers can find False Claims Act whistleblower attorneys and law firms online.
Several qui tam whistleblower attorneys and law firms have won large settlements
against U.S. defense contractors over the past several decades.

Healthcare professionals and staff working inside practices, hospitals, pharmacies, and telemedicine companies may witness fraud that puts them in a difficult position. Under the False Claims Act, individuals with firsthand knowledge of fraud against the government can file what’s known as a Qui Tam lawsuit. These lawsuits typically involve billing fraud, false documentation, or misuse of programs like Medicare and Medicaid. The person who brings the case, is called a relator, and must collect detailed evidence, including dates, documents, and witness names. That information is then used to create a disclosure statement, which becomes the foundation of the claim. If the government accepts the case and it succeeds, the relator may receive a portion of the recovery.

Filing a Qui Tam requires legal counsel with experience in complex civil litigation, federal healthcare fraud and whistleblower claims. These cases must be built carefully to meet strict legal standards, and they are filed under seal to allow government review. Chapman Law Group represents both relators and healthcare providers nationwide in federal matters and handles both federal compliance issues, and those that are state specific in Florida and Michigan. Our attorneys guide clients through every step, from evidence collection to disclosure preparation and government interaction. If you're considering a Qui Tam or responding to one, contact us before taking your next step.

metadata.title: FinCEN Proposed Regulations
metadata.author: Fraud in America
metadata.shortDescription: In this episode, we explore the FinCEN Whistleblower Program, its recent regulatory updates, and how it aims to incentivize reporting of financial crimes like money laundering and sanctions evasion. Experts Poppy Alexander and Andrew Feller share insights on the program's structure, protections, and areas for improvement.

segments.text: Hello and welcome back to Fraud in
America. I am Jackie Dear, your host.
Um, today we are going to be exploring
the Financial Crimes Enforcement
Networks or Fininsen's whistleblower
program. Fininsen is a bureau within the
Department of Treasury that combats
financial crimes such as moneyaundering
and sanctions evasion. Joining us today
is Poppy Alexander. She is a partner at
the law firm Whistleblower Partners. She
represents whistleblowers in a variety
of industries and under all
whistleblower programs including the
Fininsson program um the false claims
act SEC CFTC IRS programs. We also have
with us Andrew Feller. He is special
counsel at cone and Kabinto. He has over
20 years of experience in securities and
commodities laws. He comes from a
background in the SEC where he was

operations in the financial regulation

treasury, OFAC, which is the office of

anti-money laundering act a few years

Whistleblower program was created as

violations as well. So the law was

that's what we've been involved in
andrew can you talk a little bit about
what it is what that process does.

uh the trading with the enemy act and

[clears throat] prohibit certain types

videos.full_text: Hello and welcome back to Fraud in America. I am Jackie Dear, your host. Um, today we are going to be exploring the Financial Crimes Enforcement Networks or Fininsen's whistleblower program. Fininsen is a bureau within the Department of Treasury that combats financial crimes such as moneyaundering and sanctions evasion. Joining us today is Poppy Alexander. She is a partner at the law firm Whistleblower Partners. She represents whistleblowers in a variety of industries and under all whistleblower programs including the Fininsson program um the false claims act SEC CFTC IRS programs. We also have with us Andrew Feller. He is special counsel at cone and Kabinto. He has over 20 years of experience in securities and commodities laws. He comes from a background in the SEC where he was investigating and litigating securities fraud matters as a senior counsel in the division of enforcement and has a deep background in the understandings of operations in the financial regulation space. So, they're going to help us unpack how the whistleblower program works, what the new proposed rules might mean for potential whistleblowers, and what loo loopholes might need to be closed um and how you can safely report financial fraud. So, let's dive in there. Can you give us a big picture of what Fininsen is and what it does? Pinson is a subd department within the department of treasury and they are tasked with stopping the movement of dirty money through the US banking system sort of most broadly and there's a number of ways that they do that sort of probably the best known is that if there is any questionable money transactions that happen in a a financial institution that financial institution has to file what's called a SAR a suspicious activity report those SARS go to Fininsson. Fininsson collects all of this data about a potential suspicious money movements and then uses that for investigations or farms it out to its investigative partners to try to stop various criminal activity. Because of that, Fininsson isn't responsible for ensuring that banks and other financial institutions comply with what's called the Bank Secrecy Act, which is the law that governs all of the rules around what banks and other financial institutions have to do to try to stop dirty money. What's interesting, and you know, as you mentioned, Jackie, in your introduction, Finson does not cover sanctions violations. However, the Fininsson whistleblower program does because they work with their sister organization within the department of treasury, OFAC, which is the office of foreign asset control. Um, and that is the agency responsible for governing sanctions. So, correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe that this whistleblower program was actually enacted through the anti-money laundering act a few years ago, and these new proposals are um implementing regulations for that whistleblower program. Is that right? >> So yes. So the original Finson Whistleblower program was created as part of the NDAA a number of years ago and that only covered bank secrecy act violations. And that program came as somewhat of a surprise. No one knew that this was going to be part of the law, but Finson was very excited about the program. They stood up in office and they started it. However, the original law, there were some basic issues that hadn't been resolved and it was narrow and that it only covered violations of the Bank Secrecy Act. In 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine, it became abundantly clear to a number of members of Congress that we needed something more robust and we needed to have whistleblowers incentivized to come forward and to know where to go to tell people about violations of sanctions violations as well. So the law was expanded as part of the anti-moneyaundering act to both expand it to cover sanctions violations and to resolve some of the loopholes that had been put in. But yes, that's only the first part to have the statute. We then also need the regulations which tells people how that statute is going to be interpreted and how it's going to be enforced. And that is now what we have here. These proposed regulations were released a couple of months ago and Taff Coalition uh our organization submitted comments on the proposed rules and so there's a process called a notice and comment process that happens here and that's what we've been involved in andrew can you talk a little bit about what it is what that process does. >> Sure. Under what's called the Administrative Procedure Act, the APA, there's a process under which agencies have to move forward with adopting rules to implement statutes. So the statute sets the the broad parameters of the program and then tasks a particular agency in this case Fininsen with with adopting rules to implement the broad parameters of the program. So what they do is they first draft and release what's called a proposed rule and that that is usually the product of just internal drafting and deliberation on what they imagine the program will look like. But then there's something called a notice and comment period where the public is invited to comment on the proposed rules and provide input on what on the AY's analysis as well as the public's views on on how the program should look. The agency is then required under the APA to consider the public comments in shaping its final rule. So the the comment process is really important and you'll often see lots of types of interested parties participating in in the public comment on proposed rules. That can include organizations like the TAF coalition or business organizations or members of the public whistleblowers really can be anybody who has some relevant views or experience. Comments are publicly available. They're submitted via a a website. There's a centralized government website for notice and comment on proposed rules across the government. And so it's a really important part of sharing with the responsible government agency lessons that that interested parties have had with similar rules and real life application of the types of processes that the that the agencies are contemplating. So in this case, because CAF coalition members are members of the whistleblower bar who've dealt with a wide variety of whistleblower programs, whether it's the SEC, the CFTC, the IRS, or the False Claims Act. Our members had a lot of views on how what best practices are for a government whistleblower program. uh we're able to to look at the proposed rule through that lens and then craft some comments intended to uh share our knowledge with Fininsen and partner with them in making this really a best-in-class program which they have the opportunity to be. >> Yes. Excellent. Thank you. So the proposed rules, they basically establish a Bolure program that will offer incentives to individuals to come who will come forward with information about violations of a few different statutes. And so maybe we can just go through and talk about what the kinds kinds of crimes are that we're talking about under this program. The violations include the Bank Secrecy Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, that's called AIPA. The Bank Secrecy Act is abbreviated BSA. I'm going to give you guys all these these upfront so that you know what we're talking about when we're talking about it later. Trading with the Enemy Act is TWWA and the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act which is the Kingpin Act. So all of those are covered um under these proposed rules. Can you go through kind of some like common violations of the Bank Secrecy Act for instance? >> Sure. So, the Bank Secrecy Act is the rule uh the rules that govern all of the compliance obligations banks and other financial institutions which are known as money services businesses or MSBs have to try to stop dirty money moving through their system. And generally speaking, there's sort of two buckets of rules. One is the compliance obligations banks and financial institutions have upfront to try to stop suspicious people from joining their institutions. So that's things like the know your customer rules or know your business rules. It's the reason all of us have to show a driver's license or some other ID before we open a bank account. It's those sorts of rules. The second half, the second bucket is the rules about what happens when there is a transaction that sends up a red flag or should send up a red flag. This is a very complicated process just to be very upfront about it and every bank has implemented it in a very different way. But generally speaking, they have to have some sort of system where in the, you know, millions or billions of transactions that happen a day, there's some way that the ones that are weird get flagged and that then goes to someone who then looks at it and says, "Yes, this is weird. No, this isn't." You know, Andrew has never sent $10,000 to Jackie, you know, before, and maybe there's something going on that we should know about. that then sort of goes up the chain and ultimately someone makes a decision about whether they need to report it to the government and that is the suspicious activity report or SAR. So the bank secrecy act largely covers banks but it also then covers money services businesses which are any business that facilitates the transaction of money. So it's the western unions of the world but it's also the PayPal of the world and it is many crypto companies because they are in fact facilitating the transaction of money as well. So those the MSBs have slightly different rules than the banks but generally speaking they have the same obligations to check for suspicious money. The last sort of part of it which is also part of the you know suspicious transaction process is what's called the CTRs or the currency transaction reports where banks are obligated to report to the government every time there is a transaction of more than $10,000 within a reasonable period of time and that is not fully defined but all the banks have different ways of checking. So, you know, you can't what's called structure your transaction where you do $9,000 one day and $1,000 the next. That will get reported. And again, these are all just different mechanisms to try to have some sort of check for all the different transactions to try to stop criminal proceeds from moving through our banking system. And what about AIPA? What are the some of the violations of AIPA that are common? I think for AIPA uh the trading with the enemy act and the kingpin act in all those cases you're talking about statutes that allow the government to designate particular entities or individuals as as sanctioned individuals or entities and and [clears throat] prohibit certain types of commerce or interaction with those entities or individuals. And so I think the broadly across those statutes, the violations that you're looking at, evasions or attempts to evade the the particular sanctions on the particular individuals or entities who have been designated under those under those statutes and under the processes that those statutes lay out. >> So let's kind of get into what the um proposed rules said and what is good, what might need to be changed in order to protect whistleblowers. I'll just start with there's a a proposed rule that says that there's a presumption that whistleblowers will automatically receive the maximum 30% share if the enforcement action is $15 million. So, how does that rule kind of protect smaller whistleblowers and make the program more efficient than other government programs? >> So, that builds off a provision that was adopted by the CC in 2020, I believe. And actually recently the CFTC proposed a similar rule in line with the SEC's rule. The SEC's rule applies to awards $5 million or or lower whereas Fininsen has proposed to set the limit at $15 million recognizing that that the cases and the dollar values that come through the Fininsen program are expected to be larger than the ones that that come through the SEC program. Interestingly, I was at the SEC when when the SEC equivalent of this rule was proposed. I was working for a commissioner at that time and reviewed that proposal. I was not sure how well it would work, but I am happy to say it it it really proved to be quite effective at moving some significant percentage of award claims through much more efficiently than they had been. It it really reduced the administrative burden for for issuing awards. So, I was happy to see this provision in the Fininsen rule. I was also happy to see the higher dollar amount. Well, actually, I think they didn't estimate how many of their cases would follow fall under that provision because there just isn't enough track record for the for the Fininsen program. I know that uh the CFTC recently in their proposal to to adopt a similar rule estimated that something like 80% of their awards historically would have fallen under this provision. So the hope is that this will create real efficiencies in the program. >> And then so also in the program um there in order to receive an award you need to provide original information and that looks different under different programs and in this proposal they proposed that to provide original information the whistleblower doesn't have to be the sole source of the information. It just contributes to the kind of mosaic of evidence that is out there. Why is that distinction kind of crucial for insiders who might only see one piece of the puzzle? >> I think that that is particularly important in the Fininsson context because as you said insiders do only see one piece of the puzzle particularly if they're in a financial institution which tend to be very everybody gets one part one piece of the puzzle and there tends to be you know a lot of process and a lot of different departments that touch every single transaction. And I think the other reason that it's really important in this particular context is because of all of the obligations banks have to report self-report all sorts of information. There is in fact a lot of information in Fininsson's hands already about a lot of the transactions that we're talking about. However, they're often lacking that last key that shows them where they need to look. And that's what whistleblowers can bring forward and need to bring forward. And so yes, maybe you know a particular whistleblower isn't the isn't quote unquote the source of information that you know a bank is failing to look at suspicious activity that relates to you know ATMs for example but they can be a source because they can point to Fininsson to the reams and reams of data that they have and say look you know this is where you need to be looking. >> Another good piece here is that they really encourage internal compliance reporting. So a lot of corporate whistleblowers want to give their company a chance to do the right thing first. And that these proposed rules pres preserve the elig eligibility of whistleblowers to receive an award even if the information reaches didn't send through a subsequent internal compliance report. How does that rule kind of balance the desire for strong internal compliance with the need to protect whistleblowers ultimate reward? This question of the extent to which rules are designed to either encourage or compel internal reporting before award eligibility has been an issue in the adoption of every whistleblower program. I think there's there are a variety of provisions in this proposal that relate to internal reporting and and it's probably a mixed bag altogether. That's part of what Taft Coalition is is weighing in on based on our experience with whistleblowers and based on real life knowledge of what can happen to whistleblowers who want to do the right thing, want to report internally, but may be aware that either the the mechanism is flawed, the internal reporting mechanism is flawed, or the person to whom they might be reporting uh is in some way complicit in the wrongdoing. and therefore reporting to them would be feudal or worse. So I I think there's a mix of good and bad as there is in almost every whistleblower program and I think a number of the comments beyond Taffft coalition related to this same tension and how to strike the appropriate balance. >> One I think one of the concerns is that the whistleblowers would be retaliated against after they report. So I think on the whole it's a very positive step to get this proposal out and and to invite public comment on on how they've structured it. There's an email address that you can send it to or there's a form online. It goes to the Fininsson whistleblower office. They then look at the information and determine which agencies are implicated by the information. And here's one of those, I think, quirks of the Finson program and maybe our banking laws generally. There's a lot of overlapping jurisdiction between different agencies. And so there's a lot of people who potentially are going to ultimately have some interest in a tip. So tips come in and then it gets farmed out. So if it's sanctions related, it goes to OFAC. If it's bank related, it's going to go to the OC. the office of the controller of the currency. It will probably also go to the Federal Reserve. It's then going to be sent over to the Department of Justice to whatever they're now calling the moneyaundering division, which I know the name has changed recently. We've had some that have been sent to the Department of Commerce. We've had some that have been sent to other parts of Treasury. So, you know, there's a lot of different people that ultimately may consider a tip, but there will ultimately be someone who is in charge and who's responsible, who's going to be taking the lead. Then there's going to be an enforcement action, we hope, and at that point, the whistleblower will submit an award submission to Fininsson and and that process is laid out in these proposed regulations. and in terms of, you know, what standards they're going to take into consideration when they're considering an award tip. And those standards, I think it's fair to say, are largely based on the SEC standards. Um, and are very similar in a lot of the ways that they're structured because it's ultimately going to be the Finson Whistleblower Office who's going to consider any whistleblowers award submission. It's really really important that any whistleblower keep the Finson whistbler office apprised of all the communications you're having with the all these different government agencies because often times you'll submit to Finson but then it's going to be OFAC who you're talking to but it's going to be Fininsson ultimately that is managing the award submission process. So you have to remember that which is a little bit complicated but I think the agencies do work together. Ultimately, they're all fairly small agencies and they all know each other. And so, you know, there's no reason to think that's going to be an issue, but it is something to remember. The whistleblower is entitled to an award of 10 to 30%, but only if they're per and that percentage depends on how much the agencies use their information, how valuable that information was. And so, that communication is going to be really important. Okay. Well, let's get into some of the things that we think could be improved with the proposed rules. And let's start with um how a whistleblower's award might be impacted by the bankruptcy of the company that's that's in question here. So, if a whistleblower exposes for instance like a startup or a a lightly capitalized firm, that firm goes bankrupt because of the fraud. What happens to the whistleblower's reward under the current proposal? I believe they would get no award. Unfortunately, this is an issue that has come up in the SEC context. And the SEC's program does not define collected proceeds of of an enforcement matter to include amounts distributed in bankruptcy, which means that if a company goes into bankrupt before bankruptcy before the SEC is able to to collect its sanctions, in all likelihood, there won't be a a payout to a whistleblower. Unfortunately, this the the Fininsson's proposal did not address that loophole in its in in the proposed rule. Some of our comments and the comments of others encourage them to address that in in any final rule so that we don't get in the same situation. As you referenced in your question, there are particular types of companies or industries where there's a higher likelihood of bankruptcy if there's an enforcement action. And our view is that Fininsen nevertheless should want to encourage reporting on those types of companies and industries and they are less likely to get the reports they want if they don't fix this bankruptcy loophole. >> So confidentiality is obviously very important to whistleblowers. Is there anything in these proposed rules that concern you about the confidentiality of whistleblowers identities? Yeah, I I think you're obviously right about the importance of confidentiality in terms of both whistleblower's anonymity, but also how their the information they submit will be treated because in many cases just the nature of the information is sufficient for someone knowledgeable to identify the whistleblower. So that was something we looked very carefully at the rules about and unfortunately there's some language in in the proposal that they made that suggests either Fininsen or the agencies that that use the information may be willing to to share the information for purposes that that we think are probably a little loosely defined and and potentially put whistleblowers at risk, frankly. And that includes some language in the proposal suggesting that they they might uh share information whistleblower information with with defendants to facilitate settlement discussions which could be could be very risky to whistleblowers and is is honestly one of our biggest concerns with with this proposal. So we've we've suggested changes to that language. I know I don't think we were the only commenters to raise this issue either. There were others from the whistleblower bar who raised it. I don't think the intention of the agency was to suggest that they would be in any way cavalier with whistleblower information, but I think in trying to preserve their flexibility, they may have gone a little little further than than we're comfortable with. And if if that's not changed in the final rule, I think we're going to have some very interesting conversations within the whistleblower bar about how to counsel clients in terms of of using this program at all. >> The proposed rules state that if you obtain information in violation of any state or federal law, you might be completely disqualified from an award. Just is that disincentivizing people from coming forward that might have the best evidence? >> So, this is one of the areas where I think T had quite a number of comments. So, first of all, just taking a step back, there's all sorts of rules already that would prevent someone from receiving an award if the criminal activity we're talking about related to the actual um, you know, bad acts by the company. That's not what's at concern here for us. I think the big concern is that we know a lot of people gather evidence in ways that may be considered at least criminally questionable under various state or local laws. None of which any of us are fully familiar with because that's not what we do and it's not something that our clients are going to be uh fully familiar with. There's also potentially concerns. there's um you know there's always companies that make claims about you know trademark materials and trade secrets and what have you which are not usually good arguments but that doesn't mean that they can't go to some local prosecutor and try to convince them that there is something there. So this is I think a real risk and something that we I don't think Fininsson intended for the full consequences of this potential restriction and is really important you know so for example recording laws there's all sorts of different recording laws there's one party states and there's two party states uh federal law generally speaking is a one party recording rule which means basically as long as one of the parties in the conversation is consenting to the recording it's okay but that's not true honestly state level and it's potentially not true on at the level of you know local laws or other rules. So for example in California where I am they you know a company can bring a civil acts against someone for an illegal recording and so they have an incentive to potentially try to convince a DA to go after someone for this. So, you know, all of these reasons make this very complicated and disincentivizing to a whistleblower who might be very nervous about their potential criminal liability for ultimately only trying to gather evidence to tell the government about a fraud that's happening and potentially much much more serious criminal activity. I I would just add, you know, this is particularly relevant in situations where where some of the evidence that a whistleblower may gather could be considered by by their company to be trade secrets or or intellectual property belonging to the to the company. And you know, this isn't just hypothetical. I it was probably about 10 years ago. was a software engineer who left Goldman Sachs and took took some code and that he wasn't he wasn't blowing the whistle. So, I want to be clear about that distinction, but nevertheless, it seemed like Goldman Sachs was able to convince the New York State prosecutors to to bring a criminal case against him for trade secret theft. You know, basically to protect Goldman Sachs's own interests. And so when incentives like that exist out there, this sort of broad and undescerning standard of of any, you know, evidence gathered in violation of any state or local law is just very risky for uh for whistleblowers. >> All right, let's move on to like a couple of technical standards that we think we might might need to change. The government wants whistleblowers to certify that their initial tip is complete. That's kind of unworkable in reality. Why is a whistleblower's first tip rarely complete and what standard do we propose instead? >> Well, first of all, no one knows what complete means, right? No whistleblower is going to show up with all the data that is potentially relevant to some particular bad act that would require them to present all of the data and that's that's not workable. So that that sort of like on a general level is a problem. I think on a specific level, there's all sorts of reasons and very good reasons and reasons the government wants to encourage that whistleblowers do not provide all the information in their possession when they first go in through the door. One, the government doesn't want terabytes of data if that's something in the whistleblower's possession. They want the good stuff. two, government really, really doesn't want anything that could potentially be considered attorney client privileged because that could potentially taint the entire government investigations team. So, the whistleblower, if they have that kind of information, should be withholding that um until they can work with the government on some sort of solution, potentially setting up a taint process or just segregating that information entirely. And then three, you know, whistleblowers, particularly whistleblowers working without counsel, may just simply not know what the important information is. They, you know, might be focused on one issue and not looking at another or might not understand that the government needs data related to showing that the senior leadership at the bank or the financial institution knew about the particular issue. And so maybe they're presenting, you know, all of the statistical data that shows that, you know, they're not filing sufficient SARS, but they're not showing the information showing that the, you know, the CEO or what have you knew about it. So that's not bad. That's just simply Whistler are doing what they're supposed to do, which is work with the government as a partner to figure it out. And I would point out just sorry to interrupt but I would point out that that when in drafting their award criteria among the things they look at are a whistleblower's ongoing assistance to the government which clearly contemplates that, you know, they're not going to be able to provide everything they know in one neat package up front. I I think the the idea of complete is certifying that a initial submission is complete is just sort of as Poppy said, no one knows what it means. >> And you just mentioned Poppy that some of people are filing tips without a lawyer. The rule allows for people to submit tips anonymously without hiring a lawyer, but we think that that's probably a bad idea. That could clog up the system with a bunch of AI generated spam. um and that we think lawyer representation is a good way to prevent that. Can you kind of explain why having counsel is so vital for an anonymous filer? Many of the other whistleblower programs have a provision that allow people to file anonymously as long as they're represented by council. And the reason for that is that we all as lawyers have to all sorts of ethical obligations and we have to make certifications to the court. And so what we can do therefore is we can certify to the agency that yes, we've verified this person's identity. They are in fact who they say they are. And we can act as a backs stop essentially for the agency in guaranteeing that the person, you know, Tom Jones is Tom Jones and is not an AI bot or, you know, and someone else who is stealing someone's identity or or even not something malicious. is just, you know, someone who thinks they know a lot more than they actually do. It's really important that we have that level of certification so that the government can trust the information that's being presented to them, particularly when they don't have someone's name attached to it. >> Can each of you identify maybe one more like big red flag that we want to make sure we get fixed in these proposed rules? I want to draw attention to actually some comments that that we referenced in the letter but were submitted by some colleagues of ours in the in the whistleblower bar. There there was a letter from TAF coalition members Caleb Hayes Deets, Jason Zuckermanman and Matt Stock that talked about the designation of of certain funds under the >> the US victims of state sponsored terrorism fund. >> That is correct. And I thought their comment was really important because it it it both pointed out some of the the way in which the the interpretation suggested by by Fininsen was was inconsistent with the statute which which ultimately controls. But it also pointed out from a policy perspective how it would undermine some of the objectives of the program. And I thought that was a really important comment given the importance of of those types of cases and that fund and our desire to to partner with Finins to to achieve the objectives they set out. And so that was why we we flagged that in our letter and and I would encourage others to take a look at that letter and and reach out to Finsen to the extent that they believe it's important. >> What about you Poppy? One other thing that struck me as important is that, you know, to to earn an award, you have to have a covered action, which is an action where the agency recovers at least a million dollars. But figuring out how to get to that threshold of a million dollars, the the proposed regulations provide that many actions can be combined as long as they're at quote substantially the same time. But first of all, no one really knows what that means. Substantially at the same time can mean many things. And secondly, that's not how these kinds of actions often resolve, particularly if there's both civil and criminal liability in there or if there's liability for individuals and for a company. Sometimes related actions are separated by a period of years. And so I think that that's something that should be changed and that can be changed from, you know, looking at the way, for example, that the SEC does. >> Yeah, agreed. Um, and you know, my big takeaway from this is that this is wonderful that there are proposed rules out here and we've been waiting a little while to get them. So, we are excited for these proposed rules to be out here. We hope that the agency really takes into account our comments on these rules. We have we do have a unique ability to to inform the agency about how these programs have been working the best under other programs like the SEC and CFTC programs. Um, do you guys have any other big takeaways that we should be thinking about or that whistleblowers should be thinking about as they're looking at this program? >> I think as I said before, it's exciting that they've put this out there. It's exciting that we're moving forward, but the but the details matter. I've worked on comment letters in a variety of of context. Sometimes what you're doing is looking at big big picture sort of directional issues and sometimes it's these really technical details that that make a huge difference. In this case, we focused our comment letter on a lot of those technical details because that's what we have experience with and uh we really do want to partner with Vincent to make this work. We have whistleblower clients who are excited by the possibility of being able to to report to Fininsen on on all of these matters and and to have a predictable process to deal with which is which is really important both for whistleblowers and their council. I'm hopeful that they will receive these comments in the spirit in which they were intended to to improve the program and make it work for for all sides, but we'll have to see and we'll be prepared to to advise clients no matter which way it goes. >> Any last thoughts, Poppy? >> This program is so important and, you know, honestly just becomes more and more important as the multitude of ways to send and receive money continues to multiply. And you know, we really need to be incentivizing whistleblowers to come forward to tell the government about anything that's not going the way it's supposed to be going because we all rely on it. We all rely on there being a functional financial, you know, system where we know that there's checks on criminal activity. And because these things always happen in the dark, we really need lawyers to come forward and tell about it. I'm really encouraged by all the ways that this proposal shows how important the agencies recognize whistleblowers are to that process. And I think we're going to continue to see that. And what will be really interesting is what happens when they issue their first award and you know when these regulations start taking effect and we have sort of the further guidance on what this program is actually going to look like. But it's exciting. It's great. >> Absolutely. Thank you Andrew. Thank you Poppy for joining us on Fraud in America. Thank you to our sponsor Getnick Law. And we will see you next time on Fraud in America. Our annual sponsor is Getnik Law, a boutique Manhattan law firm dedicated [music] to fighting fraud and promoting business integrity. Learn more about the firm at www.getniklaw.com. [music] If you believe you've witnessed fraud against the government or on the financial markets, or want to learn more about the [music] laws that exist to fight fraud, visit taf.org where you can [music] find a directory of whistleblower attorneys who work across the country. On our website, [music] you can find information about the nation's whistleblower laws and programs and a way to donate [music] to our organization as we continue to fight attacks on whistleblowers and these laws. [music] Fraud in America is presented by the anti-fraud coalition. Jaclyn Demar [music] is our host. The website for fraud in America was designed by Wideey Creative. Our artwork is by [music] PPA agency and our theme song is by spatial relations.

metadata.title: What Is the False Claims Act and Why Does It Matter?
metadata.author: Melissa Green Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
If you’ve ever suspected that your employer is defrauding the government — overbilling Medicare, submitting false invoices on a federal contract, or misusing grant money — you may have wondered whether anyone would care, would actually listen, and whether coming forward would be worth the risk.

The answer to both questions is often yes. And the law that makes that possible is the False Claims Act. 31 U.S.C. §§ 3729–3733.

To read the full blog or to learn more visit melissagreenlaw.com.

This video is for general informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. If you have specific questions about a potential False Claims Act case, please contact our office for a confidential consultation.

segments.text: What if you knew your employer was
stealing from the government? And the
law not only wanted you to speak up, but
could pay you to do it?
That is the promise of the False Claims
Act.
President Abraham Lincoln signed the
False Claims Act in 1863 during the
Civil War.
Defense contractors were selling the
Union Army sick horses [music] and
sawdust-filled gunpowder, forcing
Congress to enlist ordinary citizens
against fraud. [music]
More than 160 years later, the same law
remains the federal government's most
powerful tool against fraud. Its central
idea is simple.
People inside organizations may know
what government investigators cannot
see.
The law makes it illegal to knowingly
submit a false or fraudulent claim for
payment to the federal government.
It follows federal money wherever it
flows, including healthcare, contracts,
grants, loans, disaster relief, and
pandemic relief.
Examples include billing Medicare for
procedures never performed, [music]
upcoding services, paying kickbacks,
falsely certifying compliance, misusing
grants, or misrepresenting defense
equipment and costs.
The key tam provision lets a private
individual, called a relator, [music]
file a lawsuit on the government's
behalf, even when the government never
knew about the fraud.
That is what makes this law unusually
powerful.
First, you hire an attorney and file
[music] a sealed complaint in federal
court.
The government investigates while the
case stays sealed. Then it may intervene
or let you proceed. [music] If fraud is
proven, recovery follows.
Since Congress significantly
strengthened the law in 1986, the
Department of Justice has recovered more
than $75 billion through False Claims
Act cases.
Many recoveries were driven by
whistleblower lawsuits.
Whistleblowers typically receive between
15% [music] and 30% of the government's
recovery.
The depends on the whistleblower's
contribution [music] and on whether the
government intervenes in the case.
Recent cases have held pharmaceutical
companies, hospitals, defense
contractors, technology companies, and
employers accountable for conduct
involving healthcare, federal contracts,
cybersecurity requirements, and COVID-19
relief funds.
These cases waste taxpayer money,
undermine programs people depend on, and
give dishonest actors an unfair
advantage over competitors who follow
the rules.
Reporting can protect public resources
and program integrity. [music] Federal
law prohibits employers from firing,
demoting, or harassing employees who
report fraud or participate in a key
lawsuit.
Retaliation victims may also pursue
reinstatement, double back pay plus
interest, and additional compensation.
A viable case generally needs evidence
of a specific false claim submitted to
the government, not only a general
feeling.
The information must be original, and
another whistleblower cannot already
have filed the case.
Timing, documentation, and legal
strategy matter enormously.
Early decisions, including whether to
report internally first, can
significantly affect the outcome.
Speaking with a False Claims Act
attorney before acting is critical.
Congress [music] recognized a simple
truth. The people most likely to know
about fraud against the government
[music] are often the people on the
inside.
You do not have to figure out what comes
next alone. [music] If you believe you
have witnessed fraud against the
government, contact Melissa Green Law
for a consultation.
Get informed before acting, understand
your options, and decide on a careful
path forward.

A plain English primer on healthcare fraud and abuse law: the False Claims Act, qui tam whistleblower lawsuits, the Anti-Kickback Statute, the Stark Law, and what an effective compliance program looks like under HHS-OIG guidance. The show notes list the source for every legal point.

Main site: https://andrew-hillman.com/
Healthcare compliance expert witness page: https://andrew-hillman.com/healthcare-compliance-expert-witness/

Educational only. Not legal advice. Andrew Hillman is not an attorney, and this content creates no attorney-client relationship. The law varies by jurisdiction and facts. Consult a licensed attorney of your choice about your situation. Views are the host's own and do not represent any employer, client, or organization. This podcast does not accept tips, evaluate cases, or make attorney referrals. To report suspected fraud in a federal health care program, visit https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/report-fraud/.

Narrated by an AI voice (synthetic narration). No real person's voice or likeness is used.

segments.text: Welcome to The Hillman Letter Podcast.
This episode is a plain English primer on healthcare
fraud and abuse law.
We cover the False Claims Act,
qui tam whistleblower lawsuits,
the Anti-Kickback Statute, and the Stark Law.
Your host's notes come from Andrew Hillman,
Dallas, who works in healthcare compliance as
a Senior Paralegal and an expert witness retained
through counsel.
Andrew Hillman is not an attorney.
This episode is general education about federal
law.
It is not legal advice.
Listening does not create an attorney-client
relationship or any professional relationship.
The law changes, and it varies by state and by
facts.
For your own situation, talk to a licensed attorney
of your choice.
The views here are Andrew's own.
They do not speak for any employer,
client, or organization.
Start with the numbers.
In January 2026 the Department of Justice reported
that False Claims Act settlements and judgments
passed six point eight billion dollars in fiscal
year 2025.
Of that amount, over five point seven billion
dollars related to matters involving the health
care industry.
DOJ called that total the highest single year
in the history of the False Claims Act.
Whistleblowers also filed one thousand two hundred
ninety seven qui tam lawsuits,
the most ever in a single year.
The False Claims Act is a federal civil statute.
Under section 3729 of title 31 of the U.S..
Code, a person can be liable for knowingly presenting
a false claim for payment to the government,
or for knowingly making a false record that is
material to a false claim.
Knowingly has a broad meaning.
It covers actual knowledge,
deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard
of the truth.
The statute says no proof of specific intent
to defraud is required.
A person who is liable can owe three times the
government's damages, plus a civil penalty for
each claim.
Those penalty amounts are adjusted for inflation
by regulation.
Qui tam is the part of the law that lets a private
person bring a case on behalf of the United States.
That person is called the relator.
Under section 3730 the complaint is filed under
seal for at least sixty days,
and it is not served on the defendant until the
court orders it.
Meanwhile, the government decides whether to
intervene.
If the government proceeds,
the relator generally receives at least fifteen
but not more than twenty five percent of the
recovery.
If the government declines and the relator goes
forward, the range is generally twenty five to
thirty percent.
The statute also protects employees,
contractors, and agents from retaliation for
lawful acts in furtherance of a False Claims
Act case, or other efforts to stop a violation.
It bars some cases based on information already
publicly disclosed.
And section 3731 sets time limits,
generally six years, with a longer window in
some cases, but no more than ten years after
the violation.
Now the Anti-Kickback Statute,
at section 1320a-7b of title 42.
In short, it makes it a crime to knowingly and
willfully offer, pay, solicit,
or receive any remuneration to induce or reward
referrals of items or services paid for by a
federal health care program.
Remuneration means anything of value,
not just cash.
One provision ties this law to the False Claims
Act:
a claim that includes items or services resulting
from a kickback violation is a false claim.
A separate provision says a person does not need
actual knowledge of the Anti-Kickback Statute,
or specific intent to violate it.
Regulations at part 1001 of title 42 of the Code
of Federal Regulations set out safe harbors.
Arrangements that meet every element of a safe
harbor are protected.
Failing a safe harbor does not make an arrangement
automatically illegal.
OIG looks at the totality of the facts and circumstances,
including intent.
The Stark Law, at section 1395nn of title 42,
deals with physician self referral.
If a physician, or an immediate family member,
has a financial relationship with an entity,
the physician may not refer Medicare patients
to that entity for designated health services,
unless an exception applies.
The entity may not bill Medicare for services
furnished under a prohibited referral.
Unlike the Anti-Kickback Statute,
the basic Stark prohibition does not turn on
intent.
That is why the exceptions,
and the paperwork behind them,
matter so much.
So what does good compliance look like?
The HHS Office of Inspector General published
its General Compliance Program Guidance in November 2023
The guidance is voluntary and nonbinding,
and it describes seven elements.
Written policies and procedures.
Compliance leadership and oversight.
Training and education.
Open lines of communication,
including a way to report concerns.
Enforcing standards through consequences and
incentives.
Risk assessment, auditing, and monitoring.
And responding to problems with corrective action.
A practical first step is simple.
List every referral source and every paid relationship,
and confirm each one has a written agreement
and a documented legal basis.
Where does Andy fit in?
His LinkedIn profile describes healthcare compliance
work for counsel.
That includes Stark Law, Anti-Kickback,
and HIPAA compliance, internal investigations,
document review, and support for expert reports.
He works as a Senior Paralegal,
and as an expert witness he is retained through
counsel.
He is not an attorney, and he does not give legal
advice.
This podcast does not take tips,
evaluate cases, or refer anyone to a lawyer.
If you have a concern about fraud in a federal
health care program, you can report it to the
HHS Office of Inspector General at oig dot h
h s dot gov, or speak with a licensed attorney
of your choice.
Once more:
this episode is education, not legal advice.
Andrew Hillman is not an attorney.
Nothing here creates an attorney-client relationship.
For advice on your situation,
talk to a licensed attorney of your choice.
Thanks for listening to The Hillman Letter Podcast.

videos.full_text: Welcome to The Hillman Letter Podcast. This episode is a plain English primer on healthcare fraud and abuse law. We cover the False Claims Act, qui tam whistleblower lawsuits, the Anti-Kickback Statute, and the Stark Law. Your host's notes come from Andrew Hillman, Dallas, who works in healthcare compliance as a Senior Paralegal and an expert witness retained through counsel. Andrew Hillman is not an attorney. This episode is general education about federal law. It is not legal advice. Listening does not create an attorney-client relationship or any professional relationship. The law changes, and it varies by state and by facts. For your own situation, talk to a licensed attorney of your choice. The views here are Andrew's own. They do not speak for any employer, client, or organization. Start with the numbers. In January 2026 the Department of Justice reported that False Claims Act settlements and judgments passed six point eight billion dollars in fiscal year 2025. Of that amount, over five point seven billion dollars related to matters involving the health care industry. DOJ called that total the highest single year in the history of the False Claims Act. Whistleblowers also filed one thousand two hundred ninety seven qui tam lawsuits, the most ever in a single year. The False Claims Act is a federal civil statute. Under section 3729 of title 31 of the U.S.. Code, a person can be liable for knowingly presenting a false claim for payment to the government, or for knowingly making a false record that is material to a false claim. Knowingly has a broad meaning. It covers actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, and reckless disregard of the truth. The statute says no proof of specific intent to defraud is required. A person who is liable can owe three times the government's damages, plus a civil penalty for each claim. Those penalty amounts are adjusted for inflation by regulation. Qui tam is the part of the law that lets a private person bring a case on behalf of the United States. That person is called the relator. Under section 3730 the complaint is filed under seal for at least sixty days, and it is not served on the defendant until the court orders it. Meanwhile, the government decides whether to intervene. If the government proceeds, the relator generally receives at least fifteen but not more than twenty five percent of the recovery. If the government declines and the relator goes forward, the range is generally twenty five to thirty percent. The statute also protects employees, contractors, and agents from retaliation for lawful acts in furtherance of a False Claims Act case, or other efforts to stop a violation. It bars some cases based on information already publicly disclosed. And section 3731 sets time limits, generally six years, with a longer window in some cases, but no more than ten years after the violation. Now the Anti-Kickback Statute, at section 1320a-7b of title 42. In short, it makes it a crime to knowingly and willfully offer, pay, solicit, or receive any remuneration to induce or reward referrals of items or services paid for by a federal health care program. Remuneration means anything of value, not just cash. One provision ties this law to the False Claims Act: a claim that includes items or services resulting from a kickback violation is a false claim. A separate provision says a person does not need actual knowledge of the Anti-Kickback Statute, or specific intent to violate it. Regulations at part 1001 of title 42 of the Code of Federal Regulations set out safe harbors. Arrangements that meet every element of a safe harbor are protected. Failing a safe harbor does not make an arrangement automatically illegal. OIG looks at the totality of the facts and circumstances, including intent. The Stark Law, at section 1395nn of title 42, deals with physician self referral. If a physician, or an immediate family member, has a financial relationship with an entity, the physician may not refer Medicare patients to that entity for designated health services, unless an exception applies. The entity may not bill Medicare for services furnished under a prohibited referral. Unlike the Anti-Kickback Statute, the basic Stark prohibition does not turn on intent. That is why the exceptions, and the paperwork behind them, matter so much. So what does good compliance look like? The HHS Office of Inspector General published its General Compliance Program Guidance in November 2023 The guidance is voluntary and nonbinding, and it describes seven elements. Written policies and procedures. Compliance leadership and oversight. Training and education. Open lines of communication, including a way to report concerns. Enforcing standards through consequences and incentives. Risk assessment, auditing, and monitoring. And responding to problems with corrective action. A practical first step is simple. List every referral source and every paid relationship, and confirm each one has a written agreement and a documented legal basis. Where does Andy fit in? His LinkedIn profile describes healthcare compliance work for counsel. That includes Stark Law, Anti-Kickback, and HIPAA compliance, internal investigations, document review, and support for expert reports. He works as a Senior Paralegal, and as an expert witness he is retained through counsel. He is not an attorney, and he does not give legal advice. This podcast does not take tips, evaluate cases, or refer anyone to a lawyer. If you have a concern about fraud in a federal health care program, you can report it to the HHS Office of Inspector General at oig dot h h s dot gov, or speak with a licensed attorney of your choice. Once more: this episode is education, not legal advice. Andrew Hillman is not an attorney. Nothing here creates an attorney-client relationship. For advice on your situation, talk to a licensed attorney of your choice. Thanks for listening to The Hillman Letter Podcast.

I thought it appropriate, at this point, to spend some time on how illegal and inaccurate coding and billing can result in significant consequences for a physician and practice. I will address the False Claims Act, HIPAA and HITECH in the next videos.

First the False Claims Act.

The False Claims act [FCA] has been the federal government’s primary tool for combating fraud in federal government programs.

The FCA applies to all efforts to fraudulently have the government pay out money.

Liability under the FCA attaches to the individual or healthcare entity seeking a government payout at the moment a fraudulent claim is submitted to the government.

Submitting fraudulent claims to Medicare or Medicaid is a good way for a practice to get caught up in the liability of the FCA.

metadata.title: SEC Whistleblower Attorneys - Overview
metadata.author: Silver Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
The U.S. government recognizes that ordinary citizens and corporate insiders can make huge contributions to prosecuting securities and investment fraud. The SEC relies on information and assistance from whistleblowers to help them.
So who is a whistleblower? A whistleblower is anyone who provides new material information about a federal securities violation. If the information provided leads to an enforcement action of more than $1 million in sanctions, rewards will be between 10% and 30% of the sanctions.

Congress created the SEC Whistleblower Program to provide financial incentives for people to come forward when they suspect violations of federal securities laws and to provide protection for the whistleblowers.

Scott Silver of Silver Law explains more about the Whistleblower Program. He says:
“In order to be eligible for the SEC incentives, you can be a current employee of the company that you report, a victim of an investment scheme, or even an outside analyst who voluntarily provides new information. You need not submit the information yourself. It is possible and often advisable to submit the information through a securities whistleblower attorney.”

Silver continues to explain that various securities violations can give rise to whistleblowing. 

Violations can include:
Insider trading 
Misrepresentations in securities sales
Brokerage firm malfeasance
Fraud in buying or selling investments
(and) Market manipulation. 

The Securities Whistleblower program protects your interests, however, it is not easy to navigate. If you suspect, or if you have suffered losses, due to a securities violation, the experienced team at SEC Whistleblower Attorneys are ready to protect and advance your interests.

One of their attorneys, Scott Silver, previously worked as a defense attorney on Wall Street, and he now uses insights gained from that experience to fight for the rights of whistleblowers and investors. 

Another of their attorneys, David Chase, has gained substantial insights from previously working as Senior Counsel in the SEC's Enforcement Division, prosecuting violations of securities laws.

If you have information and are considering becoming a whistleblower, visit Scott Silver and David Chase at securitieswhistleblowerattorneys.com or call them toll-free at 800-975-4345.

metadata.title: Medicare Scam: Nurse Billed 24+ Hours a Day in Free Cancer Test Scheme
metadata.author: Money vs. The System
metadata.shortDescription:
This Medicare scam used a "free" cheek swab to bill for visits that never happened. One nurse practitioner billed Medicare for more than 24 hours a day — and got 20 years.

On many days in 2020, a Miami nurse practitioner billed Medicare for more than 24 hours of video visits — visits that never happened. A federal jury convicted her, she was sentenced to 20 years, and on July 31, 2026 the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit affirmed. This is how the "free genetic test" Medicare fraud works, step by step, from the phone call ("Medicare covers it") to the cheek swab, the signature and the lab — told through three federal cases: United States v. Hernandez (affirmed on appeal), United States v. Joyner (affirmed on appeal) and United States v. Patel / LabSolutions (convicted at trial; appeal pending). At the end: how to check your Medicare Summary Notice and where to report senior scams like this one — for yourself or for aging parents.

Patel's appeal is pending and he has asked for a new trial; the facts about LabSolutions in this video are what the jury found and what the Justice Department reported. Scenes are AI-generated reconstructions. No real people are shown.
