metadata.title: FCA Consumer Duty Explained | Delivering Good Outcomes for Customers!
metadata.author: Business with Mr. G
metadata.shortDescription:
What is Consumer Duty and how does it change financial regulation in the UK?

In this episode of the FCA REGULATIONS Masterclass, we break down:

• What Consumer Duty is
• Principle 12 and the new Consumer Principle
• The cross-cutting rules
• The four Consumer Duty outcomes
• Price and value requirements
• Consumer understanding expectations
• Supporting vulnerable customers
• Governance and board accountability
• Why Consumer Duty represents a shift to outcomes-based regulation

Consumer Duty marks one of the most significant changes in UK financial services regulation in recent years. It moves firms from technical compliance toward proactive delivery of good customer outcomes.

Whether you work in compliance, financial advice, banking, mortgage services, fintech, wealth management or governance, understanding Consumer Duty is essential.

This video is part of the FCA REGULATIONS series — a structured deep dive into UK financial regulation and supervisory expectations.

Subscribe for professional-level regulatory clarity.

► Financial Conduct Authority link: https://fincrimeintelligence.com/glossary/financial-conduct-authority/
► The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) refers to the United Kingdom’s conduct regulator for financial services, responsible for promoting market integrity, effective competition, and appropriate consumer protection. In the financial crime environment, the FCA is especially important because its supervisory expectations sit at the intersection of consumer harm, market abuse, firm governance, and financial crime controls.

From a compliance and financial crime perspective, the FCA shapes how regulated firms design, operate, monitor, and evidence their controls across areas such as money laundering, terrorist financing, fraud, sanctions, bribery and corruption, market abuse, transaction reporting, and wider conduct risk. Its guidance, thematic findings, enforcement actions, supervisory priorities, and Financial Crime Guide influence how firms assess risk, strengthen governance, improve surveillance, and remediate control weaknesses.

An effective FCA-aligned compliance framework requires strong governance, risk-based systems and controls, market abuse surveillance, fraud prevention, sanctions screening, AML oversight, regulatory reporting controls, training, independent testing, and clear escalation processes. For financial crime teams, the FCA is a key regulatory reference point for understanding what credible, proportionate, and effective controls should look like in the UK financial services sector.

segments.text: In this video we'll talk about the role of the FCA, one of the UK main financial services
regulators.
You will learn: Who is the Financial Conduct Authority, which are the FCA's primary responsibilities,
why firms are regulated by the FCA, and the Legal powers of this UK regulator.
So let's jump right into, today's video.
Hi and welcome to FinCrime Agent my YouTube channel where every week I publish a new video
to boost your awareness about AML and Financial Crime prevention.
Today we will learn more about the role of the FCA one of the UK financial services regulators.
If you are working or are starting a career within the financial services sector, having
the knowledge of the regulatory environment in which you work is vital, regardless of
the field of finance or the size of company you are working for.
The United Kingdom, has one of the largest financial services sectors in the world and
is the headquarter to several of the world's most prominent financial institutions.
In the UK there are 3 key regulators within the Financial Markets.
Those are the Financial Policy Committee, The Prudential
Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority (the FCA).
This video will help you understand the role of the FCA which is a must if your profession
is within the financial sector.
So let me start with the basics:
Who is the FCA?
"The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) regulates the financial services industry in the UK.
Its role includes protecting consumers, keeping the industry stable, and promoting healthy
competition between financial service providers."
The FCA is the government agency in charge of regulating all financial services operations
that take place in the [image 8] United Kingdom or involve UK-based firms, persons, or organisations.
[image 9] Trading firms, banks, currency exchange companies or accounting firms just to mention
a few, [footage 10] all must have frameworks and rules that they establish and update on
a regular basis in line with the FCA guidance and regulations.
Being in breach or not following the FCA regulations will have serious consequences for your business
and career, and in most scenarios may as well put you in prison.
Also is worth noting that, without the FCA's permission, you will be unable to legally
perform financial services operations in the United Kingdom.
With that in mind, let's take a closer look at the role of the FCA to see what the Financial
Conduct Authority does and how their mandate affects you.
FCA's primary responsibilities
The first thing to note is that the public interest is always at the centre of any activities
completed by UK regulators.
The FCA's primary responsibility is to prevent financial services businesses from engaging
in wrongdoing.
They'll look into and prosecute traditional forms of wrongdoing like:
insider dealing, unregulated banking activities which are also known as Shadow Banking, breach
within the broader financial crime space, but that's not all.
They also strive to prevent anti-competitive practices such as monopoly formation, financial
product misselling, and market manipulation.
The FCA badge Let's now talk about the FCA budge that you
often see on the page of regulated UK firms.
The FCA oversees the behavior of 51,000 financial services businesses and financial markets
in the United Kingdom, according to the FCA's website.
[slide 8] Having the the FCA badge for a firm that operates within the financial services
sector in the UK is a way to demonstrate that is legally operating under the FCA rules.
This provides a degree of trust for to their customers and is also a requirement for most
firms operating within the financial services sector in the UK.
The majority of the revenue required by the FCA to carry out its statutory obligations
comes from fees which are paid to the FCA by those businesses.
The application fee starts from £1,500 for the so called "Straightforward" application
up to £25,000 for the more "Complex" applications.
Additionally, firms regulated by the UK FCA would also pay annual fees which are are determined
by the sort of regulated activities carried out by a business, the volume of those activities,
and the FCA's regulatory expenses.
So if you wish to do business in the financial services within the United Kingdom, joining
the FCA and paying a membership fee is the first step to legally operate.
The FCA Investigation of Legal Matters
Let's now talk about the legal powers of the FCA for investigations that are related to
financial crime.
Instead of sending possible cases of wrongdoing to the police, the FCA has significant enforcement
powers and may start investigations against firms and people.
The FCA, as an arm of the UK government, has in fact the authority to investigate any person
or company for whom they have a reasonable suspicion of financial crime.
The FCA's investigations may result in license suspensions, multi-million-pound penalties,
and the arrest and imprisonment of individuals convicted of a crime by a British court.
As a result, adherence to the FCA rules and regulations is a critical aspect for all UK
firms and individuals operating within the financial services sector.
Conclusions KEY TAKEAWAYS:
- The FCA is in charge of the financial markets in the United Kingdom.
- The FCA's mission is to safeguard consumers, defend financial markets, and promote competition
in order to maintain honest and fair markets.
- The FCA is a government agency that reports to the Treasury and Parliament of the United
Kingdom.
- The FCA also is paid by fees from the businesses it oversees and regulate.
- The Role of the FCA is also to investigate firms to ensure full compliance with their
rules.
With that I am at the end of today's video.
If this video was useful to you, you can show your appreciation and support my channel by
subscribing to FinCrime Agent and press the thumb up.
Also remember to check the description to find some useful links including how to become
part of our community on Patreon.
Lastly, thank you for watching, I hope you enjoyed my video and until next time: See you soon!

**HJ Collection Investors – Independent Community | Video 2**

Have you invested in HJ Collection or Hunter Jones loan notes?

This video explains how concerned investors can contact the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), what documents they should prepare, and how to organise their evidence.

**FCA investor contact:**
AvillConsumers@fca.org.uk

**Official FCA announcement:**
https://www.fca.org.uk/news/press-releases/fca-takes-hunter-jones-high-court-over-alleged-unauthorised-activity

Documents to consider preserving include:
- Loan note agreements and investment certificates
- Bank transfer confirmations
- Marketing brochures and promotional material
- Emails and correspondence
- Interest payments and repayment information
- A chronological summary of events

On 21 September 2026, the FCA announced High Court proceedings concerning alleged unauthorised regulated activity by Osborne Baldwin Limited, trading as Hunter Jones and Hunter Jones Group. The allegations have not been determined by the court.

Contacting the FCA does not automatically initiate a compensation claim. Investors should also consider appropriate bank and insolvency processes.

Our independent community supports factual information, organised evidence and fair treatment of investors.

Hunter Jones loan note?
This short guide explains how to contact
the Financial Conduct Authority and how
to organize the evidence you send. On
the 21st of September 2026 the FCA
announced high court proceedings against
Osborne Baldwin Limited trading as
Hunter Jones and Hunter Jones Group
alleging unauthorized regulated
activity.
These are allegations, not findings by
the court. The FCA invited concerned
Hunter Jones investors and anyone with
relevant information to make contact.

FCA's official website. The dedicated
email address is
avilconsumers@fca.org.uk.

fca.org.uk.

announcement before sending. Use a clear
subject line such as Hunter Jones/HJ
Collection Investor Information and
Documents.
Briefly state your name, the product or
collection you invested in, how much you
paid, and when. Include copies of signed
loan notes, investment applications,
welcome letters, certificates, and
documents identifying the issuing
company, trustee, or security
arrangements if you have them. Add
payment confirmations or bank transfer
records with payment dates and recipient
names.

metadata.title: Risk Prevention Strategies: FCA Risk Prevention for Government Contractors
metadata.author: PilieroMazza PLLC
metadata.shortDescription:
With over $2.2 billion in recoveries for the Department of Justice (DOJ) in settlements and judgments from civil cases involving fraud and the False Claims Act (FCA) in 2020, statistics confirm that the FCA remains an effective and important enforcement tool for the DOJ.  Government contractors and companies that do business with government contractors should be wary of being the target of potential enforcement action in 2021 and beyond.  In this webinar, PilieroMazza’s Matt Feinberg and Camilla Hundley, attorneys in the Firm’s False Claims Act Group, discuss essential protocols companies should follow to avoid or mitigate FCA risk.

The presentation will focus on, among other things:

- latest trends in FCA enforcement for government contractors;
- the importance of an FCA compliance plan for government contractors, including small businesses and participants in the U.S. Small Business Administration’s (SBA) set-aside programs; and
- how to handle whistleblower complaints before they become FCA cases.

Disclaimer
This communication does not provide legal advice, nor does it create an attorney-client relationship with you or any other reader. If you require legal guidance in any specific situation, you should engage a qualified lawyer for that purpose. Prior results do not guarantee a similar outcome.
 
Attorney Advertising
It is possible that under the laws, rules, or regulations of certain jurisdictions, this may be construed as an advertisement or solicitation.

metadata.title: How Can I Make a Strong False Claims Act Case? | Tony Munter Attorney at Law
metadata.author: Tony Munter Attorney at Law
metadata.shortDescription:
Visit: http://whistleblower-quitam-attorney.net/false-claims-act-lawyer/

False Claims Act Lawyer Tony Munter explains what makes a good FCA case. As you can find on his website, or in his other videos, there are numerous legal definitions and requirements that need to be met in order to have a successful False Claims Act case. And, for nontraditional FCA cases, it is important to keep a close eye on how those legal elements match up with the facts. In an obvious FCA case, however, there are two main, common-sense elements that need to be met.

First, a good False Claims Act case needs to scream out fraud to anyone looking over the facts. If it is clear that a person, entity, or even multiple parties are getting ripped off, then you are halfway to having a strong False Claims Act case. Put differently, for a good FCA case you need to be able to easily explain how there was fraud and who was being defrauded. This is in contrast to some nontraditional or harder FCA cases where it is difficult to explain the complex relationships between actors and who, if anyone, was defrauded. 

This is not to say that a False Claims Act case is the same as common law fraud. Still, if you are unable to clearly explain how someone has gotten ripped off, it is unlikely that you have a good FCA case or a case that will work out. If you are able to easily explain where and how the fraud occurred, or if the facts of your case clearly scream out fraud, then you need to look at the second of these basic, common-sense elements.

The second necessary element of a good FCA case is that there must have been government money at stake. Or, put differently, a strong False Claims Act case involves a government agency that has been ripped off. This element is not only true for good federal False Claims Act cases, but for State False Claims cases, as well. Good FCA cases must, at some level, involve government money. This can include cases where the government is paying contractors, where government funding is involved through programs like Medicaid or Medicare, or even where the sub-contractors are being paid by contractors who are paid by the government. For a good False Claims Act case, you must be able to clearly show how government money is at stake, and this usually means that you can point to precisely which government agency is being ripped off by the actions described in the first element.

This means that if the case before you clearly has someone being ripped off, but that someone is a big private firm, then it very unlikely you have a False Claims Act case. In such a situation, your actions as a whistleblower will likely take a different form by, for example, reporting to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) whistleblower office.

If, on the other hand, you can clearly explain the fraud in your case and how government money is involved, it is very likely you have a strong False Claims Act case. If you do have a good FCA case, then it is more than likely that False Claims Act Lawyers would be happy to speak with you about your options. metadata.title: Exposing Customs Fraud: Hidden Schemes and How to Stop Them
metadata.author: Stephen Teller - Teller Law
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode Summary:
In this episode of False Claims, Real Consequences, attorney Stephen Teller breaks down the mechanics of customs fraud and how whistleblowers are vital in bringing these deceptive practices to light. Stephen shares stories from real cases involving tariff evasion, misclassification, country-of-origin fraud, and more. From smuggling goods to underreporting import values, Stephen highlights the legal risks importers take and how honest insiders can stop them — often with life-changing rewards.

Key Timestamps:
00:01 – Introduction to the episode and Stephen Teller
01:25 – How rising tariffs incentivize customs fraud
02:14 – Methods companies use to avoid tariffs: smuggling, misclassification, false declarations
04:10 – Example: misdeclaring roof racks as car seats to change tariff code
05:50 – Underreporting item value to reduce tariff percentage
06:18 – The Bid-Buy truck case: falsified prices and repeated fraud
08:30 – DOJ involvement and consequences of even “small” cases
09:45 – Aluminum import case: anti-dumping duties and willful underreporting
11:35 – Real-world consequences: company fined $3.4 million
12:50 – How the False Claims Act can lead to triple damages
13:45 – The blurred line between mistake and fraud
14:50 – Country-of-origin fraud: labeling and assembly loopholes
16:40 – Difficulty in proving origin-shifting fraud in multi-country assembly
17:55 – Whistleblower rewards: potential 15–25% share in government recovery
19:05 – Cable company case: $6.5 million payout to a whistleblower
20:10 – What to do if you see shady import activity in your job
21:25 – When to speak to your boss vs. when to call a lawyer
22:40 – How to protect yourself legally when speaking up
24:00 – Importance of documenting fraud reports and understanding your rights

About the Show:
False Claims, Real Consequences dives into the world of federal fraud litigation and whistleblower cases. The show features legal experts like Stephen Teller who shine a light on the inner workings of fraud schemes — and how the False Claims Act empowers insiders to stop them. Each episode delivers real-world legal insights, high-stakes case stories, and actionable advice for professionals navigating compliance, ethics, and justice.

#CustomsFraud #WhistleblowerLaw #FalseClaimsAct #ImportFraud #TariffEvasion #FederalLaw #DOJEnforcement #TradeCompliance #LegalPodcast #StephenTeller #WhistleblowerRights

Welcome to False Claims, Real Consequences, the podcast that breaks down highstakes fraud cases with the legal experts who fight them. I'm John Clemens. I'm here with Steve Teller, a national whistleblower attorney who has helped recover millions in cases involving tariff fraud, import scams, and federal violations. Uh, again, I'm I'm excited to talk about this because I'm hearing words that I've heard in the media, tariffs and customs. So, I'm excited to learn a little bit more. >> Yeah, it's been a um quite a roller coaster that way. >> It sure has. It really increases the incentives for them to be dishonest. I mean, their business model is built on the old tariffs. >> They're gonna they picked a price point based on the old tariffs, you know, all of that. So, >> so that's a really good point. What does this dishonesty or or fraud look like in in the world of customs? >> Well, there's a few different ways that a company could pretend and pay less tariffs. You know, they could commit fraud essentially and and pay less tariffs. And they can they can hide the country of origin because tariffs depend on where the where the item is coming from often. um they could pretend that the item is really a different kind of item. You know, sometimes it's hard to tell whether uh you know, we're talking about let's say um roof racks or you know, car seats, right? In terms of this harmonized tariff schedule, uh because the tariffs vary depending on the type of um thing you're importing. And then of course there's also just, you know, smuggling where you're not declaring the actual thing at all and uh and just hiding it, bringing it over somehow pretending it's something else completely um or just not not declaring it, bringing it on a private boat or something like that. And so, you know, and the fourth way of um committing customs fraud is just misdeclaring the value of the thing that's being imported, right? So I say that it's worth much less than it actually is and so my tariff percentage is way smaller. >> Yeah. Right. Right. And so you mentioned I want to dig in on one thing you mentioned. Uh you know maybe you've got a shipping container full of roof racks but it's really actually car seats. So is that would that be considered like misclassification or like using a wrong tariff code? Is the IRS Whistleblower program a waste of time? Maybe, depending on your potential case and how it is handled. On this week's podcast, Eric is joined by Bryan Skarlatos from Kostelanetz LLP, a true heavyweight in tax controversy. They bring their extensive experiences to the discussion and offer insights into what they think works, what doesn't, and why whistleblower cases often take years to resolve. If you're considering becoming a whistleblower or dealing with one, this episode delivers the hard truths you need. 

If you're a CPA, EA, accountant or an attorney, you're in a great position to help people by becoming a Tax Rep Network member. Visit Tax Rep Network: https://taxrepllc.com/ and book a call to get started: https://calendly.com/kevin-s-mw/trn-intro-call

Watch for cutting-edge IRS rep training to save taxpayers and make more money. Equip yourself with the skills and knowledge necessary to effectively advocate for taxpayers before the Internal Revenue Service with the best tax representation training including:

Comprehensive Tutorials on tax representation strategies, case studies, and best practices.

Expert Interviews with industry leaders sharing their secrets and experiences.

Live Q&A Sessions to address your burning questions and provide real-time advice.

Update Alerts on the latest tax laws, regulations, and procedures.

Chapters:
Is It Worth Bringing A Whistleblower Case? [02:48]
Why Whistleblower Cases Take So Long To Process [07:30]
Challenges Of Large Whistleblower Claims At The IRS [10:32]
The Inherent Tension In The Whistleblower Program [16:37]
Limited Workarounds In Complex Whistleblower Cases [20:07]
Understanding Section 6103 In Whistleblower Cases [22:58]
Is The Whistleblower Claim Worth Your Time? [25:48]
Proposed Bill To Revamp The Whistleblower Program [31:26]

metadata.title: IRS Whistleblower to Financial Empowerment: Dr. Sherry Peel Jackson's Journey #irs #tbws2024
metadata.author: The Brad Weisman Show
metadata.shortDescription:
Former IRS agent Dr. Sherry Peel Jackson joins us to reveal her eye-opening journey from the bowels of the IRS to becoming a whistleblower and GOING TO JAIL for financial justice. Dr. Jackson's story sheds light on the pressures faced within the IRS to target mom-and-pop operations harshly, while large corporations often skate by unscathed. Her courageous transformation from an IRS insider to a vocal advocate for tax reform highlights the need for transparency and the audacity required to stand up to such a formidable institution. #sherrypeeljackson 

Join us as Dr. Jackson unravels the complexities of federal income tax laws and the controversies surrounding their legitimacy. Drawing from her rich experiences and significant court cases, she navigates the murky waters of income tax fraud, challenging the often-misunderstood differences between personal earnings and corporate income. With real-world examples, Dr. Jackson provides a thought-provoking perspective on the ongoing debate about the constitutionality of federal income taxes, fostering a deeper understanding of the challenges and potential avenues for change. 

Embark on a journey towards financial empowerment with Dr. Jackson’s KPG system—Keep, Protect, and Grow what you earn. Discover actionable strategies for escaping the "rat race," reducing debt, and investing wisely in hard assets like real estate and precious metals. Uncover how meticulous record-keeping and awareness of audit red flags can secure your financial future. By navigating the tax code for personal benefit, listeners gain insights into achieving financial freedom and confronting the societal issues that stifle economic progress for many. Tune in now to harness the knowledge that could reshape your financial destiny.

"Stick it to the IRS", is the theme of this episode and the name of her book!  My guest Dr. Sherry Peel Jackson was once an IRS Agent, and now she questions the legitimacy of it.  She refused to pay/file her Federal Income Taxes for 4 years and ended up in jail because of it.  She shares "the red flags" to avoid an audit and shares the qualifications that the IRS looks for to work there" - Brad Weisman

metadata.title: The DOJ’s New Agenda: What Every Business Should Know About the False Claims Act
metadata.author: DarrowEverett LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
In this recorded DarrowEverett webinar, we explored the evolving landscape of the False Claims Act (FCA) and its growing impact across industries. Many businesses assume they’re beyond the reach of FCA scrutiny—but recent shifts under the Trump Administration signaled a renewed focus on corporate accountability and white-collar enforcement from the Department of Justice.

Led by Evan J. Gotlob, a respected litigator and thought leader in corporate compliance, this session breaks down what the FCA really means for companies today.

In this webinar, we covered:

How the False Claims Act works—and why it matters more now than ever

DOJ’s current enforcement priorities and their implications for businesses

Practical steps to strengthen compliance and manage risk

Originally presented live, this session includes a Q&A segment addressing real-world concerns from attendees.

metadata.title: Trends and Developments Related to the False Claims Act
metadata.author: American Health Law Association
metadata.shortDescription: Joe Wolfe, Attorney, Hall Render Killian Heath & Lyman PC, speaks with Robert S. Salcido, Partner, Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld LLP, about the current landscape of the False Claims Act (FCA) in the health care industry. They discuss the recent district court opinion declaring the FCA’s qui tam provisions unconstitutional (Zafirov v. Florida Medical Associates LLC), enforcement trends and case law developments, the impact of Loper Bright, trends related to Civil Investigative Demands and self-disclosures, and emerging hot topics. Robert is author of AHLA’s False Claims Act & the Health Care Industry, Fifth Edition. From AHLA’s Fraud and Abuse Practice Group.

metadata.title: Josh Drew on What’s New with the False Claims Act [Podcast]
metadata.author: ComplianceVideos
metadata.shortDescription:
By Adam Turteltaub (mailto:adam.turteltaub@corporatecompliance.org) 



Despite being a Civil War era statute, the False Claims Act (FCA) always has something new going on.  To find out what’s hot these days, we spoke with Joshua Drew (LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/in/joshuawdrew/) ), a former federal prosecutor and chief compliance officer and currently a Member at Miller & Chevalier (https://www.millerchevalier.com/professional/joshua-drew) .



Lately, he explains, there has been a steady stream of activity.


     
     
  •  May:  The Civil Rights Fraud Initiative was announced by the administration and proposes to use the FCA against any federal funding recipient that it believes are operating DEI initiatives that violate antidiscrimination laws.
     
     
  •  July:  A new working group was created between the DOJ and HHS to focus on healthcare and life sciences.  It encouraged whistleblowers to file action in areas such as Medicare Advantage, drug device and biologics pricing and barriers to patient access, amongst others.
     
     
  •  August:  A trade task force was created to encourage whistleblowing against tariff violators.
     
     


All of this occurs against a backdrop of activity by the Administration to identify and fight waste, fraud and abuse.



Listen in to learn more about where the Administration is focusing and what compliance teams can learn from recent actions.

metadata.title: The Truth About Whistleblower Cases Nobody Tells You
metadata.author: Against The Fraud
metadata.shortDescription:
What actually makes something a False Claims Act case?

Marianne Hamilton, a whistleblower attorney with Miller Law Group, PLLC, joins Joseph Belsin on Against the Fraud to explain how whistleblower cases work from the attorney's perspective.

In this conversation, Marianne explains how attorneys:

Separate critical facts from a complicated whistleblower story
Determine whether evidence actually supports a False Claims Act case
Evaluate government money, materiality, intent, and insider knowledge
Help whistleblowers document concerns safely
Navigate retaliation and professional consequences
Work with clients during investigations that can last years
Use insider knowledge to show investigators where to look
Decide what evidence actually matters
Protect confidential information before a case is filed

Marianne also shares an important warning for potential whistleblowers about putting confidential information into publicly available AI systems.

One of the simplest explanations from the conversation:

A False Claims Act claim is essentially "a lie attached to a dollar."

You need the alleged falsehood and the connection to government money.

This episode is for educational purposes only and is not legal advice. Anyone who believes they may have information concerning fraud should speak directly with a qualified attorney.

Guest: Marianne Hamilton
Firm: Miller Law Group, PLLC
Podcast: Against the Fraud

Transcript Timeline

Approximate chapter timestamps based on the transcript flow.

00:00 Introduction to Marianne Hamilton and the False Claims Act
01:20 From the U.S. Navy, PhD, writing and editing to becoming an attorney
03:14 Public service and lessons from the Navy
05:15 Why Marianne chose whistleblower and False Claims Act law
07:20 How attorneys untangle complicated whistleblower stories
09:50 How long a qui tam case can actually take
11:48 How whistleblowers should safely document concerns
13:53 How much evidence does a whistleblower need?
15:51 Healthcare fraud vs. defense contracting and other industries
18:19 Why insider knowledge can make a case much stronger
21:39 Retaliation, career consequences and the human cost of whistleblowing
26:09 What a strong attorney-whistleblower relationship looks like
27:48 How insiders help government investigators know where to look
29:05 What to do before making a major decision
29:35 "A lie attached to a dollar" explained
31:02 Why Marianne warns whistleblowers about putting confidential data into AI
32:56 Final advice and how to reach Marianne Hamilton
34:00 Closing

#FalseClaimsAct #Whistleblower #QuiTam #GovernmentFraud #WhistleblowerAttorney #FraudInvestigation #WhistleblowerProtection #HealthcareFraud #FCA #AgainstTheFraud

metadata.shortDescription:
In our latest episode, healthcare attorney Patricia Graham and I break down the strict federal compliance laws that every healthcare entrepreneur must know.

As a healthcare attorney, I focus on highly specific practice areas, and I work with surgeons and medical doctors often. A critical truth for founders is that standard business marketing models are an absolute compliance minefield in medicine. Standard business attorneys often lack the highly specific knowledge needed to navigate these complex regulations safely.

First, we unpack the Anti-Kickback Statute, which makes it illegal to exchange anything of value for patient referrals. While other industries use referral bonuses, healthcare practices cannot. This ensures medical choices are based strictly on clinical need. Next, we look at the Stark Law, a strict rule prohibiting doctors from referring patients to businesses where they or their immediate family hold a financial interest.

To enter the medical space, unlicensed entrepreneurs utilize Management Services Organizations to handle non-clinical tasks like technology, branding, and billing. However, MSO agreements require precise structuring. Critical violations include tying management fees to patient volume or revenue percentages, and giving physicians bonuses for ordering more tests.

At Holt Law, we act as a one-stop-shop across the USA, teaming up with expert professionals to provide a holistic approach to legal compliance. Compliance is facing immense scrutiny right now, especially in states like California where regulations are tightening.

Tune into our latest masterclass to master the strict rules of federal healthcare compliance. Watch full episode now!

metadata.title: Stark Law: Latest Trends and Developments
metadata.author: American Health Law Association
metadata.shortDescription:
Joe Wolfe, Attorney, Hall Render Killian Heath & Lyman PC, speaks with Charles Oppenheim, Partner, Hooper Lundy & Bookman PC, about the current landscape surrounding the Physician Self-Referral Law, also known as the Stark Law. They discuss why the Stark Law is so complex and the kinds of issues that attorneys face in this area, how CMS has introduced more flexibility under Stark and ways that health care organizations can incorporate these new flexibilities into their contracting policies, best practices for analyzing arrangements that may overlap with other areas of the law, CMS’ efforts to clarify the “Big 3,” and issues related to value-based exceptions. Charles is the co-author of AHLA’s The Stark Law: Comprehensive Analysis and Practical Guide, Eighth Edition. From AHLA's Fraud and Abuse and Hospitals and Health Systems Practice Groups.

Learn more about The Stark Law: Comprehensive Analysis and Practical Guide, Eighth Edition: https://store.lexisnexis.com/ahla/products/ahla-the-stark-law-comprehensive-analysis-and-practical-guide-ahla-members-grpussku59066.html

Learn more about AHLA’s Fraud and Abuse Practice Group: https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/practice-groups/practice-groups/fraud-and-abuse

Learn more about AHLA’s Hospitals and Health Systems Practice Group: https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/practice-groups/practice-groups/hospitals-and-health-systems 

Subscribe to AHLA's Speaking of Health Law: https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/education-events/speaking-of-health-law-podcasts

Learn more about AHLA and the educational resources available to the health law community: https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/

Get all your health law news from the major media outlets on AHLA's Health Law Daily podcast, exclusively for AHLA Comprehensive members. To subscribe and add this private podcast feed to your podcast app, go to https://www.americanhealthlaw.org/dailypodcast

So, as we evaluate, you know, we've mentioned fair market value or market rate or market rent you know, throughout this discussion. So, what does that really mean, right? And fair market value is a key requirement under both the Stark Law and the Anti-Kickback Statute. I know I mentioned before that you don't have to necessarily meet every element of an Anti-Kickback Statute safe harbor in order for an arrangement to be compliant and that is true. However, the every almost every Anti-Kickback Statute safe harbor does have an element that requires fair market value and that is one that we would say you should always meet because failure to meet the fair market value requirement is a very difficult burden to then overcome with respect to um you know, proving you did not have an improper intent, right? Um because why would you pay above or below, depending on the circumstance, uh fair market value unless it was to you know, curry favor with with that business relationship. Or that's what the government would say. I'm not saying there couldn't be other reasons, but um so so what does that mean then practically, right? So rent must reflect market rates in an arms-length transaction. There are certain factors that we would not want to consider in rental rates um or or lease arrangements, right? So for one that we see often in the real estate space would be, well, but we want again, kind of going back to this example, uh we want this physician practice to be on our campus or closer to our facility so that they do more cases here. So we're willing to charge them below market rent um for that space, and that that would not be an appropriate um negotiation in arms-length, right? Um because that would be influenced by the referral relationships or location convenience. And so um it's not a requirement to get a a third-party appraisal or assessment um or fair market value review. Um it can be beneficial, particularly maybe if it's a new market or a building that's new to you. Um or if if we are maybe pushing um what we think the fair market value might be, right? Sometimes getting an outside third party who's experienced in health care valuations to come in and do that assessment or appraisal can be beneficial. Um and and there are under Stark, there are specific definitions of fair market value, specifically as it relates to real estate that are important that your valuation, if you do use a third party, that that third party knows those and is referencing those appropriately throughout its assessment to make sure that it is factoring in the things that are appropriate and is not factoring in any of the things that the Stark law would say should not be considered. Um, you know, we've we've seen this before um where an entity will get a will get evaluation or get an appraisal, which is great, um but they maybe use an organization that does a lot of appraisals but maybe not for health care. And so they may factor in some of those things that the Stark law or the anti-kickback statute would say that we shouldn't. And then that probably the only thing that's more problematic uh than, you know, not not paying fair market value is is is having an assessment that shows it's fair market value, but only if you factor in these things that we we shouldn't be factoring in, right? And so so that can be problematic. So that's that's just something to keep in mind. Make sure um that if you are engaging a third party that they're aware of the health care regulatory constraints. We often will do engagements of valuation firms or appraisers um through the law firm, for example, for our clients so that then that work product um so it's an engagement a three-party engagement, but so it's protected by the attorney-client privilege. Um and so you know, that appraisal and that information, the valuation, are are protected by the attorney-client privilege, which can, depending on the facts and circumstances, can be beneficial. Um and then, you know, again, just kind of taking a step back, thinking about fair market value typically is expressed as a range, right? So it doesn't mean that there's just one number that's fair market value. Um it's typically a range. So if we're talking about a price per square foot for a large space, right? That range could be more more significant overall. Um but just something to keep in mind, right? And then within that range, you can land on the higher end or the lower end within that fair market value range and it doesn't necessarily mean that one is more compliant than the other as long as you're within that determined range of a fair market value. And then with commercial reasonableness, you know, the government CMS has said that in order to be commercially reasonable, an arrangement must serve a legitimate business purpose. Um It can commercial reasonableness can vary based on certain factors of the parties, like their size, their type, their scope, their specialty, their geographic location. There's not necessarily a one-size-fits-all. Um and also maybe not as relevant to real estate arrangements specifically or or leases at least, um but very relevant to health care arrangements more generally. Several years ago, um in some updated regulations, uh CMS said that an arrangement does not necessarily need to be profitable in order to be commercially reasonable. So, we see that come up again more in the services space, but with certain specialties that historically operate at a loss, right? Um psych, burn units, right? There are several that kind of historically operate at a loss across most organizations. Um and the and CMS did actually issue in its commentary for the regulations um guidance that that says just because something does not make a profit does not mean that it that you're paying above or below fair market value, right? It It can still be commercially reasonable. It's just something to keep in mind, right? As a guidepost. So. And with that Oh, sorry. Go ahead. >> I was just going to say and we're also talking about just defining square footage, which can be a seemingly simple concept, but nearly everything on your lease in your lease is going to depend on it. So, we have base rent is calculated based on square footage, operating expenses. There's like comparisons to the market and then the valuation itself. So, if the square footage is wrong, it's going to effectively put the arrangement out of It could potentially put the arrangement out of compliance as well because the tenant could be paying for more space than it has or less space than it has um and could create a compliance issue. So, that's something we want to be careful of as well is that when when we're structuring these agreements, needing to be sure of what the square footage is. So, the lease should say how the space is measured, um what's specifically included, how many common areas are allocated. So, are there Is it just a a a space where you have direct entry into that suite or is the tenant potentially walking through a building using an elevator, using common restrooms? Like these types of things are important to delineate in your agreement because otherwise it could be viewed as again someone receiving a benefit that they're not otherwise paying for. Um common areas specifically get tricky um because we don't always differentiate the in an agreement usable square footage and rentable square footage. So, usable square footage is the four walls that the tenant is actually using in their space. That's what they're actually occupying, where they're going to be seeing patients. The rentable square footage is going to be kind of was like I was talking earlier, it's going to be that lobby, the corridors, the restrooms, the elevators, any mechanical or IT rooms that the tenant has access to. And so, the difference between the two is usually expressed as a load factor. Sometimes, understandably, landlords don't know the um specific square footage calculation. So, what they'll do is they'll add on a load factor onto the rent amount. And I would say I see standard load factors between 15 and 20% being added on. So, for example, if you have uh physicians are in a 2,000 square foot space, we'll add on that 15% load factor, so now their square footage is going to be billed as 2,300. So, they're going to pay rent on that 2,300 square feet to make sure that the lease is encompassing everything that they're actually using. Um again, we're going to see problems when we forget to account for this. The business team is going to agree on a rate for the suite. Everyone focuses on that, but they kind of forget to take into account these common areas. It's a common mistake that we see made. So, as lawyers, we kind of try to raise that issue and point it out, "Hey, is this number the usable square foot or is it the rentable square foot that we're leasing space here in?" Um in a typical commercial deal, uh a business point that the landlord may simply leave on the table is something like this square footage that they might not take into account uh the common area situation. And I think on the next slide, we're going to talk about other specific lease provisions that are important to think about in the context of are we paying for everything that we're getting as a benefit? So, for example, in the assignment and subletting provision, um these are important because they can really determine who can end up in the space. So, we analyze these with scrutiny because we don't want uh a transfer to potentially create a new relationship with the referral source that no one has independently reviewed. So, watch out for those provisions. Um rights of first offers or rights of first refusal, maybe it's to purchase the building, maybe it's to lease space in the building, but those have real economic value um which should be included under the commercial reasonableness and fair market value analysis that um people are undertaking when they're leasing a space. There's also the subordination and estoppel provisions, which matter for financing and any future sale. And then renewals and holdover, those are also a frequent problem. Um, if a tenant is going to stay past their expiration, they may be paying rent at a rate that was supported at the time by evaluation. But we commonly see that sometimes these arrangements are forgotten about and so let's say it's a an arrangement that was entered into in 2020. Uh, everything looked good. There was a fair market value determination that was done in 2020. And then the lease term was let's say for 3 years, but the physician just has been in the space up until 2026. You can have a problem then because if they're still in the space and paying that same rental rate that was set in 2020, whether or not it's going to be compliant is going to be dependent on the situation, but something we need to be aware of. It's best practice again to not have a physician or any entity stay over and holdover in their space without reanalyzing it um, when the term expires. Additionally, we have the surrender provisions that can hold some value. Who's going to keep the improvements? Um, who's going to keep the equipment? Who's going to pay to restore the space? So those are kind of like some hidden elements that can be baked into a lease that might hold some economic value depending on the circumstances. And then um, next let's talk about the practical drafting tips. So here things that we want to just be aware of and where we can minimize our non-compliant arrangements by focusing on these things. They seem somewhat simple on their face, but obviously in practice they could get more convoluted and more complicated as we know things come up and we're not always thinking about these things. So first is make sure that every agreement is signed before an arrangement begins. This is a basic thing, but there are so many times where leases are unsigned and it's a common issue that we see. So a kind of a tip for this is to have some type of a tracking system. So for example, if I'm working with a hospital and they are the tenant in a space, I'm not going to sign out or like mark my job complete until I make sure I receive the signed copy back. So that's kind of a way where we add value to our clients by making sure we're tracking those agreements, making sure they're signed, and then we say, "Okay, we're going to close out this assignment." So either internally or with your counsel, kind of making sure that that gets done. As we talked about earlier, we're going to make sure that the premises is clearly identified with a suite number. Specifically, if you can attach a floor plan, that makes things a lot easier because we can make sure we're going to know where the space is located if anything ever changes. Um as Alyssa talked about earlier, we're going to want to make sure the rent is consistent with fair market value, and as she said, a a determination is not required, a third-party determination, but some type of logic as to how you arrived at the rent is going to need to be at least have thought been thought out and best practice is to have that documented. So that if there ever is a time where it comes into question, "Hey, is this rent fair market value?" you'll at least have something to provide to say, "Yes, we did think about this and this is why we came up with the rent that we did." >> [clears throat and cough] >> Then we are going to talk about Oops, sorry, I'm not quite done with that slide. Um let's see. One-year term, there's one year that we talked about earlier, the one-year term that's required for most arrangements. Make sure that it is included there, and then if you're going to terminate the agreement for any reason and have an early termination option, you can't enter into another agreement within that same year. So typically we'll include language in our agreements to that effect to make sure it's caught if if for whatever reason the original agreement is terminated. Um and I think yep, and then we said proper administration throughout the lease term, which obviously everyone's um aware of. Okay, and now we'll talk about some issues spotting. So, here these are just kind of the things we've all just we've talked about this before, but providing physicians with items or services for free or less than fair market value, that's going to be something that we're going to have a red flag around. Want to make sure we're paying for the services that we're actually receiving or providing. Um relieving physicians of financial obligations they would otherwise incur. So, this can come up in arrangements where I see commonly there's an agreement that's set in place and it's for a term of 5 years. The rent was supposed to escalate every year um throughout the term and for whatever reason it didn't the rent never increased. The hospital system never pointed it out. The physician never paid the increase. So, then we're going to kind of have an issue. We can't just relieve this obligation um that they would otherwise have had to pay and it'll have to be kind of raised to that higher level of scrutiny and compliance would have to evaluate kind of what we could agree to in that situation. Um but making sure that we're not kind of relieving a financial obligation uh out that they would otherwise be responsible for. Um another issue that comes up is inflating compensation paid to physicians for items and services. So, if a physician is in a time-share arrangement receiving um a receptionist to assist them kind of with shuffling their patients in and out and scheduling, we need to make sure that they're paying a specific rate for that receptionist if it's included in their arrangement. And then, last but not least, a lease agreement that's going to include more space than is needed for a tenant's business and we talked about that earlier um, and how we can kind of fall into that. And any questions? I know we covered a lot. We've got several minutes left for for any questions that that folks may have. >> Good good point, Alyssa. One question in the chat Chris has answered. Many of you wanted to know if the presentation would be shared, and Chris will send this presentation out to everybody, you know, that registered for the event. There are none directly in the in the question box, Alyssa and Sadie, >> Okay. >> a couple of questions I got in advance. If a hospital has a lease with another hospital that's going to be used for specialist physician clinic days, does that arrangement need to comply with Stark law? >> Good question, and I'm I'm happy to to take that one, and and Sadie, feel free to chime in as well. So, if we have a a lease arrangement really between two hospitals where one is providing some of its specialists, the the arrangement, the contract itself would really be subject more to the anti-kickback statute, would not have to comply with Stark. Um, the one sort of caveat that we that we would put on that because as Sadie mentioned earlier, as attorneys, we can never just say yes or no. Um, is is that and we didn't get into this today, under the Stark law, there is a concept of indirect compensation relationships, as well. Um, so if those physicians who were coming on site in that space happened to have a compensation formula that varied based on their referrals to the landlord, so to the location where they were going, um, that could potentially implicate Stark. That's pretty unlikely and and pretty unusual. So, I think the safe answer is no. We would not have to worry about Stark. Um, but but in the regulatory space of healthcare, there's never just an absolute no. So, um, but but we would mostly be concerned about any anti-kickback statute um, implications of that relationship. >> Thanks. Another question, uh, can several physicians or physician groups share the same time share suite? >> I'm happy to field this one. Um, so yes, the answer there is yes. Sharing is really the point of a time share. So, it's going to be a non-exclusive arrangement. The hospital can let the physician use the space or they can use it when the physician isn't scheduled. It's part of why a time sharing arrangement is very valuable. So, it's says, "Hey, we can still use the space Thursday through Friday, but another physician can come in Monday through Wednesday and use the space." Um, the key thing here is that obviously we're documenting those arrangements and then I can also see from a um, like an implementation standpoint, the everyone needs to work together. Be that legal and business and operations to make sure functionally it's administered properly. To make sure the space isn't promised to one physician at one time and another physician at the same time. That's where you would run into issues. >> [snorts] >> Another question, our hospital just found a physician lease that actually expired six months ago and the tenant is still there. What should we do? >> I'm happy to field this one as well as it's more of a real estate standpoint. So, this this comes up a lot um, in day-to-day practice. So, before um, jumping any conclusions, don't panic. Let's gather the facts before we're going to decide anything. So, I would say first and foremost, have someone confirm the lease is actually expired. Make sure there's no automatic renewal provision baked in or any type of letter agreement or even an email that extended the term in any way. So, under Stark, there's any type of writings can be met by the collections of documents rule, and so there might it might be better you might be better off than you previously thought. So, that would kind of be my first set of advice. And then I would say, "Okay, let's look. What does the agreement actually say?" Typically, there is a holdover provision that's going to address what happens when a tenant stays in a space longer than they should. And these are permitted under Stark so long as your continuing the arrangement on the same um terms and conditions as you originally entered into it. Um and then if there is no holdover provision or for whatever reason you're not compliant with that, um then I would say like let's try to fix the gap right away, uh paper a new lease or an extension that is gets the agreement um current and in fair market value at the time of the new term starts. Um and then kind of retroactively looking at it to see, "Hey, if there was this period of non-compliance, we need to kind of assess. We might have to elevate that to compliance to take a look to say, 'Hey, is there anything that we need to disclose here um and how can we fix it?'" >> How often do people need to get a new fair market value appraisal? >> So, I'm happy to to weigh in here, and and Sadie, feel free to as well. There's no legal requirement of of how often you have to get an appraisal. Oftentimes, when appraisers issue their report, they they include a duration of how long you can rely on that report for. Um so, first I would I would look to any sort of appraisal that you have and see if it has a a I'm going to use the phrase expiration date, right? Or kind of a a valid um period of time that you can rely on that. Um from a regulatory perspective, ultimately what matters and what the government or a regulator would look at is whether or not factually your arrangement um if it's an ongoing arrangement is fair market value. And so certainly within that range of the appraisal, that should be you know, it should be valid. If for some reason it's a very volatile market um geographic area with a lot of change, it might make sense to reconsider even earlier. But typically whatever date the appraiser puts in their report would be a good a good starting point. Um just because you don't reassess after that doesn't necessarily mean that you have a violation. It just means again, you're going to be looking at those facts and circumstances um and potentially having to defend your rate if it if it hasn't changed and the report is is outdated. >> Yeah, I agree with everything Alyssa said. I think it just sometimes comes down to as well like what's the risk tolerance from the client? Um like like she said, the appraisals have an end date. You have I have some clients I work with where we're kind of saying, "Hey, rent needs to be FMV. It's it's up to you whether or not this is you believe that this is still within the time frame or you think it's still um going to be a valid thing that you can defend moving forward." >> [snorts] >> Well, we're right at the top of the hour. Alyssa and Sadie, we can't thank you enough. What an excellent presentation. You've answered some good questions. Uh I think uh people are looking forward to getting your presentation. Yeah, we're getting people in the chat saying thank you and thumbs up and clapping. Um but we we really do appreciate uh this excellent presentation. This is going to conclude our webinar, but you do have Alyssa and Sadie's email on the screen. If you've got further questions or you want to follow up, feel free to visit them at Hall Render. I'm sure they'll be glad to work with you. But on behalf of the Hospital Council, Alyssa and Sadie, thank you. Excellent presentation. And Sadie, again, enjoy that parade tomorrow for that World Series win. >> Yes, go Bears. >> Right. Thank y'all and everyone have a good evening. >> Thank you.

metadata.title: Compliance into the Weeds: The DOJ Whistleblower Incentive Program
metadata.author: Compliance Podcast Network
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, Tom Fox and Matt Kelly take a deep dive into the recently announced Department of Justice (DOJ) Whistleblower Incentive Program.

Last week, the DOJ announced a whistleblower pilot program, offering monetary rewards to whistleblowers who report corporate misconduct. Whistleblowers can receive up to 30% of the net proceeds of a settlement resulting from their tip. The program covers various types of corporate crime, including bribery, healthcare fraud, and Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) violations.

This program puts pressure on compliance programs to quickly investigate and address reported misconduct. It also raises questions about how whistleblowers will be rewarded in cases where there is a declination or non-prosecution agreement. The SEC case involving a whistleblower award highlights the importance of handling whistleblower reports effectively.

Connect with the Compliance Podcast Network at:

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/compliance-podcast-network/

YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@CompliancePodcastNetwork
Twitter: https://twitter.com/tfoxlaw
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/voiceofcompliance/
Website: https://compliancepodcastnetwork.net/

metadata.title: Bessent Unveils $30,000 Whistleblower Reward as Trump Escalates Fraud Crackdown | APT
metadata.author: APT
metadata.shortDescription:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announces a new $25 million Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program as part of President Donald Trump's 'War on Fraud'. Under the programme, eligible whistleblowers could receive rewards of up to $30,000 for information leading to convictions or enforcement actions.

Bessent also claims the Trump administration has uncovered more than $260 billion in fraud since January 2025, while revealing that FinCEN identified over $8 billion in potentially suspicious foreign agent-directed payments between 2021 and 2025.
